q.v: A 28-year-old man participates in a nutritional study evaluating the sequential digestion of a meal rich in complex starches. Samples aspirated from the oral cavity show rapid initial cleavage of polysaccharides, whereas samples aspirated from the gastric lumen show an abrupt cessation of this enzymatic activity. Activity resumes strongly in the duodenum following pancreatic secretion. Which of the following best describes the primary disaccharide generated by the initial oral and subsequent duodenal enzyme, as well as the specific brush-border enzyme required to yield its absorbable monosaccharides?
o: Maltose; Maltase
Sucrose; Sucrase
Lactose; Lactase
Glucose; SGLT-1
Fructose; GLUT-5
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that salivary and pancreatic alpha-amylase digest starch/glycogen, and salivary amylase is inactivated by low gastric pH) -> Step 2 (Determine that amylase breaks starch down into the disaccharide maltose, which is subsequently cleaved into 2x glucose by the brush-border enzyme maltase).

r.B: Sucrose is a dietary disaccharide cleaved by sucrase into glucose and fructose, not the primary breakdown product of starch digestion by amylase.
r.C: Lactose is a disaccharide cleaved by lactase into glucose and galactose, and is not generated from starch by salivary or pancreatic amylase.
r.D: Glucose is a final monosaccharide product rather than a disaccharide intermediate, and SGLT-1 is a membrane transporter rather than a hydrolytic enzyme.
r.E: Fructose is a monosaccharide absorbed via the GLUT-5 transporter, neither of which is involved in the amylase-mediated breakdown of starch.

q.s: Slide 4 & Slide 5: SLO1 Big Picture Metabolism / Digestion and Absorption of Carbohydrates

q.v: A 6-month-old infant is evaluated for severe watery diarrhea and dehydration that occurs shortly after being fed a standard formula containing glucose and galactose, but resolves when fed a specialized formula containing only fructose as the carbohydrate source. Intestinal biopsy reveals normal mucosal architecture and intact brush-border disaccharidase activities, prompting suspicion of a congenital defect in an apical membrane transport protein. A defect in this specific transporter directly impairs the apical cotransport of these sugars alongside which of the following ions, and what basolateral transporter would normally export all three monosaccharides into the circulation?
o: Sodium (Na+); GLUT-2
Potassium (K+); GLUT-5
Calcium (Ca2+); GLUT-4
Sodium (Na+); GLUT-1
Chloride (Cl-); GLUT-3
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that apical absorption of glucose and galactose in the enterocyte occurs via SGLT-1, while fructose uses GLUT-5) -> Step 2 (Connect SGLT-1 function to Sodium [Na+] cotransport on the luminal membrane and identify GLUT-2 as the basolateral transporter that exports glucose, galactose, and fructose into the circulation).

r.B: Potassium channels are involved in pancreatic beta-cell depolarization rather than intestinal sugar cotransport, and GLUT-5 is an apical fructose transporter.
r.C: Calcium influx triggers insulin vesicle fusion in beta cells, and GLUT-4 is an insulin-regulated transporter in muscle and adipose tissue.
r.D: While SGLT-1 cotransports sodium, GLUT-1 is responsible for basal glucose uptake in tissues like erythrocytes rather than basolateral intestinal export.
r.E: Chloride is not cotransported by SGLT-1, and GLUT-3 is a high-affinity transporter primarily important in neuronal tissues.

q.s: Slide 5 & Slide 6: SLO1 Digestion and Absorption of Carbohydrates

q.v: A 30-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus administers her mealtime insulin injection prior to eating dinner. Within 30 minutes, glucose uptake markedly increases in her skeletal muscles and adipose tissue, while the rate of glucose transport into her erythrocytes remains unchanged at its baseline level. The insulin-mediated increase in skeletal muscle glucose uptake relies on a signaling cascade that triggers the exocytosis of intracellular vesicles containing a transporter with which of the following kinetic profiles, compared to the transporter responsible for basal uptake in her erythrocytes?
o: Higher Vmax and Km of ~6.5 mM vs. Low Vmax and Km of ~5 mM
Lower Vmax and Km of ~1.5 mM vs. High Vmax and Km of ~17 mM
Higher Vmax and Km of ~17 mM vs. Low Vmax and Km of ~1.5 mM
Lower Vmax and Km of ~5 mM vs. High Vmax and Km of ~6.5 mM
Higher Vmax and Km of ~1.5 mM vs. Low Vmax and Km of ~5 mM
q.p: Step 1 (Identify GLUT-4 as the insulin-regulated transporter translocated via exocytosis in skeletal muscle/adipose, and GLUT-1 as the basal transporter in erythrocytes) -> Step 2 (Match GLUT-4 to a high Vmax and Km of ~6.5 mM, and GLUT-1 to a low Vmax and low Km of ~5 mM).

r.B: A low Vmax and Km of ~1.5 mM describes neuronal GLUT-3, while a high Vmax and Km of ~17 mM describes hepatic/pancreatic GLUT-2.
r.C: A high Vmax and Km of ~17 mM characterizes bidirectional GLUT-2 in the liver and kidney, not insulin-inducible GLUT-4 in skeletal muscle.
r.D: This option reverses the kinetic properties of GLUT-1 and GLUT-4; GLUT-4 has a high Vmax to accommodate postprandial glucose uptake.
r.E: GLUT-4 has a moderate Km of ~6.5 mM rather than the very low Km of ~1.5 mM seen in neuronal GLUT-3.

q.s: Slide 9 & Slide 12: SLO2 Transport of Glucose into Tissues

q.v: In an isolated organ perfusion experiment, researchers measure the rate of bidirectional glucose transport across the plasma membrane of hepatocytes and renal tubular epithelial cells as extracellular glucose concentration is progressively increased from fasting levels (4 mM) to severe postprandial hyperglycemia (20 mM). They observe that the transport rate does not saturate at physiological fasting concentrations, but instead continues to rise linearly with increasing glucose concentration. Which of the following kinetic combinations accounts for the behavior of the transporter expressed in these tissues?
o: High Km (~17 mM) and high Vmax, conferring low affinity and high capacity
Low Km (~1.5 mM) and low Vmax, conferring high affinity and low capacity
Low Km (~5 mM) and low Vmax, conferring high affinity and low capacity
Moderate Km (~6.5 mM) and high Vmax, regulated by vesicular translocation
Low Km (~1.5 mM) and high Vmax, conferring both high affinity and high capacity
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the bidirectional transporter in liver, renal tubular, small intestinal epithelial, and pancreatic beta cells as GLUT-2) -> Step 2 (Deduce that GLUT-2 has a high Km [~17 mM] and high Vmax, which translates to low affinity and high capacity).

r.B: A low Km (~1.5 mM) and low Vmax describes GLUT-3, which ensures constant basal glucose uptake by the brain even when blood glucose levels are low.
r.C: A low Km (~5 mM) and low Vmax describes GLUT-1, which mediates basal glucose uptake in erythrocytes and most mammalian tissues.
r.D: A Km of ~6.5 mM regulated by insulin-stimulated vesicular translocation describes GLUT-4 in cardiac/skeletal muscle and adipose tissue.
r.E: No GLUT transporter described in the lecture combines the lowest Km (~1.5 mM) with a high Vmax; GLUT-3 has a low Vmax.

q.s: Slide 9 & Slide 11: SLO2 Transport of Glucose into Tissues

q.v: A 40-year-old healthy volunteer undergoes a 16-hour overnight fast. During this fasting state, her hepatocytes actively synthesize glucose via gluconeogenesis to maintain normoglycemia. To prevent a futile cycle in which newly synthesized glucose is immediately re-phosphorylated back into glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) within the hepatocyte, the liver relies on two distinct regulatory mechanisms for its glucose-phosphorylating isozymes. Which of the following correctly pairs the mechanism that limits glucokinase activity during fasting with the mechanism that limits hexokinase activity?
o: Nuclear sequestration by GK regulatory protein (GKRP); Direct product inhibition by G6P
Direct product inhibition by G6P; Nuclear sequestration by GK regulatory protein (GKRP)
Allosteric inhibition by fructose-1-phosphate (F1P); Phosphorylation by protein kinase A (PKA)
Vesicular endocytosis from the plasma membrane; Allosteric inhibition by citrate
Dephosphorylation by insulin-stimulated phosphatases; Competitive inhibition by galactose
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that hepatocytes express both glucokinase and hexokinase to phosphorylate glucose to G6P) -> Step 2 (Identify that during fasting, glucokinase is sequestered in the nucleus by GKRP [dissociating only when glucose or F1P is high], while hexokinase is directly inhibited by its product, G6P).

r.B: This reverses the two mechanisms; hexokinase is inhibited by G6P, whereas glucokinase is not inhibited by G6P and instead relies on GKRP sequestration.
r.C: Fructose-1-phosphate (F1P) actually causes glucokinase to dissociate from GKRP to become active in the cytoplasm, rather than inhibiting it.
r.D: Vesicular translocation regulates GLUT-4 at the plasma membrane, and citrate allosterically inhibits PFK-1 rather than hexokinase.
r.E: Insulin-stimulated phosphatases activate glycolytic regulatory enzymes in the fed state, and galactose does not serve as the physiological regulator of hepatic hexokinase.

q.s: Slide 14 & Slide 15: SLO3 Hexokinase and Glucokinase in Liver

q.v: A 52-year-old man is being evaluated for a pancreatic disorder characterized by impaired insulin secretion in response to oral glucose loads. In healthy pancreatic beta-islet cells, extracellular glucose enters via GLUT-2 and is phosphorylated by glucokinase, leading to increased glycolytic flux, citric acid cycle activity, and oxidative phosphorylation. What is the immediate downstream consequence of the resulting change in the intracellular ATP concentration that directly triggers voltage-dependent calcium (Ca2+) channel opening and insulin granule exocytosis?
o: Closure of ATP-gated K+ channels, leading to plasma membrane depolarization
Opening of ATP-gated K+ channels, leading to plasma membrane hyperpolarization
Activation of Na+/K+ ATPase pumps, leading to intracellular potassium accumulation
Direct phosphorylation of voltage-dependent Ca2+ channels by glucokinase
Release of intracellular calcium from the nucleus via GK regulatory protein
q.p: Step 1 (Trace beta-cell glucose sensing: high glucose -> GLUT2 -> glucokinase -> glycolysis/TCA/oxidative phosphorylation -> increased ATP) -> Step 2 (Identify that high ATP closes ATP-gated K+ channels -> causes membrane depolarization -> opens voltage-dependent Ca2+ channels -> Ca2+ uptake -> vesicle fusion/insulin release).

r.B: Increased intracellular ATP closes rather than opens K+ channels, causing membrane depolarization rather than hyperpolarization.
r.C: Beta-cell depolarization is driven by the closure of passive ATP-gated K+ channels preventing K+ efflux, not by Na+/K+ ATPase activation.
r.D: Voltage-dependent Ca2+ channels open in response to membrane depolarization, not via direct phosphorylation by glucokinase.
r.E: Calcium enters from the extracellular space through voltage-dependent plasma membrane channels rather than being released from the nucleus via GKRP.

q.s: Slide 16: SLO3 Insulin is released in response to high blood glucose

q.v: Researchers studying cellular bioenergetics isolate the cytoplasmic fraction of mammalian cells and supply it with glucose, ADP, inorganic phosphate, and NAD+ to measure the isolated activity of the 10-step glycolytic pathway. For every single molecule of glucose completely oxidized to two molecules of pyruvate through this cytoplasmic pathway, what is the exact number of ATP molecules consumed during the activation phase (steps 1–3), the gross number of ATP molecules generated during the production phase (steps 4–10), and the specific glycolytic intermediate that acts as a feed-forward allosteric activator of the final ATP-generating enzyme?
o: 2 ATP consumed; 4 ATP produced; Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate
1 ATP consumed; 2 ATP produced; Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate
2 ATP consumed; 2 ATP produced; Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate
2 ATP consumed; 6 ATP produced; 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate
4 ATP consumed; 6 ATP produced; Phosphoenolpyruvate
q.p: Step 1 (Determine the energy balance of cytoplasmic glycolysis: 2 ATP utilized in the activation stage [steps 1-3] and 4 ATP produced in the production phase [steps 4-10] for a net of 2 ATP) -> Step 2 (Identify the final ATP-generating enzyme as pyruvate kinase [step 10] and recognize from the regulation chart that Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate [F1,6BP] is its positive allosteric regulator).

r.B: 2 ATP are consumed and 4 ATP are produced per glucose molecule (yielding a net of 2 ATP), and F2,6BP activates PFK-1 rather than pyruvate kinase.
r.C: While 2 ATP are consumed, 4 gross ATP are produced during the production phase, and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate is not the allosteric activator of pyruvate kinase.
r.D: Approximately 6 ATP are produced from the 2 NADH via the mitochondrial electron transport chain, not directly by the cytoplasmic production phase of glycolysis.
r.E: Only 2 ATP are utilized during the priming reactions (by hexokinase/glucokinase and PFK-1), and phosphoenolpyruvate is the direct substrate for pyruvate kinase.

q.s: Slide 19, Slide 20 & Slide 22: SLO4 Glycolysis Overview and Regulation

q.v: A 19-year-old collegiate runner is 18 hours into a water-only fast and goes for a morning training run, causing her plasma glucagon and epinephrine levels to surge. In her hepatocytes, these counter-regulatory hormones bind to their respective receptors and stimulate protein kinase A (PKA) activity, leading to the phosphorylation of key regulatory enzymes. Simultaneously, intracellular levels of acetyl-CoA and alanine are elevated due to ongoing lipolysis and proteolysis. How do the PKA-mediated phosphorylation of the bifunctional enzyme (PFK-2/FBPase-2) and the elevated levels of acetyl-CoA and alanine coordinate to regulate hepatic glycolytic enzymes?
o: FBPase-2 phosphatase activity is stimulated to break down F2,6BP (decreasing PFK-1 activity), while acetyl-CoA and alanine allosterically inhibit pyruvate kinase
PFK-2 kinase activity is stimulated to synthesize F2,6BP (increasing PFK-1 activity), while acetyl-CoA and alanine allosterically inhibit hexokinase
FBPase-2 phosphatase activity is inhibited to preserve F2,6BP (decreasing PFK-1 activity), while acetyl-CoA and alanine allosterically activate pyruvate kinase
PFK-2 kinase activity is inhibited to reduce F1,6BP (decreasing glucokinase activity), while acetyl-CoA and alanine allosterically inhibit PFK-1
FBPase-2 phosphatase activity is stimulated to synthesize F2,6BP (increasing gluconeogenesis), while acetyl-CoA and alanine allosterically activate hexokinase
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that high glucagon/epinephrine -> increased PKA -> phosphorylation of PFK-2/FBPase-2 -> activates FBPase-2 phosphatase domain to break down F2,6BP to F6P, removing positive regulation of PFK-1) -> Step 2 (Connect elevated ATP, acetyl-CoA, and alanine [the amino acid form of pyruvate] to the direct allosteric inhibition of pyruvate kinase).

r.B: Glucagon and PKA phosphorylation activate the FBPase-2 phosphatase domain to break down F2,6BP, whereas insulin promotes PFK-2 kinase activity.
r.C: Glucagon activates the breakdown of F2,6BP via FBPase-2, and both acetyl-CoA and alanine serve as negative allosteric inhibitors of pyruvate kinase.
r.D: Acetyl-CoA and alanine specifically inhibit pyruvate kinase at the final step of glycolysis, whereas PFK-1 is inhibited by ATP and citrate.
r.E: FBPase-2 breaks down F2,6BP into Fructose-6-phosphate rather than synthesizing it, and hexokinase is inhibited by G6P.

q.s: Slide 21, Slide 22 & Slide 24: SLO4 Hormonal Control and Glycolysis Regulation

q.v: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with severe tissue hypoxia and a high anion gap metabolic acidosis (lactic acidosis) following a near-drowning incident. Because oxygen is unavailable to support mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation in his peripheral tissues, pyruvate is diverted away from the irreversible pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex and is instead acted upon by lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). Which of the following accurately describes the proton dynamics of the isolated LDH enzymatic reaction itself, as well as the fate of the resulting lactate if it is taken up by well-oxygenated cardiac myocytes or neurons?
o: The LDH reaction actually consumes protons while generating NAD+; lactate can be converted back to pyruvate to fuel the TCA cycle in cardiac and neuronal tissues
The LDH reaction directly releases free protons as a byproduct of NADH oxidation; lactate must be excreted by the kidneys because the LDH reaction is irreversible
The LDH reaction consumes protons while reducing NAD+ to NADH; lactate can only be metabolized by the liver via the Cori cycle for gluconeogenesis
The LDH reaction neither consumes nor produces protons; lactate is directly converted into acetyl-CoA by cytoplasmic LDH in neurons
The LDH reaction releases protons via ATP hydrolysis; lactate is irreversibly converted into ketone bodies and triacylglycerols in cardiac tissue
q.p: Step 1 (Examine the anaerobic glycolysis slide note: although anaerobic conditions + the lactate-proton shuttle generate lactic acidosis, the LDH reaction itself [Pyruvate + NADH + H+ -> Lactate + NAD+] actually consumes protons and generates NAD+) -> Step 2 (Identify that because LDH is reversible, lactate removed from cells can be used as fuel for other cells like neurons and cardiac tissue by converting it back to pyruvate for the TCA cycle, or sent to the liver for the Cori cycle).

r.B: The isolated LDH reaction consumes protons rather than releasing them (acidosis results from the anaerobic condition and lactate-proton shuttle), and the LDH reaction is fully reversible.
r.C: LDH oxidizes NADH to generate NAD+ (to keep glycolysis going) rather than reducing NAD+, and lactate can be used directly as fuel by neurons and cardiac tissue in addition to the hepatic Cori cycle.
r.D: The reduction of pyruvate to lactate by LDH consumes a proton, and conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA requires the mitochondrial PDH complex rather than LDH.
r.E: LDH does not hydrolyze ATP or release protons, and it is acetyl-CoA (produced aerobically via the irreversible PDH complex) that serves as a precursor for fatty acids, TAG, and ketone bodies.

q.s: Slide 28 & Slide 29: SLO5 Fate of Pyruvate and Anaerobic Glycolysis

q.v: A 38-year-old woman presents with chronic fatigue, splenomegaly, and jaundice. Laboratory evaluation reveals a normocytic hemolytic anemia, and specialized enzymatic testing of her erythrocytes confirms a severe deficiency in pyruvate kinase (PK). Although matured erythrocytes lack mitochondria and rely entirely on cytoplasmic glycolysis for ATP production, clinical symptoms of tissue hypoxia in patients with PK deficiency are often milder than expected for their degree of anemia. Based on the glycolytic pathway, a block at step 10 (pyruvate kinase) causes an upstream accumulation of which intermediate in Step 6/7, and why is the enzyme name 'pyruvate kinase' biochemically a misnomer for the physiological reaction it catalyzes in glycolysis?
o: 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (1,3-BPG); The enzyme transfers a phosphate group from PEP to ADP rather than phosphorylating pyruvate with ATP
Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (F1,6BP); The enzyme functions as a phosphatase that hydrolyzes inorganic phosphate from pyruvate
Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (GAP); The enzyme catalyzes an isomerization reaction rather than a phosphate transfer
Glucose-6-phosphate (G6P); The enzyme requires NAD+ as a cofactor rather than an adenosine nucleotide
Dihydroxyacetone-phosphate (DHAP); The enzyme irreversibly carboxylates pyruvate during the activation phase
q.p: Step 1 (Trace the glycolytic pathway upstream from step 10 [PEP -> Pyruvate via PK]: a block at step 10 causes accumulation of upstream production-phase intermediates including 2-PG, 3-PG, and 1,3-BPG, which compensates for reduced RBC number) -> Step 2 (Answer the slide prompt 'Why does the enzyme name PK not make sense?': kinases are named for adding a phosphate from ATP to a substrate, whereas in glycolysis PK catalyzes the irreversible transfer of a phosphate from PEP to ADP to generate pyruvate and ATP).

r.B: Pyruvate kinase is a transferase (kinase) that generates ATP from ADP and PEP, not a phosphatase that releases free inorganic phosphate.
r.C: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate is upstream of the NADH-generating step 6, and PK transfers a high-energy phosphate group to ADP rather than catalyzing an isomerization.
r.D: Glucose-6-phosphate is in the early activation phase, and PK utilizes ADP/ATP rather than NAD+/NADH (which is used at step 6).
r.E: DHAP is an early triose phosphate isomer (step 4/5), and PK catalyzes dephosphorylation of PEP in the final step (step 10) of the production phase.

q.s: Slide 20: SLO4 Glycolysis 3 Irreversible Steps (Pyruvate Kinase prompt and diagram)

q.v: A 21-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a 4-month history of abdominal pain, bloating, excessive gas, and watery diarrhea that consistently occur within an hour of eating ice cream or drinking milk. She notes that she had no difficulty consuming dairy products during childhood. Her physical examination is unremarkable, and she has no weight loss or bloody stools. Which of the following best describes the normal enzymatic reaction that is impaired in this patient's small intestine?
o: Cleavage of starch into maltose by salivary alpha-amylase
Cleavage of maltose into two glucose molecules by maltase
Cleavage of sucrose into glucose and fructose by sucrase
Cleavage of lactose into glucose and galactose by lactase
Cleavage of starch dextrins into maltose by pancreatic alpha-amylase
q.p: Step 1 (Adult-onset symptoms after dairy ingestion indicate lactase deficiency) -> Step 2 (Lactase normally cleaves the disaccharide lactose into glucose and galactose; unabsorbed lactose is fermented by intestinal bacteria)

r.A: Salivary alpha-amylase begins the digestion of starch and glycogen into maltose in the mouth before being inactivated by low gastric pH.
r.B: Maltase is a brush-border enzyme that cleaves the disaccharide maltose into two molecules of glucose.
r.C: Sucrase is a brush-border enzyme that cleaves the disaccharide sucrose into one molecule of glucose and one molecule of fructose.
r.E: Pancreatic alpha-amylase continues the luminal digestion of starch and glycogen into disaccharides and trisaccharides in the small intestine.

q.s: SLO 1 / Slide 4: Carbohydrate Digestion

q.v:
A 14-month-old boy is brought to the pediatrician by his parents due to recurrent episodes of abdominal cramping, flatulence, and watery diarrhea that began after he was transitioned from breast milk to solid foods and fruit juices. The parents report that his symptoms are particularly severe after he eats sweetened cereals or drinks beverages sweetened with table sugar, whereas he tolerates plain milk and unsweetened rice cereal without difficulty. A duodenal biopsy is performed and essays of brush-border enzyme activities are obtained:
  Lactase activity: normal
  Maltase activity: normal
  Sucrase activity: markedly decreased
After this patient ingests a meal rich in table sugar, absorption of which of the following monosaccharides via the apical GLUT-5 transporter of enterocytes will be most directly reduced?
o: Galactose
Fructose
Glucose
Maltose
Lactose
q.p: Step 1 (Decreased sucrase activity impairs hydrolysis of sucrose into glucose and fructose) -> Step 2 (Reduced luminal free fructose directly decreases fructose uptake via the apical GLUT-5 transporter)

r.A: Galactose is a monosaccharide product of lactose cleavage by lactase and is transported across the apical enterocyte membrane via SGLT-1.
r.C: Glucose is transported across the apical membrane of the enterocyte by the sodium-dependent SGLT-1 cotransporter rather than GLUT-5.
r.D: Maltose is a disaccharide composed of two glucose units and cannot be transported intact by the monosaccharide transporter GLUT-5.
r.E: Lactose is a disaccharide composed of glucose and galactose that must be hydrolyzed by lactase prior to monosaccharide absorption.

q.s: SLO 1 / Slides 4-5: Digestion and Absorption of Carbohydrates

q.v: A 29-year-old woman is participating in a supervised 36-hour fast for a metabolic research study. At hour 30 of the fast, her Fingerstick blood glucose concentration is 3.8 mmol/L (low-normal), yet she remains fully alert, oriented, and displays normal cognitive function. Meanwhile, her liver is net exporting glucose rather than taking it up for glycogen synthesis. Which of the following combinations of glucose transporter kinetics best explains how her brain maintains continuous glucose uptake while hepatic glucose uptake is minimized during this fasting state?
o: Brain GLUT-1 (high Km, high Vmax) / Liver GLUT-2 (low Km, low Vmax)
Brain GLUT-2 (high Km, high Vmax) / Liver GLUT-3 (low Km, low Vmax)
Brain GLUT-3 (low Km, low Vmax) / Liver GLUT-2 (high Km, high Vmax)
Brain GLUT-3 (high Km, low Vmax) / Liver GLUT-4 (low Km, high Vmax)
Brain GLUT-4 (low Km, high Vmax) / Liver GLUT-1 (high Km, low Vmax)
q.p: Step 1 (Fasting lowers blood glucose concentration below the Km of GLUT-2 but above the Km of GLUT-3) -> Step 2 (Neuronal GLUT-3 has a very low Km ~1.5 mM ensuring high-affinity basal uptake, whereas hepatic GLUT-2 has a high Km ~17 mM and low affinity)

r.A: GLUT-1 is expressed in erythrocytes and most mammalian tissues with a low Km (~5 mM) and low Vmax, rather than a high Km and high Vmax.
r.B: GLUT-2 is the high-Km transporter in the liver and pancreatic beta cells, whereas GLUT-3 is the low-Km transporter in neuronal tissues.
r.D: GLUT-3 has a low Km (high affinity) rather than a high Km, and GLUT-4 is the insulin-responsive transporter in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue.
r.E: GLUT-4 mediates insulin-stimulated glucose uptake in muscle and fat cells, whereas GLUT-1 mediates basal uptake in erythrocytes and other tissues.

q.s: SLO 2 / Slides 9-11: Transport of Glucose into Tissues

q.v: Which of the following glucose transporters is correctly paired with its primary tissue distribution and physiological feature?
o: GLUT-1: Skeletal and cardiac muscle; translocated to the plasma membrane in response to insulin
GLUT-2: Erythrocytes; high-affinity basal glucose uptake with a low Km
GLUT-3: Renal tubular and small intestinal epithelial cells; high-capacity bidirectional transport with a high Vmax
GLUT-4: Pancreatic beta cells; high-Km glucose influx involved in signaling insulin release
GLUT-1: Erythrocytes and most mammalian tissues; low-Km, low-Vmax basal glucose uptake
q.p: Step 1 (Identify GLUT-1 properties from the transporter comparison table) -> Step 2 (GLUT-1 has a low Km ~5 mM and low Vmax, providing basal glucose uptake that is especially important in erythrocytes)

r.A: Translocation to the plasma membrane in skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, and adipose tissue in response to insulin is the defining feature of GLUT-4.
r.B: Erythrocytes rely on GLUT-1 for low-Km basal glucose uptake, whereas GLUT-2 has a high Km (~17 mM) and is expressed in the liver, kidney, intestine, and pancreas.
r.C: Bidirectional transport in renal tubular cells, small intestinal enterocytes, hepatocytes, and pancreatic beta cells with a high Km and high Vmax is mediated by GLUT-2.
r.D: Glucose influx into pancreatic beta cells for insulin-release signaling is mediated by the high-Km, low-affinity transporter GLUT-2.

q.s: SLO 2 / Slide 9: Transport of Glucose into Tissues

q.v:
A researcher isolates hexokinase and glucokinase from a human hepatocyte homogenate and measures their initial reaction velocities across a range of glucose concentrations, both in the presence and absence of 5 mmol/L glucose-6-phosphate (G6P). The kinetic data are summarized below:
  Isozyme X: Km = 0.2 mmol/L; Vmax = low; Velocity with G6P = Decreased by 85%
  Isozyme Y: Km = 10 mmol/L; Vmax = high; Velocity with G6P = Unchanged
When a healthy individual transitions from the fed state to the fasting state, how do hepatocytes prevent Isozyme Y from phosphorylating newly synthesized glucose and creating a futile cycle during gluconeogenesis?
o: Allosteric inhibition of Isozyme Y by accumulating glucose-6-phosphate
Allosteric inhibition of Isozyme Y by elevated cytoplasmic AMP
Sequestration of Isozyme Y in the nucleus by glucokinase regulatory protein (GKRP)
Internalization of Isozyme Y into cytoplasmic endocytic vesicles
Dephosphorylation of Isozyme Y by insulin-activated protein phosphatases
q.p: Step 1 (Isozyme Y is glucokinase, identified by its high Km, high Vmax, and lack of G6P inhibition) -> Step 2 (During fasting, GKRP sequesters glucokinase in the hepatocyte nucleus to prevent a futile cycle with gluconeogenesis)

r.A: Product inhibition by glucose-6-phosphate regulates hexokinase (Isozyme X) to prevent a futile cycle, whereas glucokinase (Isozyme Y) is not inhibited by G6P.
r.B: AMP is a low-energy signal that allosterically activates phosphofructokinase-1 and pyruvate kinase rather than inhibiting glucokinase.
r.D: Internalization into cytoplasmic vesicles regulates the membrane abundance of the GLUT-4 transporter in muscle and adipose tissue, not hepatic glucokinase.
r.E: Insulin-stimulated dephosphorylation regulates enzymes such as PFK-2/FBPase-2 and pyruvate kinase in the fed state, not nuclear sequestration of glucokinase during fasting.

q.s: SLO 3 / Slides 14-15: Hexokinase and Glucokinase Regulation

q.v: A 35-year-old man consumes a dinner rich in sucrose and high-fructose corn syrup, resulting in a rapid rise in portal vein glucose and fructose concentrations. Within his hepatocytes, rising intracellular glucose and fructose-1-phosphate (F1P) concentrations promote the rapid phosphorylation of incoming glucose for glycogen synthesis and glycolysis. By what mechanism do elevated intracellular glucose and F1P increase the cytoplasmic activity of glucokinase in the fed state?
o: They stimulate protein kinase A (PKA) to phosphorylate glucokinase
They cause glucokinase to dissociate from glucokinase regulatory protein (GKRP) and exit the nucleus
They decrease the Km of hexokinase by relieving glucose-6-phosphate product inhibition
They trigger the exocytosis of glucokinase-containing vesicles to the hepatocyte plasma membrane
They allosterically inhibit fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase to prevent gluconeogenesis
q.p: Step 1 (In the fasting state, hepatic glucokinase is bound to GKRP and sequestered inside the nucleus) -> Step 2 (In the fed state, high glucose and F1P from fructose metabolism cause glucokinase to dissociate from GKRP and translocate to the cytoplasm)

r.A: Protein kinase A is activated by glucagon and epinephrine during the fasting state to phosphorylate metabolic enzymes, not by glucose or F1P in the fed state.
r.C: Hexokinase is regulated by glucose-6-phosphate product inhibition, whereas glucose and F1P regulate the nuclear-cytoplasmic shuttling of glucokinase.
r.D: Exocytosis of intracellular vesicles to the plasma membrane is the mechanism by which insulin stimulates GLUT-4 glucose transport in muscle and adipose tissue.
r.E: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, rather than glucose or F1P, acts as the direct negative allosteric regulator of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase.

q.s: SLO 3 / Slide 15: Sequestration of Glucokinase by GKRP

q.v: A 27-year-old man eats a high-carbohydrate lunch after a morning of classes. Thirty minutes later, his plasma insulin concentration is significantly elevated and his plasma glucagon concentration is suppressed. Within his hepatocytes, insulin signaling increases the activity of protein phosphatases that dephosphorylate the bifunctional enzyme phosphofructokinase-2/fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase (PFK-2/FBPase-2). Which of the following best describes the resulting enzymatic activity of this bifunctional enzyme and the downstream effect on hepatic glycolysis?
o: Increased FBPase-2 phosphatase activity -> decreased fructose-2,6-bisphosphate -> inhibition of PFK-1
Increased PFK-2 kinase activity -> increased fructose-2,6-bisphosphate -> activation of PFK-1
Increased PFK-2 kinase activity -> increased fructose-1,6-bisphosphate -> inhibition of pyruvate kinase
Increased FBPase-2 phosphatase activity -> increased fructose-6-phosphate -> activation of hexokinase
Increased PFK-2 kinase activity -> decreased fructose-2,6-bisphosphate -> activation of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase
q.p: Step 1 (High insulin in the fed state activates phosphatases that dephosphorylate PFK-2/FBPase-2, activating its PFK-2 kinase domain) -> Step 2 (PFK-2 converts fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, a potent positive allosteric regulator of PFK-1 that drives glycolysis)

r.A: Activation of FBPase-2 phosphatase activity occurs when glucagon stimulates PKA-mediated phosphorylation in the fasting state, breaking down fructose-2,6-bisphosphate.
r.C: PFK-2 synthesizes fructose-2,6-bisphosphate rather than fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, and fructose-1,6-bisphosphate is an allosteric activator of pyruvate kinase.
r.D: FBPase-2 converts fructose-2,6-bisphosphate back to fructose-6-phosphate during fasting when glucagon is high, not in response to insulin.
r.E: Active PFK-2 kinase increases rather than decreases fructose-2,6-bisphosphate levels, and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is a negative regulator of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase.

q.s: SLO 4 / Slides 21-25: Hormonal Regulation of Glycolysis by PFK-2/FBPase-2

q.v: Which of the following correctly pairs one of the three regulated, irreversible enzymes of glycolysis with its allosteric activators and allosteric inhibitors?
o: Hexokinase: Activated by glucose-6-phosphate; Inhibited by AMP
Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1): Activated by ATP and citrate; Inhibited by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate
Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1): Activated by alanine and acetyl-CoA; Inhibited by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate
Pyruvate kinase: Activated by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate and AMP; Inhibited by ATP, acetyl-CoA, and alanine
Pyruvate kinase: Activated by ATP, acetyl-CoA, and alanine; Inhibited by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate and AMP
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the three irreversible glycolytic enzymes: hexokinase, PFK-1, and pyruvate kinase) -> Step 2 (Pyruvate kinase is feed-forward activated by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate and AMP, and allosterically inhibited by high-energy signals ATP, acetyl-CoA, and alanine)

r.A: Hexokinase is allosterically inhibited by its product, glucose-6-phosphate, and is not inhibited by AMP.
r.B: PFK-1 is allosterically activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, and allosterically inhibited by high-energy signals ATP and citrate.
r.C: Alanine and acetyl-CoA are allosteric inhibitors of pyruvate kinase, whereas fructose-1,6-bisphosphate is the product of PFK-1 and an activator of pyruvate kinase.
r.E: ATP, acetyl-CoA, and alanine signal abundant energy and building blocks to inhibit pyruvate kinase, while fructose-1,6-bisphosphate and AMP activate it.

q.s: SLO 4 / Slides 20, 22-23: Glycolysis Regulation

q.v:
A 19-year-old male track athlete performs repeated 400-meter sprints at maximal effort. During the final sprint, oxygen delivery to his quadriceps muscles is insufficient to meet the rate of ATP demand, and pyruvate can no longer be efficiently oxidized by the mitochondrial pyruvate dehydrogenase complex. Arterial blood gas and venous blood studies obtained immediately after the sprint show:
  Arterial pH: 7.26 (normal: 7.35-7.45)
  Venous lactate: 11.2 mmol/L (elevated)
Which of the following statements best explains the biochemistry of the reaction converting pyruvate to lactate in his skeletal muscles and its relationship to the observed acidosis?
o: The lactate dehydrogenase reaction is irreversible and directly releases two protons per lactate molecule formed
The lactate dehydrogenase reaction oxidizes pyruvate to lactate while consuming NAD+ and generating NADH
The lactate dehydrogenase reaction is reversible and consumes protons while regenerating NAD+, whereas the anaerobic condition and lactate-proton shuttle generate the acidosis
The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex reverses direction during hypoxia to convert acetyl-CoA and NADH into lactate
The conversion of pyruvate to lactate occurs exclusively in the mitochondrial matrix and prevents lactate from being used by the heart or neurons
q.p: Step 1 (During hypoxia, cytoplasmic lactate dehydrogenase reversibly reduces pyruvate to lactate using NADH, regenerating NAD+ to sustain glycolysis) -> Step 2 (The LDH reaction itself consumes protons, while the underlying anaerobic state and lactate-proton cotransport cause lactic acidosis)

r.A: The conversion of pyruvate to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase is reversible and actually consumes protons rather than releasing them.
r.B: Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate while oxidizing NADH back to NAD+ so that glycolysis can continue.
r.D: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex catalyzes the irreversible conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA under aerobic conditions and cannot reverse.
r.E: Anaerobic glycolysis and the lactate dehydrogenase reaction occur in the cytoplasm, and exported lactate can serve as fuel for neurons and cardiac tissue or enter the hepatic Cori cycle.

q.s: SLO 5 / Slides 28-29: Fate of Pyruvate and Anaerobic Glycolysis

q.v: A 58-year-old man is being evaluated for an enlarging retroperitoneal mass discovered on an abdominal CT scan. To assess for malignancy, the oncologist orders a positron emission tomography (PET) scan utilizing a radiolabeled glucose analog. Although the patient's arterial oxygen saturation is 99% and the mass is well-vascularized, the retroperitoneal mass demonstrates intense radiotracer uptake compared to the surrounding normal tissues, reflecting a markedly elevated rate of glycolysis and lactate production despite the presence of ample oxygen. Which of the following terms best describes this metabolic phenomenon in the tumor cells?
o: Cori cycle
Pasteur effect
Warburg effect
Futile cycling
Substrate-level phosphorylation
q.p: Step 1 (Tumor cells exhibit high rates of glucose uptake and glycolysis with lactate production even in the presence of oxygen) -> Step 2 (This aerobic glycolysis in cancer cells is known as the Warburg effect and forms the basis for FDG-PET imaging)

r.A: The Cori cycle refers to the physiological transport of lactate from anaerobic tissues like skeletal muscle or erythrocytes to the liver for gluconeogenesis.
r.B: The Pasteur effect is not the term taught for high rates of aerobic glycolysis in cancer cells visualized on PET imaging.
r.D: Futile cycling occurs when opposing catabolic and anabolic pathways run simultaneously, such as if glucokinase were not sequestered by GKRP during hepatic gluconeogenesis.
r.E: Substrate-level phosphorylation refers to the direct generation of ATP from phosphorylated intermediates by phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase during glycolysis.

q.s: SLO 5 / Slides 30-31: Anaerobic Glycolysis and Warburg Effect

q.v: A 42-year-old agricultural worker presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and profound muscle weakness after accidentally ingesting a pesticide containing arsenic. Laboratory evaluation reveals a severe anion gap metabolic acidosis with markedly elevated serum lactate and pyruvate levels. Which of the following hormonal or enzymatic mechanisms directly counteracts the inhibition of the targeted multienzyme complex under normal physiological conditions?
o: Phosphorylation by specific regulatory kinases
Allosteric activation by elevated intracellular NADH
Dephosphorylation mediated by insulin-stimulated phosphatases
Allosteric inhibition by intracellular calcium ions
Direct transport of oxaloacetate across the inner mitochondrial membrane
q.p: Step 1 (Arsenic targets and inhibits the pyruvate dehydrogenase [PDH] complex, blocking the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA) -> Step 2 (PDH is physiologically activated by insulin via phosphatases, whereas kinases inhibit it)

r.A: Kinases phosphorylate and inhibit the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex rather than activating it.
r.B: Elevated NADH signals a high-energy state and allosterically inhibits the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.
r.D: Intracellular calcium ions released during muscle use drive and activate the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex rather than inhibiting it.
r.E: Oxaloacetate does not have a direct transporter to cross the inner mitochondrial membrane and must be converted to malate.

q.s: Slide 5: Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex (PDH)

q.v: A 58-year-old man with a history of severe substance abuse and poor nutritional intake is admitted to the hospital with dyspnea, orthopnea, and bilateral lower extremity edema. Chest radiography reveals significant dilatation of the right heart consistent with high-output heart failure. The deficient micronutrient responsible for this patient's cardiac manifestations is also required as a cofactor for a specific enzyme within the tricarboxylic acid cycle. What is the immediate downstream product generated by this specific tricarboxylic acid cycle enzyme?
o: Acetyl-CoA
Citrate
Alpha-ketoglutarate
Succinyl-CoA
Fumarate
q.p: Step 1 (Patient has wet beriberi due to thiamine deficiency, which impairs PDH, transketolase, and the alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex) -> Step 2 (In the TCA cycle, the alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex converts alpha-ketoglutarate into succinyl-CoA)

r.A: Acetyl-CoA is the product of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, which links glycolysis to the TCA cycle but is not inside the TCA cycle itself.
r.B: Citrate is generated by citrate synthase, an enzyme that does not require thiamine as a cofactor.
r.C: Alpha-ketoglutarate is the product of isocitrate dehydrogenase and serves as the substrate, not the product, of the thiamine-dependent TCA cycle enzyme.
r.E: Fumarate is generated from succinate by succinate dehydrogenase, which relies on FAD rather than thiamine.

q.s: Slide 4: Beriberi & Slide 7: The TCA Cycle

q.v: An investigator is studying hepatocyte metabolism during a prolonged fast. Tracing radiolabeled mitochondrial pyruvate reveals that it is first carboxylated into a 4-carbon intermediate inside the mitochondrial matrix before its carbon skeleton can be utilized in the cytosol to synthesize phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP). Because the inner mitochondrial membrane lacks a direct transporter for this initial 4-carbon intermediate, it must be temporarily converted into which of the following molecules to exit the mitochondrial matrix?
o: Citrate
Malate
Succinate
Fumarate
Isocitrate
q.p: Step 1 (During gluconeogenesis, mitochondrial oxaloacetate must reach the cytosol to be converted to PEP, but lacks a direct membrane transporter) -> Step 2 (Oxaloacetate is converted to malate, which has a transporter to cross into the cytosol before being converted back to oxaloacetate)

r.A: Citrate moves from the mitochondria to the cytosol when acetyl-CoA builds up to synthesize lipids, not to supply oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis during fasting.
r.C: Succinate is a 4-carbon TCA cycle intermediate that is oxidized to fumarate in the mitochondria and does not serve as the transport shuttle for gluconeogenesis.
r.D: Fumarate is hydrated to malate within theTCA cycle, rather than being the molecule directly formed from oxaloacetate for cytosolic transport.
r.E: Isocitrate is a 6-carbon intermediate oxidized in the matrix by isocitrate dehydrogenase and does not transport carbons for gluconeogenesis.

q.s: Slide 9: The mitochondrial matrix contains & Slide 14: TCA interacts with many other cycles

q.v: A 64-year-old woman presents to the clinic with progressive fatigue, pallor, and shortness of breath. A complete blood count reveals macrocytic anemia with megaloblasts on peripheral smear, and the physician seeks to differentiate between a vitamin B9 (folate) deficiency and a vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency. Measuring the accumulation of methylmalonic acid confirms a vitamin B12 deficiency. This accumulated diagnostic metabolite is derived directly from an intermediate that normally enters the tricarboxylic acid cycle from the catabolism of which of the following substrates?
o: Even-chain fatty acids and ketone bodies
Glucose-6-phosphate and ribulose-5-phosphate
Glutamate and alpha-ketoglutarate
Odd-chain fatty acids and valine, isoleucine, threonine, and methionine
Citrate and cytosolic acetyl-CoA
q.p: Step 1 (Vitamin B12 is required to convert methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, causing methylmalonic acid to build up in B12 deficiency) -> Step 2 (This pathway is fed by propionyl-CoA derived from the breakdown of odd-chain fatty acids and VITM amino acids)

r.A: Even-chain fatty acids and ketone bodies are metabolized via acetyl-CoA rather than propionyl-CoA and methylmalonyl-CoA.
r.B: Glucose-6-phosphate and ribulose-5-phosphate are intermediates of the pentose phosphate pathway and do not form methylmalonyl-CoA.
r.C: Glutamate is interconverted with alpha-ketoglutarate by glutamate dehydrogenase, which does not require vitamin B12 or pass through methylmalonyl-CoA.
r.E: Citrate and acetyl-CoA participate in lipid synthesis when energy is abundant and do not feed into the propionyl-CoA pathway.

q.s: Slide 12: TCA interacts with many other cycles (B12 deficiency)

q.v: A 38-year-old man consumes a meal rich in carbohydrates and fats, leading to a high-energy state within his hepatocytes with elevated intracellular ATP and NADH concentrations. As a consequence, flux through the tricarboxylic acid cycle is significantly downregulated, causing an accumulation of acetyl-CoA inside the mitochondria. Which of the following metabolic processes is directly stimulated by the resulting buildup of mitochondrial acetyl-CoA and citrate?
o: Movement of excess citrate into the cytosol to synthesize lipids
Allosteric activation of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex
Inhibition of pyruvate carboxylase to prevent oxaloacetate formation
Direct conversion of acetyl-CoA into glucose via gluconeogenesis
Activation of isocitrate dehydrogenase to clear excess citrate
q.p: Step 1 (High energy states [ATP, NADH] inhibit the TCA cycle, causing acetyl-CoA and citrate to build up) -> Step 2 (When acetyl-CoA builds up, excess citrate moves to the cytosol to build lipids, and acetyl-CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase)

r.B: Acetyl-CoA signals a high-energy state and allosterically inhibits, rather than activates, the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.
r.C: Acetyl-CoA allosterically activates pyruvate carboxylase to replenish oxaloacetate rather than inhibiting it.
r.D: Acetyl-CoA cannot be used as a substrate for gluconeogenesis because the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction is irreversible and the two carbons entering the TCA cycle leave as CO2.
r.E: Isocitrate dehydrogenase is strongly inhibited during high-energy conditions by elevated ATP and NADH.

q.s: Slide 10: Citric acid and oxaloacetate in lipid metabolism & Slide 15: TCA cycle regulation

q.v: During a laboratory experiment studying isolated hepatocyte mitochondria, a researcher removes several tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates to simulate their diversion into amino acid synthesis and gluconeogenesis. To prevent the cycle from stalling, the mitochondria are supplied with pyruvate and high levels of acetyl-CoA to drive anaplerotic replenishment. Which of the following cofactors or ions are directly required by the enzyme that catalyzes the single-step replenishment of the necessary 4-carbon TCA cycle intermediate from pyruvate?
o: Thiamine pyrophosphate and lipoic acid
Biotin and magnesium (Mg2+)
Cobalamin (B12) and FADH2
NADP+ and riboflavin (B2)
Coenzyme Q and iron
q.p: Step 1 (TCA cycle replenishment from pyruvate is catalyzed by pyruvate carboxylase, which adds a carbon to pyruvate to generate oxaloacetate and is activated by acetyl-CoA) -> Step 2 (As shown in the reaction diagram, pyruvate carboxylase requires ATP, CO2, biotin, and Mg++)

r.A: Thiamine pyrophosphate and lipoic acid are cofactors for the pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complexes, not pyruvate carboxylase.
r.C: Cobalamin (B12) is required for the conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, whereas FADH2 is a product of succinate dehydrogenase.
r.D: NADP+ is utilized in the oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway, and riboflavin (B2) is a cofactor for PDH and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
r.E: Coenzyme Q accepts electrons from FADH2 via succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II) in the electron transport chain.

q.s: Slide 16: TCA replenishment

q.v: An investigator is analyzing the metabolic flux of the pentose phosphate pathway in newly isolated mature human erythrocytes. Because these cells lack nuclei and mitochondria, they have no ongoing requirement for DNA or RNA synthesis, yet they maintain high activity through the oxidative branch of the pathway to combat oxidative stress. What occurs to the 5-carbon sugar produced at the end of the oxidative phase in these erythrocytes?
o: It is irreversibly decarboxylated into a 4-carbon sugar and CO2
It is shunted through reversible carbon rearrangements to form fructose-6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate
It is transported into the mitochondrial matrix to replenish succinyl-CoA
It is oxidized by 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase to generate additional NADPH
It accumulates intracellularly to directly allosterically inhibit glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
q.p: Step 1 (The oxidative phase of the PPP produces ribulose-5-phosphate [5C] and NADPH; in RBCs, there is no need for nucleotide [DNA/RNA] synthesis) -> Step 2 (The non-oxidative phase is very active in RBCs, using reversible transketolase and transaldolase reactions to convert the 5C sugars into 6C [fructose-6P] and 3C [glyceraldehyde-3P] glycolytic intermediates)

r.A: Oxidative decarboxylation occurs in the irreversible oxidative phase when 6-phosphogluconate (6C) is converted to ribulose-5-phosphate (5C), not afterward.
r.C: Mature red blood cells do not have mitochondria and cannot perform the TCA cycle.
r.D: 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase catalyzes the formation of ribulose-5-phosphate from 6-phosphogluconate, rather than oxidizing ribulose-5-phosphate.
r.E: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase is regulated by the NADPH:NADP+ ratio, not by the accumulation of ribulose-5-phosphate.

q.s: Slide 19 & Slide 20: Pentose Phosphate Pathway (SLO4 & SLO5)

q.v: In a well-fed hepatocyte actively synthesizing fatty acids and sterols, glucose-6-phosphate is directed into the oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway to generate reducing power. The resulting 5-carbon intermediates are subsequently rearranged via the non-oxidative branch using enzymes that transfer 2-carbon and 3-carbon units. Accumulation of the 6-carbon product formed by these non-oxidative rearrangements exerts an indirect inhibitory effect on which of the following hepatic enzymes?
o: Glucokinase
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
Pyruvate carboxylase
Citrate synthase
Glutathione reductase
q.p: Step 1 (The non-oxidative phase of the PPP uses transketolase [2C transfer] and transaldolase [3C transfer] to generate glyceraldehyde-3P [3C] and fructose-6P [6C]) -> Step 2 (In hepatocytes, fructose-6P indirectly inhibits glucokinase)

r.B: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase is inhibited by a high NADPH:NADP+ ratio, whereas low NADPH:NADP+ promotes it.
r.C: Pyruvate carboxylase is an anaplerotic mitochondrial enzyme activated by acetyl-CoA.
r.D: Citrate synthase is the first enzyme of the TCA cycle and is inhibited by citrate, NADH, succinyl-CoA, and ATP.
r.E: Glutathione reductase uses NADPH in red blood cells to regenerate reduced glutathione and is not inhibited by fructose-6-phosphate.

q.s: Slide 20: Pentose Phosphate Pathway (SLO5)

q.v: A 29-year-old man presents to the urgent care clinic with acute onset of dark urine, scleral icterus, and back pain 24 hours after starting an antimalarial medication for an upcoming trip. Peripheral blood smear demonstrates normocytic red blood cells with characteristic bite cells. The patient's underlying X-linked enzymatic defect leads to hemolysis because his erythrocytes cannot provide the reducing equivalents directly required by which of the following enzymes?
o: Glutathione peroxidase
Glutathione reductase
6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase
Transaldolase
Succinate dehydrogenase
q.p: Step 1 (The patient has G6PD deficiency, which impairs the first step of the PPP and prevents the generation of NADPH in RBCs) -> Step 2 (NADPH is directly used by glutathione reductase to convert oxidized glutathione [GSSG] back into reduced glutathione [2 GSH])

r.A: Glutathione peroxidase uses reduced glutathione (GSH) to convert H2O2 into H2O, whereas glutathione reductase is the enzyme that directly uses NADPH.
r.C: 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase requires NADP+ as a substrate to produce NADPH, rather than consuming NADPH.
r.D: Transaldolase catalyzes a reversible 3-carbon transfer in the non-oxidative phase of the PPP and does not use NADPH.
r.E: Succinate dehydrogenase is a mitochondrial TCA cycle enzyme absent in red blood cells and utilizes FAD rather than NADPH.

q.s: Slide 22: Case & Slide 23: G6PD Deficiency

q.v: A 4-year-old boy is evaluated in the immunology clinic for a history of recurrent severe bacterial and fungal infections and the formation of large tissue granulomas. Diagnostic testing confirms chronic granulomatous disease caused by the deficiency of an enzyme that normally consumes NADPH to generate reactive oxygen species. In normal human cells, the same electron-donating cofactor required by this deficient enzyme is also directly required for which of the following metabolic conversions?
o: Reduction of oxidized lipoic acid in the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex
Oxidation of isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate
Reduction of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate in folate metabolism
Conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA
Carboxylation of pyruvate to oxaloacetate
q.p: Step 1 (Chronic granulomatous disease is caused by a lack of NADPH oxidase, which normally uses NADPH to produce ROS) -> Step 2 (Other uses of NADPH include fatty acid/steroid synthesis, cytochrome P450 reactions, and the reduction of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate in folate metabolism)

r.A: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex utilizes NAD+ and FAD to transfer electrons, generating NADH rather than consuming NADPH.
r.B: Isocitrate dehydrogenase is a TCA cycle enzyme that reduces NAD+ to NADH, not NADPH.
r.D: The conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA is an isomerization requiring vitamin B12, not NADPH.
r.E: The carboxylation of pyruvate to oxaloacetate by pyruvate carboxylase requires ATP, biotin, and magnesium, not NADPH.

q.s: Slide 25: Other uses of NADPH

q.v:
A 48-year-old man with a long history of alcohol abuse and poor nutritional intake is brought to the emergency department with confusion, difficulty breathing, and generalized muscle weakness. Physical examination reveals loss of reflexes in the knees and feet, painful tender calf muscles, and bilateral foot drop. Laboratory studies show:
  Serum glucose: 38 mg/dL
  Serum lactate: elevated
Before administering intravenous glucose, the physician orders 100 mg of intravenous thiamine. Administration of glucose prior to thiamine in this patient would most directly worsen his condition by increasing the conversion of pyruvate into which of the following compounds?
o: Acetyl-CoA
Citrate
Lactate
Malate
Oxaloacetate
q.p: Step 1 (Thiamine deficiency impairs pyruvate dehydrogenase complex activity) -> Step 2 (Administering glucose increases pyruvate, which cannot be converted to acetyl-CoA and is instead shunted to lactate, worsening lactic acidosis)

r.A: Without thiamine (TPP), the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex cannot convert pyruvate into acetyl-CoA.
r.B: Citrate generation requires acetyl-CoA entry into the TCA cycle, which is blocked when pyruvate dehydrogenase is inactive.
r.D: Malate is a TCA cycle intermediate downstream of acetyl-CoA entry and is not the primary toxic byproduct of impaired pyruvate oxidation.
r.E: Oxaloacetate is generated via biotin-dependent pyruvate carboxylase rather than accumulating from thiamine deficiency.

q.s: SLO 1, Slide 3-4: Beriberi and Pathways of Pyruvate

q.v: A 35-year-old woman with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought to the clinic for routine metabolic follow-up. After administering her prescribed dose of mealtime insulin, intracellular signaling cascades are activated within her skeletal muscle and liver cells to promote glucose oxidation. Which of the following mechanisms directly mediates the activation of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex in response to insulin?
o: Allosteric activation by acetyl-CoA
Allosteric activation by NADH
Covalent dephosphorylation by phosphatases
Covalent phosphorylation by kinases
Inhibition of mitochondrial pyruvate transport
q.p: Step 1 (Insulin signaling stimulates intracellular phosphatases) -> Step 2 (Phosphatases dephosphorylate and activate the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex)

r.A: Acetyl-CoA signals a high-energy state and acts as an allosteric inhibitor, not an activator, of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.
r.B: NADH signals a high-energy state and inhibits both the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and the TCA cycle.
r.D: Kinases phosphorylate and inhibit the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex rather than activating it.
r.E: Pyruvate must be moved into the mitochondrial matrix via a transporter for the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex to convert it to acetyl-CoA.

q.s: SLO 1, Slide 5: Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex (PDH)

q.v: A 51-year-old woman with a history of chronic alcohol abuse presents to the clinic with numbness of the feet, wrist drop, and confusion. Laboratory evaluation confirms severe deficiency of vitamin B1 (thiamine). In addition to the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, which of the following pairs of enzymes directly requires the cofactor derived from this vitamin for catalytic activity?
o: Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex and transketolase
Citrate synthase and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
Isocitrate dehydrogenase and transaldolase
Pyruvate carboxylase and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase
Succinate dehydrogenase and glutathione reductase
q.p: Step 1 (Vitamin B1 is converted to thiamine pyrophosphate) -> Step 2 (Thiamine is required by three enzymes: PDH, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex in the TCA cycle, and transketolases in the PPP)

r.B: Citrate synthase and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase do not require thiamine pyrophosphate as a cofactor.
r.C: Isocitrate dehydrogenase requires NAD+ and transaldolase catalyzes a 3-carbon transfer in the PPP without thiamine.
r.D: Pyruvate carboxylase requires biotin (B7), and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase uses NADP+ rather than thiamine.
r.E: Succinate dehydrogenase utilizes FAD in the electron transport chain, and glutathione reductase utilizes NADPH.

q.s: SLO 2, Slide 4 and 15: Beriberi and TCA Cycle Regulation

q.v: Which of the following coenzymes required by both the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and the alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex is derived from vitamin B2?
o: Coenzyme A (CoA)
FADH2
Lipoic acid
NADH
Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP)
q.p: Step 1 (PDH and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase require the same 5 coenzymes) -> Step 2 (Vitamin B2, riboflavin, is the precursor for FADH2)

r.A: Coenzyme A (CoA) is derived from vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid), not vitamin B2.
r.C: Lipoic acid is one of the five required coenzymes for PDH, but it is not derived from riboflavin.
r.D: NADH is derived from vitamin B3 (niacin), not vitamin B2.
r.E: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is derived from vitamin B1 (thiamine), not vitamin B2.

q.s: SLO 2, Slide 5 and 15: Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex (PDH) and TCA Cycle Regulation

q.v:
A 70-year-old man is brought to the clinic by his daughter due to progressive fatigue, pallor, and numbness in his lower extremities. He has followed a strict vegan diet for the past decade without taking vitamin supplements. Laboratory studies show:
  Hemoglobin: 8.8 g/dL
  Mean corpuscular volume (MCV): 112 fL
  Serum methylmalonic acid: markedly elevated
  Peripheral blood smear: megaloblastic anemia
Impaired conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA into which of the following tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates best explains the laboratory findings in this patient?
o: Alpha-ketoglutarate
Citrate
Fumarate
Oxaloacetate
Succinyl-CoA
q.p: Step 1 (Vitamin B12 deficiency impairs the conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA) -> Step 2 (Methylmalonic acid builds up instead of forming succinyl-CoA to enter the TCA cycle)

r.A: Alpha-ketoglutarate is linked to glutamate metabolism via glutamate dehydrogenase rather than odd-chain fatty acid and methylmalonyl-CoA catabolism.
r.B: Citrate is formed from acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate and is exported to the cytosol for lipid synthesis when acetyl-CoA builds up.
r.C: Fumarate is generated from succinate by succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II) and does not require vitamin B12.
r.D: Oxaloacetate is formed from pyruvate via biotin-dependent pyruvate carboxylase or malate dehydrogenase.

q.s: SLO 2, Slide 12: TCA interacts with many other cycles

q.v:
A 26-year-old man is performing a maximal-effort sprint test in an exercise physiology laboratory. Biopsy of his contracting quadriceps muscle demonstrates the following intracellular metabolite profile compared to his resting baseline:
  Intracellular ADP: markedly increased
  Cytosolic and mitochondrial Ca2+: markedly increased
  Intracellular ATP: decreased
  Intracellular NADH: decreased
These acute intracellular changes directly stimulate flux through the tricarboxylic acid cycle by allosterically activating which of the following pairs of irreversible enzymes?
o: Citrate synthase and malate dehydrogenase
Isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex
Malate dehydrogenase and fumarase
Pyruvate carboxylase and succinate dehydrogenase
Succinate dehydrogenase and citrate synthase
q.p: Step 1 (Muscle contraction and low energy states increase Ca2+ and ADP) -> Step 2 (Ca2+ and ADP directly activate the irreversible TCA enzymes isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex)

r.A: Citrate synthase is regulated primarily by citrate inhibition, and malate dehydrogenase is a reversible enzyme not activated by Ca2+.
r.C: Both malate dehydrogenase and fumarase catalyze reversible steps in the TCA cycle and are not the primary Ca2+/ADP-activated regulatory points.
r.D: Pyruvate carboxylase is an anaplerotic enzyme activated by acetyl-CoA, and succinate dehydrogenase is Complex II of the electron transport chain.
r.E: Succinate dehydrogenase and citrate synthase are not the irreversible TCA cycle enzymes activated by Ca2+ and ADP.

q.s: SLO 3, Slide 15: TCA cycle regulation

q.v:
A 21-year-old man is evaluated in the sports medicine clinic for progressive fatigue, muscle cramps, and a scaly erythematous rash around his eyes and mouth. He reports eating a specialized bodybuilding diet that includes six raw egg whites daily for the past five months. Laboratory studies show:
  Fasting blood glucose: 62 mg/dL
  Serum pyruvate: elevated
  Serum lactate: elevated
Impaired replenishment of which of the following tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates best explains the laboratory abnormalities in this patient?
o: Alpha-ketoglutarate
Citrate
Isocitrate
Oxaloacetate
Succinyl-CoA
q.p: Step 1 (Biotin deficiency from raw egg white consumption impairs pyruvate carboxylase) -> Step 2 (Pyruvate carboxylase cannot add a carbon to pyruvate to generate oxaloacetate and replenish the TCA cycle)

r.A: Alpha-ketoglutarate is replenished via glutamate dehydrogenase, which does not require biotin.
r.B: Citrate is synthesized from acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate by citrate synthase, which does not utilize biotin.
r.C: Isocitrate is formed by the isomerization of citrate and is not the direct product of biotin-dependent pyruvate carboxylation.
r.E: Succinyl-CoA is replenished from propionyl-CoA and methylmalonyl-CoA in a pathway requiring vitamin B12, not biotin.

q.s: SLO 3, Slide 16: TCA replenishment

q.v: A 30-year-old woman consumes a high-carbohydrate meal, stimulating hepatic fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis. As cytosolic NADPH is rapidly consumed by these anabolic pathways, the changing intracellular NADPH/NADP+ ratio alters flux through the pentose phosphate pathway in her hepatocytes. Which of the following best describes the resulting enzymatic effect and the phase of the pathway in which it occurs?
o: Activation of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase in the irreversible oxidative phase
Activation of transketolase in the irreversible non-oxidative phase
Inhibition of 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase in the reversible oxidative phase
Inhibition of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase in the reversible oxidative phase
Inhibition of transaldolase in the reversible non-oxidative phase
q.p: Step 1 (Consumption of NADPH in lipid and sterol biosynthesis lowers the NADPH:NADP+ ratio) -> Step 2 (A low NADPH:NADP+ ratio promotes glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, the rate-limiting step of the irreversible oxidative phase)

r.B: Transketolase is part of the non-oxidative phase, which is reversible rather than irreversible.
r.C: The oxidative phase is irreversible, and a low NADPH:NADP+ ratio promotes rather than inhibits the pathway.
r.D: A low NADPH:NADP+ ratio promotes glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, and the oxidative phase is irreversible.
r.E: Transaldolase catalyzes a reversible 3-carbon transfer in the non-oxidative phase and is not the rate-limiting step regulated by the NADPH:NADP+ ratio.

q.s: SLO 4, Slide 19: Pentose Phosphate Pathway

q.v: Which of the following correctly pairs the carbon transfer reaction catalyzed by transaldolase in the non-oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway with the glycolytic intermediate produced by this phase that indirectly inhibits glucokinase in hepatocytes?
o: 2-carbon transfer; Fructose-6-phosphate
2-carbon transfer; Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate
3-carbon transfer; Fructose-6-phosphate
3-carbon transfer; Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate
3-carbon transfer; Ribulose-5-phosphate
q.p: Step 1 (Transaldolase catalyzes a reversible 3-carbon transfer in the non-oxidative phase, whereas transketolase catalyzes a 2-carbon transfer) -> Step 2 (The non-oxidative phase yields fructose-6-phosphate, which indirectly inhibits glucokinase in hepatocytes)

r.A: A 2-carbon transfer is catalyzed by transketolase rather than transaldolase.
r.B: A 2-carbon transfer is catalyzed by transketolase, and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate is not the 6-carbon intermediate that inhibits glucokinase.
r.D: Although transaldolase catalyzes a 3-carbon transfer, it is fructose-6-phosphate (6C) rather than glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (3C) that indirectly inhibits glucokinase.
r.E: Ribulose-5-phosphate is the 5-carbon product of the oxidative phase, not the 6-carbon glycolytic intermediate that inhibits glucokinase.

q.s: SLO 5, Slide 20-21: Pentose Phosphate Pathway

q.v:
A 19-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute fatigue, back pain, and dark urine two days after eating a meal containing fava beans. Physical examination reveals scleral icterus. Laboratory studies show:
  Hemoglobin: 9.1 g/dL
  Peripheral blood smear: bite cells and Heinz bodies
  Erythrocyte NADPH: decreased
The decreased concentration of NADPH in this patient's red blood cells directly impairs the activity of which of the following enzymes required to detoxify hydrogen peroxide?
o: 6-Phosphogluconate dehydrogenase
Cytochrome P450 monooxygenase
Glutathione peroxidase
Glutathione reductase
NADPH oxidase
q.p: Step 1 (G6PD deficiency reduces NADPH production in red blood cells) -> Step 2 (Without NADPH, glutathione reductase cannot regenerate reduced glutathione [GSH] from oxidized glutathione [GSSG] to allow glutathione peroxidase to detoxify H2O2)

r.A: 6-Phosphogluconate dehydrogenase produces NADPH from NADP+ in the oxidative phase rather than consuming NADPH to regenerate glutathione.
r.B: Cytochrome P450 enzymes use electrons from NADPH for detoxification and biosynthesis, not for regenerating reduced glutathione in erythrocytes.
r.C: Glutathione peroxidase uses reduced glutathione (GSH) to convert H2O2 into H2O, whereas glutathione reductase is the enzyme that directly uses NADPH.
r.E: NADPH oxidase uses NADPH to produce reactive oxygen species in phagocytes (deficiency causes chronic granulomatous disease) rather than detoxifying ROS.

q.s: SLO 6, Slide 23 and 26: G6PD Deficiency

myLectures.note: Cards picked to match the slides, checked against your 42 Bioenergetics cards (see bioenergetics_card_check.csv). Slides only, with no B&B card: redox potentials/electron affinity, complex II not pumping protons, redox state upstream/downstream of a block, the Q cycle as a superoxide source, mitochondrial genome details. Also adds your own cards (as cloze: 7 notes, 8 cards) to Anki for the facts B&B doesn't fully cover (#4, 6, 9, 13, 14, 18, 29, 30).

add.cloze: Electrons from NADH enter the electron transport chain at {{c1::complex I}}
add.extra: Complex I = NADH dehydrogenase. Electrons from FADH2 enter at complex II (succinate dehydrogenase).

add.cloze: Electrons flow "downhill" through the ETC because each successive carrier has an {{c1::increasing electron affinity (more positive redox potential)}}
add.extra: Complex I/II → CoQ → complex III → cytochrome c → complex IV → O2, the terminal electron acceptor

add.cloze: Complex II does not contribute directly to the proton motive force because it {{c1::does not pump protons}} across the inner mitochondrial membrane
add.extra: Complexes I, III and IV pump protons

add.cloze: When an ETC complex is inhibited, electron carriers upstream of the block become {{c1::highly reduced}}, while carriers downstream of the block become {{c2::oxidized}}
add.extra: Electrons pile up before the block and drain away after it

add.cloze: Antimycin A inhibits {{c1::complex III}} of the electron transport chain
add.extra: Rotenone → complex I; antimycin A → complex III; cyanide/CO → complex IV; oligomycin → ATP synthase (complex V)

add.cloze: The {{c1::hydroxyl radical (•OH)}} has no known detoxification enzyme and directly damages cells
add.extra: Formed from H2O2 by the Fenton reaction (Fe2+) or by ionizing radiation; superoxide → SOD, H2O2 → catalase / glutathione peroxidase

add.cloze: Lack of oxygen halts the ETC, so {{c1::NADH accumulates and the TCA cycle is inhibited}}
add.extra: Without O2 as the terminal electron acceptor, NAD+ isn't regenerated; pyruvate shifts to lactate
