q.v: A 28-year-old man participates in a metabolic study evaluating hepatic carbohydrate processing after consuming a meal rich in both sucrose and starch. Laboratory analysis of isolated hepatocytes reveals a transient, rapid accumulation of intracellular fructose-6-phosphate before downstream glycolytic enzymes are fully activated. What is the immediate regulatory consequence of this specific metabolite's accumulation on hepatic glucose entry and utilization?
o: It allosterically activates phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK1) to accelerate glycolysis
It promotes the binding of glucokinase regulatory protein (GKRP) to glucokinase, decreasing glucose utilization
It causes glucokinase to dissociate from its regulatory protein, increasing glucose utilization
It directly inhibits both phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK1) and phosphofructokinase-2 (PFK2)
It stimulates the transport of reduced oxaloacetate out of the mitochondrial matrix
q.p: Step 1 (Accumulation of fructose-6-phosphate indicates glycolysis is progressing and the system is temporarily saturated) -> Step 2 (Fructose-6-phosphate promotes GKRP-glucokinase binding, which indirectly inhibits glucokinase and reduces glucose utilization until F-6P works through the system)

r.A: Fructose-6-phosphate is the substrate for PFK1, not the primary allosteric activator described, and its buildup here slows upstream glucose entry via GKRP.
r.C: Fructose-1-phosphate (indicating dietary fructose entry), rather than fructose-6-phosphate, releases glucokinase from GKRP to increase glucose utilization.
r.D: Citrate is the metabolite that inhibits both PFK1 and PFK2 to decrease glycolysis, whereas fructose-6-phosphate acts on the GKRP-glucokinase complex.
r.E: Shuttling reduced oxaloacetate (malate) out of the mitochondria is a function of the malate/aspartate shuttle during gluconeogenesis, not a direct regulatory effect of fructose-6-phosphate on glucokinase.

q.s: Slide 2: Citrate and glycolysis regulation

q.v: A 6-month-old infant presents with hypotonia and fasting hypoglycemia. Biochemical assay of liver tissue demonstrates a defect in the inner mitochondrial membrane glutamate-aspartate transporter, severely impairing the malate-aspartate shuttle. In addition to impaired transfer of glycolytic NADH reducing equivalents into the mitochondrial matrix, which of the following processes will be most directly compromised in this patient's hepatocytes?
o: Export of reduced oxaloacetate from the mitochondria for gluconeogenesis
Direct transfer of electrons from Complex I to Complex II
Import of inorganic phosphate via the mitochondrial antiporter
Reduction of ubiquinone to ubiquinol by succinate dehydrogenase
Pumping of protons into the intermembrane space by Complex II
q.p: Step 1 (Defect in the glutamate-aspartate transporter impairs the malate-aspartate shuttle) -> Step 2 (Because the shuttle also transports reduced oxaloacetate, i.e., malate, out of the mitochondria, gluconeogenesis is directly compromised)

r.B: No electrons move directly from Complex I to Complex II under normal physiological conditions.
r.C: Inorganic phosphate is imported into the matrix via the phosphate translocase, which is a H2PO4-/H+ symporter, not an antiporter.
r.D: Reduction of ubiquinone to ubiquinol by Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) utilizes FADH2 and operates independently of the malate-aspartate shuttle.
r.E: Complex II does not pump protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane under any circumstances.

q.s: Slide 5: How does glycolytic NADH get into the mitochondria?

q.v: A 9-year-old girl is evaluated for progressive muscle weakness and exercise intolerance. A skeletal muscle biopsy reveals a selective deficiency in the iron-sulfur (FeS) clusters of Complex III (Coenzyme Q-Cytochrome bc1 complex), while all other electron transport chain complexes remain structurally intact. Which of the following specific molecular events is most directly impaired by this defect?
o: Oxidation of NADH to NAD+ on the matrix arm of the inner membrane
Transfer of electrons from ubiquinol (QH2) to reduce two cytochrome c molecules
Reduction of molecular oxygen to two molecules of water at the heme-Cu center
Conversion of succinate to fumarate to expand the ubiquinol pool
Rotation of the gamma and epsilon subunits within the F1F0 complex
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that the defect lies in the FeS center of Complex III / Coenzyme Q-Cytochrome bc1 complex) -> Step 2 (Complex III uses its FeS center to remove 2 electrons from reduced QH2 to reduce 2 cytochrome c molecules and deliver 4 protons to the intermembrane space)

r.A: Oxidation of NADH to NAD+ using FMN and FeS centers occurs at Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase), not Complex III.
r.C: Reduction of O2 to 2 H2O occurs at the Fe-Cu (heme-Cu) center of Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase).
r.D: Oxidation of succinate to fumarate and reduction of ubiquinone (Q) to ubiquinol (QH2) is catalyzed by Complex II (succinate-CoQ reductase).
r.E: Rotation of the c, gamma, and epsilon subunits is driven by proton flow through ATP synthase (Complex V), not electron transfer in Complex III.

q.s: Slide 10: Next Stop: Complex III (Coenzyme Q-Cytochrome bc1 complex)

q.v: A researcher is studying isolated, metabolically active mitochondria in a medium containing abundant ADP, inorganic phosphate, succinate, and oxygen. She introduces an experimental compound that selectively cross-links and immobilizes the 'c' subunits of the F0 domain of ATP synthase without obstructing the proton channel itself or affecting the inner membrane transporters. How will this compound most directly disrupt ATP synthesis in the mitochondrial matrix?
o: By preventing the adenine nucleotide translocase from exporting ATP4- in exchange for ADP3-
By halting the rotation of the alpha3-beta3 hexamer in the mitochondrial matrix
By preventing the rotation of the gamma subunit that drives conformational changes in the stationary alpha3-beta3 hexamer
By blocking the symport of H2PO4- and H+ across the inner mitochondrial membrane
By inhibiting the stationary epsilon subunit from anchoring the F1 catalytic domain to the membrane
q.p: Step 1 (Immobilization of the rotating 'c' subunits of the F0 domain of ATP synthase) -> Step 2 (Without 'c' subunit rotation, the gamma and epsilon subunits cannot rotate, failing to induce the conformational changes in the stationary alpha3-beta3 hexamer required to synthesize ATP)

r.A: Adenine nucleotide translocase is a separate inner membrane antiporter that exchanges ATP4- and ADP3- and is not part of the F0 'c' subunit ring.
r.B: The alpha, beta, a, b, and delta subunits of ATP synthase are stationary and do not rotate during catalysis.
r.D: The symport of H2PO4- and H+ is mediated by the separate phosphate translocase symporter, not the 'c' subunits of ATP synthase.
r.E: The epsilon subunit rotates along with the 'c' and gamma subunits; it is not a stationary anchoring subunit.

q.s: Slide 12: The ATP Synthase Harnesses The Energy of The Proton Gradient

q.v: During a biochemical assay of the mitochondrial electron transport chain, a scientist measures the standard reduction potentials (E0) of various isolated electron carriers. The NAD+/NADH redox pair exhibits an E0 of -0.32 volts, whereas the O2/H2O redox pair exhibits an E0 of +0.816 volts. Coenzyme Q (ubiquinone) possesses an intermediate E0 near 0.0 volts. Based on these bioenergetic properties, which of the following statements best explains the directional movement of electrons through this system?
o: Electrons gain free energy as they move from NADH to oxygen, allowing CoQ to accept low-energy electrons from Complex IV
NADH has the highest affinity for electrons, actively pushing them uphill toward carriers with more negative reduction potentials
Carriers further down the chain have a lower tendency to be reduced, requiring ATP hydrolysis to drive electron flow toward oxygen
Electrons lose energy as they pass down the chain toward carriers with increasingly positive E0 values and higher electron affinity
Coenzyme Q has a higher affinity for electrons than oxygen and can accept both high-energy and low-energy electrons from Cytochrome c
q.p: Step 1 (Analyze the E0 gradient from -0.32 V at NADH to +0.816 V at O2) -> Step 2 (A more positive E0 indicates a higher affinity for electrons and a greater tendency to be reduced, meaning electrons lose free energy as they move down the chain from NADH through CoQ to oxygen)

r.A: Electrons lose free energy as they pass down the chain, and CoQ can only accept higher-energy electrons from Complexes I and II, whereas oxygen accepts low-energy electrons.
r.B: A negative E0 (-0.32 V) means the NAD+/NADH pair has a low affinity for electrons and readily releases them to carriers with more positive E0 values.
r.C: Carriers down the chain have a greater (more positive) E0 and a greater tendency to be reduced, so electron transfer is spontaneous and does not require ATP hydrolysis.
r.E: Oxygen has the highest redox potential (+0.816 V) and electron affinity, allowing it to accept low-energy electrons, whereas CoQ can only accept higher-energy electrons.

q.s: Slide 15: Biological Redox Pairs in Energy Transfer & Slide 17: Redox Potential

q.v: A biochemist is studying electron transfer kinetics in a synthetic membrane system containing Complex I, Coenzyme Q, and Complex III. Under normal conditions, electrons flow smoothly from NADH to Cytochrome c. If the biochemist chemically modifies Coenzyme Q so that its reduction potential (E0) becomes significantly more negative than that of the flavin mononucleotide (FMN) and iron-sulfur (FeS) centers in Complex I, what will be the immediate bioenergetic consequence?
o: Coenzyme Q will exhibit an increased affinity for electrons, accelerating proton pumping at Complex I
Complex I will pump protons from the intermembrane space back into the mitochondrial matrix
The modified Coenzyme Q will spontaneously strip low-energy electrons directly from molecular oxygen
Electron transfer from Complex I to Coenzyme Q will be impaired because the modified carrier has a lower tendency to be reduced
Electrons from NADH will bypass Coenzyme Q and flow directly from Complex I into Complex II
q.p: Step 1 (Coenzyme Q's E0 is made more negative than upstream Complex I components) -> Step 2 (Because electrons flow from more negative E0 to more positive E0, a more negative E0 decreases CoQ's electron affinity and tendency to be reduced, halting electron transfer from Complex I)

r.A: A more negative E0 corresponds to a lower affinity for electrons and a greater tendency to release electrons, not accept them.
r.B: Impaired electron transfer into CoQ stops the energy input required to power the Complex I proton pump rather than reversing it.
r.C: Molecular oxygen has a large positive E0 (+0.816 V) and high affinity for electrons, so it takes electrons from pairs with less positive E0 rather than donating them.
r.E: No electrons move directly from Complex I to Complex II; they must pass through the ubiquinone (Q) pool.

q.s: Slide 16: Oxidation: Reduction (Redox) Reactions Involve Electron Transfer & Slide 17

q.v: A 42-year-old agricultural worker is brought to the emergency department with severe lethargy and tachypnea after accidentally inhaling concentrated pesticide fumes containing antimycin A. Arterial blood gas reveals a profound anion gap metabolic acidosis with markedly elevated serum lactate. In addition to the accumulation of lactate from increased glycolysis, which of the following best describes the mechanism contributing to cellular acidosis and the redox state of mitochondrial carriers in this patient?
o: Co-transport of protons from ATP hydrolysis out of the cell with lactate; Cytochrome c is predominantly oxidized
Net generation of protons during the conversion of pyruvate to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase; Ubiquinone is predominantly oxidized
Direct leakage of protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane via uncoupling channels; Cytochrome c is predominantly reduced
Blockade of the F0 proton channel causing proton buildup in the matrix; NADH/NAD+ ratio is decreased
Inhibition of Complex IV preventing water formation; all upstream electron carriers are predominantly oxidized
q.p: Step 1 (Antimycin A blocks Complex III, halting the ETC and forcing the cell to rely on glycolysis and ATP hydrolysis) -> Step 2 (Carriers downstream of Complex III like Cytochrome c become oxidized, while pyruvate-to-lactate conversion recycles NAD+ and protons from ATP hydrolysis are co-transported out of the cell with lactate)

r.B: The conversion of pyruvate to lactate actually consumes protons to recycle NADH to NAD+, and because the block is at Complex III, upstream ubiquinone (CoQ) becomes reduced, not oxidized.
r.C: Antimycin A is a Complex III inhibitor, not an uncoupler, and downstream Cytochrome c will be oxidized because it cannot receive electrons from Complex III.
r.D: Blockade of the F0 proton channel is the mechanism of oligomycin, and any ETC block increases the NADH/NAD+ ratio due to backup of reduced NADH.
r.E: Antimycin A inhibits Complex III rather than Complex IV, and carriers upstream of an ETC block become reduced, not oxidized.

q.s: Slide 19: Mitochondrial Poisons & Slide 21: Disruption of Electron Transport Chain

q.v: A 16-year-old boy is evaluated for progressive bilateral vision loss, cardiac conduction abnormalities, and chronic lactic acidosis. Genetic sequencing confirms a pathogenic point mutation in the mitochondrial genome (mtDNA), which is also identified in his mother and maternal aunt. Based on the specific characteristics of the mitochondrial genome, a subunit of which of the following complexes could be directly encoded by the mutated gene in this patient?
o: Succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II), resulting in paraganglioma
Cytochrome bc1 complex (Complex III), which lacks introns and has a mutation rate 10 times higher than nuclear DNA
Adenine nucleotide translocase (AAC), which is inherited paternally in 10-15/100,000 individuals
Citrate synthase, which is encoded by 2-10 copies of mtDNA per mitochondrion
Glucokinase regulatory protein, which requires 22 mitochondrial tRNAs for translation
q.p: Step 1 (Identify a maternally inherited mtDNA mutation causing multi-systemic disease affecting brain/eye and heart with lactic acidosis) -> Step 2 (mtDNA has no introns, mutates 10x more frequently than nuclear DNA, and encodes 13 oxidative phosphorylation subunits including Complex I, III, IV, and V, but notably NOT Complex II)

r.A: Although Complex II defects can cause Leigh syndrome, paraganglioma, and pheochromocytoma, Complex II is encoded entirely by nuclear DNA, not mitochondrial DNA.
r.C: Mitochondrial DNA is inherited exclusively maternally, and while AAC (ADP/ATP carrier) is a disease site in mitochondrial disorders, it is nuclear-encoded.
r.D: Mitochondrial DNA only encodes 13 protein subunits of the oxidative phosphorylation system, 22 tRNAs, and 2 rRNAs, not TCA cycle enzymes like citrate synthase.
r.E: Glucokinase regulatory protein is a hepatic nuclear-encoded protein involved in glycolysis regulation, not one of the 13 ox/phos subunits encoded by mtDNA.

q.s: Slide 23: Mitochondrial Diseases

q.v: During an experiment on isolated cardiac mitochondria, a researcher notes that 1% to 3% of consumed molecular oxygen is converted into a reactive intermediate during the Q cycle between Complex I and Complex III. If this reactive oxygen species is not rapidly cleared, it reacts directly with mitochondrial iron-sulfur (FeS) centers to release free iron, AND it reacts with ferric iron (Fe3+) to regenerate ferrous iron (Fe2+). What is the primary downstream consequence of these iron-mediated reactions?
o: Direct enzymatic conversion of hydroxyl radicals into water and molecular oxygen by catalase
Reaction of regenerated ferrous iron (Fe2+) with hydrogen peroxide to generate highly toxic hydroxyl radicals
Spontaneous reduction of oxidized glutathione (GSSG) back to reduced glutathione (GSH) without NADPH
Inhibition of the Fenton reaction due to the depletion of mitochondrial ferric iron (Fe3+)
Stabilization of unsaturated membrane lipids against free radical electron abstraction
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that semiquinone radicals in the Q cycle donate an electron to O2 to form superoxide anion, which releases iron from FeS centers and reduces Fe3+ to Fe2+) -> Step 2 (The regenerated Fe2+ reacts with H2O2 in the Fenton reaction to produce the dangerously reactive hydroxyl radical, OH•)

r.A: Catalase decomposes hydrogen peroxide (2 H2O2 -> 2 H2O + O2) to prevent hydroxyl radical formation; it does not act directly on hydroxyl radicals.
r.C: Reduction of GSSG back to GSH requires the enzyme glutathione reductase and NADPH; it is not driven by iron or superoxide.
r.D: Superoxide regenerating Fe2+ from Fe3+ actively promotes and sustains the Fenton reaction rather than inhibiting it.
r.E: The resulting hydroxyl radical steals electrons from membrane lipids, leaving behind a new radical on the biological molecule that leads to cell lysis.

q.s: Slide 27: Free Radicals, Slide 30: Free Radicals Form During Respiration & Slide 31

q.v: A researcher is investigating the dose-dependent effects of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and its detoxification pathways in cultured human fibroblasts. As the intracellular in vivo concentration of H2O2 is experimentally increased from 10^-8 M to 10^-6 M, and subsequently to 10^-4 M, the cells transition from proliferation to growth arrest and finally to apoptosis. To prevent the cells from reaching the 10^-4 M apoptotic threshold via the glutathione peroxidase pathway, which of the following cofactors and enzymatic steps is strictly required?
o: Superoxide dismutase to reduce oxidized glutathione (GSSG) using FADH2
Catalase to transfer unpaired electrons from hydroxyl radicals onto reduced glutathione (GSH)
Glutathione reductase and NADPH to reduce oxidized glutathione (GSSG) back to reduced glutathione (GSH)
Cytochrome c oxidase to couple H2O2 reduction with the pumping of 4 protons into the intermembrane space
Ferrous iron (Fe2+) to catalyze the breakdown of H2O2 into harmless water and molecular oxygen
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that rising H2O2 concentrations shift cellular effects from proliferation [10^-8 M] to growth arrest [10^-6 M] to apoptosis [10^-4 M], requiring detoxification by glutathione peroxidase: H2O2 + 2 GSH -> 2 H2O + GSSG) -> Step 2 (Continuous operation of this protective pathway requires glutathione reductase and NADPH to reduce GSSG back to GSH)

r.A: Superoxide dismutase combines two superoxide anions and 2H+ to form H2O2 and O2; it does not reduce GSSG or use FADH2.
r.B: Catalase converts 2 H2O2 directly into 2 H2O and O2 without using glutathione, and it does not detoxify hydroxyl radicals once formed.
r.D: Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) reduces O2 to 2 H2O using electrons from Cytochrome c, whereas H2O2 decomposition is handled by catalase and glutathione peroxidase.
r.E: Ferrous iron (Fe2+) reacts with H2O2 via the Fenton reaction to produce toxic hydroxyl radicals (•OH) and OH-, rather than harmless water and oxygen.

q.s: Slide 28: The O2 Reduction Pathway and the Family of Reactive Oxygen Species & Slide 32: Enzyme Mechanisms Protect Against High Levels of ROS

q.v: Which compound inhibits both phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK1) and phosphofructokinase-2 (PFK2) to regulate glycolysis?
o: Citrate
Fructose-1-phosphate
Fructose-6-phosphate
NADH
Succinate
q.p: Step 1 (Accumulation of citrate signals high energy status) -> Step 2 (Citrate allosterically inhibits both PFK1 and PFK2 to slow glycolysis)

r.B: Fructose-1-phosphate releases glucokinase from GKRP in hepatocytes to promote glucose utilization.
r.C: Fructose-6-phosphate promotes the binding of glucokinase to GKRP, indirectly inhibiting glucokinase.
r.D: NADH donates electrons to Complex I of the electron transport chain rather than inhibiting both PFK1 and PFK2.
r.E: Succinate donates electrons to Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) in the mitochondrial inner membrane.

q.s: Slide 2: Citrate and glycolysis regulation

q.v: A 14-year-old boy presents to the neurology clinic with progressive gait unsteadiness and bilateral drooping of his eyelids (progressive external ophthalmoplegia). Muscle biopsy reveals impaired export of newly synthesized ATP from the mitochondrial matrix into the cytosol, accompanied by decreased import of ADP into the matrix. Which of the following inner mitochondrial membrane proteins is most likely defective in this patient?
o: Phosphate translocase
Adenine nucleotide translocase
Malate-alpha-ketoglutarate transporter
Thermogenin (UCP1)
Cytochrome c oxidase
q.p: Step 1 (Identify clinical presentation of adPEO and ataxia with impaired mitochondrial ATP/ADP exchange) -> Step 2 (Link to defect in Adenine Nucleotide Translocase / ADP-ATP carrier)

r.A: Phosphate translocase is a symporter that moves H2PO4- and H+ into the mitochondrial matrix.
r.C: The malate-alpha-ketoglutarate transporter is part of the malate-aspartate shuttle that transfers reducing equivalents across the inner membrane.
r.D: Thermogenin (UCP1) is an uncoupling protein that allows protons to re-enter the matrix without synthesizing ATP.
r.E: Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) transfers electrons from cytochrome c to oxygen and pumps protons.

q.s: SLO1 / Slide 13: How Do We Get The ATP to Biological Work Sites in The Cell? & Slide 23: Mitochondrial Diseases

q.v: A 34-year-old woman is evaluated for hypertension, episodic headaches, sweating, and tachycardia. Imaging and biopsy confirm a catecholamine-secreting paraganglioma. Genetic testing identifies a pathogenic mutation in a gene encoding a component of the mitochondrial electron transport chain. Because the affected complex is encoded entirely by nuclear DNA rather than mitochondrial DNA, her children are not at risk of inheriting this mutation via maternal mitochondrial inheritance. Which of the following complexes is most likely affected in this patient?
o: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase)
Complex II (Succinate dehydrogenase)
Complex III (Cytochrome bc1 complex)
Complex IV (Cytochrome c oxidase)
Complex V (ATP synthase)
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize paraganglioma associated with an ETC complex encoded exclusively by nuclear DNA) -> Step 2 (Identify Complex II / Succinate dehydrogenase, which has 0 subunits encoded by mtDNA)

r.A: Complex I contains subunits encoded by mitochondrial DNA and is associated with Leber hereditary optic neuropathy and Leigh syndrome.
r.C: Complex III contains cytochrome b encoded by mitochondrial DNA and is associated with sporadic myopathy.
r.D: Complex IV contains subunits encoded by mitochondrial DNA and is associated with Leigh syndrome and cardioencephalomyopathy.
r.E: Complex V contains subunits (such as ATPase 6 and 8) encoded by mitochondrial DNA and is associated with encephalomyopathy.

q.s: SLO1 & SLO3 / Slide 9: Complex II: Succinate-CoQ Reductase & Slide 23: Mitochondrial Diseases

q.v: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with severe vomiting, lethargy, and hypotonia. Laboratory evaluation reveals a profound lactic acidosis. A muscle biopsy demonstrates a defect in Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) of the electron transport chain. Which of the following redox centers is directly responsible for transferring electrons from FMN through Complex I to ubiquinone (Q) to power proton pumping?
o: Heme a and a3 centers
Copper A and Copper B centers
Iron-sulfur (Fe-S) centers
Heme c1 and bL centers
Flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD)
q.p: Step 1 (NADH donates 2 electrons to FMN in Complex I) -> Step 2 (Oxidation/reduction of iron-sulfur [FeS] centers transfers electrons to Q and powers the pumping of 4 H+ into the intermembrane space)

r.A: Heme a and a3 centers are found in Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), where they participate in reducing oxygen to water.
r.B: Copper A and Copper B (Fe-Cu) centers are located in Complex IV, not Complex I.
r.D: Heme c1 and bL centers are components of Complex III (coenzyme Q-cytochrome bc1 complex).
r.E: FAD is the prosthetic group utilized by Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) to accept electrons from succinate.

q.s: SLO1 / Slide 8: First Stop: Complex I NADH Dehydrogenase (NADH-Quinone Oxidoreductase)

q.v:
A biochemist isolates mitochondrial electron transport chain components and measures their standard reduction potentials (E0) and free energy changes as electrons pass down the chain:
  NAD+/NADH: -0.32 V
  Coenzyme Q (Ubiquinone): +0.04 V
  Cytochrome c: +0.25 V
  1/2 O2 / H2O: +0.82 V
Based on these data, which of the following best explains the directional flow of electrons from NADH to oxygen?
o: Electrons gain free energy as they move toward carriers with more positive E0
Carriers with more negative E0 have the highest affinity for low-energy electrons
Coenzyme Q has a higher affinity for electrons than Cytochrome c
Electrons lose free energy as they move toward carriers with greater E0 and higher electron affinity
Oxygen only accepts high-energy electrons directly from NADH due to its positive E0
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret table showing E0 becoming progressively more positive from NADH to O2) -> Step 2 (Conclude that a greater E0 indicates higher electron affinity, causing electrons to lose energy as they flow down the chain to O2)

r.A: Electrons lose free energy (kcal/mol) as they are passed down the electron transport chain toward oxygen.
r.B: A more negative E0 (like NAD+/NADH at -0.32 V) indicates a lower affinity for electrons and a tendency to release electrons.
r.C: Cytochrome c has a more positive E0 than Coenzyme Q, meaning Cytochrome c has a higher affinity for electrons.
r.E: Because of its high redox potential (+0.82 V), oxygen can accept low-energy electrons at the end of the chain to be reduced to water.

q.s: SLO2 / Slide 15: Biological Redox Pairs & Slide 17: Redox potential and Free energy

q.v:
A 50-year-old man is rescued from a poorly ventilated home heated by a malfunctioning kerosene stove. He presents with confusion, headache, dizziness, and tachypnea. Laboratory studies show:
  Arterial pH: 7.22
  Serum bicarbonate: 13 mEq/L
  Serum lactate: 9.4 mmol/L (elevated)
  Carboxyhemoglobin: 28% (elevated)
Which of the following best explains the mechanism driving the elevated serum lactate in this patient?
o: Direct activation of pyruvate dehydrogenase by carbon monoxide
Increased conversion of pyruvate to lactate to regenerate NAD+ for glycolysis
Uncoupling of the inner mitochondrial membrane proton gradient
Enhanced oxidation of NADH by Complex I to compensate for Complex IV blockade
Inhibition of cytosolic lactate dehydrogenase by accumulated reactive oxygen species
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize carbon monoxide poisoning inhibiting Complex IV and halting the ETC) -> Step 2 (Cells rely on glycolysis for ATP, requiring conversion of pyruvate to lactate to recycle NADH back to NAD+)

r.A: Carbon monoxide inhibits Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), not pyruvate dehydrogenase.
r.C: Uncoupling of the proton gradient is caused by agents like aspirin or 2,4-dinitrophenol, whereas CO is a direct Complex IV inhibitor.
r.D: When Complex IV is blocked by CO, electron flow halts and Complex I cannot oxidize NADH.
r.E: Lactate dehydrogenase activity is increased (not inhibited) to convert pyruvate to lactate and recycle NADH to NAD+.

q.s: SLO3 / Slide 19: Mitochondrial Poisons

q.v:
A 21-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 4 hours after ingesting a large bottle of aspirin tablets. She is diaphoretic, tachypneic, and has a core body temperature of 39.4°C (102.9°F). An arterial blood gas and metabolic panel reveal:
  pH: 7.31
  PaCO2: 24 mmHg (decreased)
  Serum bicarbonate: 12 mEq/L (decreased)
  Anion gap: 24 mEq/L (elevated)
Which of the following mitochondrial mechanisms directly accounts for this patient's fever and metabolic disturbance?
o: Blockade of the F0 proton channel of ATP synthase
Inhibition of electron transfer from ubiquinol to cytochrome c
Direct passage of protons into the matrix without ATP synthesis
Irreversible binding of salicylate to the heme-copper center of Complex IV
Impaired transport of malate across the inner mitochondrial membrane
q.p: Step 1 (Identify aspirin overdose causing respiratory alkalosis followed by fever and high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis) -> Step 2 (Link to uncoupling of the ETC, allowing H+ to re-enter the matrix directly without ATP synthesis, releasing energy as heat)

r.A: Blockade of the F0 proton channel of ATP synthase (Complex V) is the mechanism of oligomycin toxicity.
r.B: Inhibition of electron transfer at Complex III is the mechanism of antimycin A.
r.D: Binding to the heme-copper (FeCu) center of Complex IV is the mechanism of cyanide and carbon monoxide toxicity.
r.E: Impaired malate transport disrupts the malate-aspartate shuttle but does not uncouple the proton gradient to cause hyperthermia.

q.s: SLO3 / Slide 22: Electron Transport Chain: Uncouplers

q.v: A 4-month-old infant is evaluated for developmental delay, hypotonia, and persistent lactic acidosis. Biochemical testing of isolated muscle mitochondria is performed to localize the defect in oxidative phosphorylation. The addition of succinate results in normal oxygen consumption and ATP synthesis, whereas the addition of pyruvate and malate (which generate NADH) results in minimal oxygen consumption and severely reduced ATP synthesis. Which of the following toxins produces an identical biochemical profile in isolated mitochondria?
o: Oligomycin
Cyanide
Antimycin A
Rotenone
2,4-Dinitrophenol
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret data: impaired NADH oxidation with preserved succinate/FADH2 oxidation indicates a Complex I block) -> Step 2 (Match Complex I inhibition to Rotenone)

r.A: Oligomycin inhibits Complex V (ATP synthase), which would block ATP synthesis from both NADH and succinate.
r.B: Cyanide inhibits Complex IV, halting oxygen consumption and ATP synthesis from both NADH and succinate.
r.C: Antimycin A inhibits Complex III, blocking electron flow from both Complex I (NADH) and Complex II (succinate).
r.E: 2,4-Dinitrophenol is an uncoupler that increases oxygen consumption while decreasing ATP synthesis for both substrates.

q.s: SLO3 / Slide 9: Complex II & Slide 21: Disruption of Electron Transport Chain

q.v: Which of the following sets of molecules is required to regenerate reduced glutathione (GSH) from oxidized glutathione disulfide (GSSG) after the detoxification of hydrogen peroxide by glutathione peroxidase?
o: Superoxide dismutase and FADH2
Catalase and NADH
Glutathione reductase and NADPH
Cytochrome c and ubiquinol
Ferrous iron (Fe2+) and oxygen
q.p: Step 1 (Glutathione peroxidase oxidizes 2 GSH to GSSG while reducing H2O2 to 2 H2O) -> Step 2 (Glutathione reductase uses NADPH to reduce GSSG back to 2 GSH)

r.A: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide radicals into hydrogen peroxide and oxygen without using FADH2.
r.B: Catalase directly decomposes hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen without requiring glutathione or NADH.
r.D: Cytochrome c and ubiquinol are mobile electron carriers in the mitochondrial electron transport chain.
r.E: Ferrous iron (Fe2+) reacts with hydrogen peroxide in the Fenton reaction to generate toxic hydroxyl radicals.

q.s: SLO4 / Slide 32: Enzyme Mechanisms Protect Against High Levels of ROS

q.v: A 58-year-old man with hereditary hemochromatosis develops progressive liver injury due to severe intracellular iron overload. Hepatocyte biopsy demonstrates extensive peroxidative damage to membrane lipids, enzyme denaturation, and nucleic acid mutations, leading to cell lysis. Elevated intracellular levels of ferrous iron (Fe2+) react directly with which of the following molecules via the Fenton reaction to generate the highly toxic hydroxyl radical (•OH)?
o: Superoxide anion (O2•−)
Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)
Hypochlorous acid (HOCl)
Molecular oxygen (O2)
Oxidized glutathione (GSSG)
q.p: Step 1 (Identify iron-mediated cellular damage via the Fenton reaction) -> Step 2 (Fe2+ reacts with H2O2 to produce Fe3+, OH-, and the highly reactive hydroxyl radical •OH)

r.A: Superoxide anion reacts with ferric iron (Fe3+) to regenerate ferrous iron (Fe2+) and O2, rather than serving as the direct substrate oxidized by Fe2+ in the Fenton reaction.
r.C: Hypochlorous acid is a non-radical reactive oxygen species, not the substrate of the Fenton reaction.
r.D: Molecular oxygen accepts a single electron during respiration (e.g., from CoQ) to form superoxide anion.
r.E: Oxidized glutathione (GSSG) is reduced by glutathione reductase and does not react with Fe2+ to form hydroxyl radicals.

q.s: SLO4 / Slide 27: Free Radicals (The Fenton Reaction) & Slide 31: Inactivation of Free Radicals Must Be Controlled

add.cloze: The first and final steps of heme synthesis occur in the {{c1::mitochondria}}, while the intermediate steps occur in the {{c2::cytosol}}
add.extra: First: ALA synthase (glycine + succinyl-CoA); final: ferrochelatase (Fe2+ into protoporphyrin IX)

add.cloze: Drugs that induce cytochrome P450 {{c1::increase hepatic heme demand}}, accelerating heme synthesis (via ALA synthase) and precipitating acute porphyria attacks
add.extra: Treat attacks with hemin and glucose, which inhibit ALA synthase

add.cloze: The clinical manifestations of the porphyrias are caused by {{c1::accumulation of the specific intermediates upstream of the deficient enzyme}}
add.extra: Early intermediates (ALA, PBG) → neurovisceral; porphyrins → photosensitivity

add.cloze: Porphyrias with neurovisceral symptoms such as abdominal pain and neuropathy are generally classified as {{c1::hepatic}} porphyrias
add.extra: e.g., acute intermittent porphyria; erythropoietic porphyrias (CEP, EPP) present with photosensitivity

add.cloze: Congenital erythropoietic porphyria (Günther disease) is due to {{c1::uroporphyrinogen III synthase}} deficiency and presents with {{c2::reddish teeth that fluoresce under UV light}} and severe blistering photosensitivity
add.extra: Also hemolytic anemia and skin scarring; early onset

add.cloze: {{c1::Variegate porphyria}} (protoporphyrinogen oxidase deficiency) presents with both blistering photosensitivity and acute neurovisceral attacks
add.extra: Generally milder than acute intermittent porphyria

add.cloze: Erythropoietic protoporphyria (ferrochelatase deficiency) presents with {{c1::painful, non-blistering}} photosensitivity
add.extra: Childhood onset; protoporphyrin in the liver → cholestasis, gallstones

add.cloze: Unconjugated bilirubin is taken up from the blood into hepatocytes by {{c1::OATP transporters (SLCO1B1 and SLCO1B3)}}
add.extra: They also take back conjugated bilirubin that leaks into the blood (defective in Rotor syndrome)

add.cloze: Conjugated bilirubin is excreted into the bile by the transporter {{c1::MRP2 (ABCC2)}}
add.extra: Deficient in Dubin-Johnson syndrome (black liver)

add.cloze: Rotor syndrome causes increased conjugated bilirubin due to defective {{c1::OATP (organic anion transport protein)}} function
add.extra: Milder than Dubin-Johnson and no black liver

add.cloze: Newborns often develop transient unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia because of {{c1::increased bilirubin production}} combined with {{c2::low UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity and immature transport}}
add.extra: Peaks around day 3-5; severe cases risk kernicterus

q.v: A 3-year-old boy living in an older home with peeling paint is evaluated for developmental delay, fatigue, and abdominal pain. Laboratory testing reveals elevated blood lead levels, increased urinary aminolevulinic acid (ALA), and elevated erythrocyte protoporphyrin. The toxic agent responsible for this child's condition directly inhibits two specific enzymes in the heme biosynthetic pathway. In which respective subcellular compartments do these two inhibited enzymatic reactions normally occur?
o: Both occur in the mitochondria
Both occur in the cytoplasm
First in the mitochondria, second in the cytoplasm
First in the cytoplasm, second in the mitochondria
First in the endoplasmic reticulum, second in the mitochondria
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that lead poisoning inhibits aminolevulinic acid dehydratase and ferrochelatase) -> Step 2 (Localize aminolevulinic acid dehydratase to the cytoplasm and ferrochelatase to the mitochondria).

r.A: While aminolevulinic acid synthase and ferrochelatase are mitochondrial, the first enzyme inhibited by lead (ALA dehydratase) is located in the cytoplasm.
r.B: Although intermediate steps like ALA dehydratase and uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase occur in the cytoplasm, the final step catalyzed by ferrochelatase occurs in the mitochondria.
r.C: This reverses the compartments; the initial rate-limiting step (ALA synthase) is mitochondrial, but lead inhibits the cytoplasmic ALA dehydratase first and mitochondrial ferrochelatase last.
r.E: The endoplasmic reticulum is not a primary compartment depicted in the heme biosynthetic pathway diagram on the lecture slides.

q.s: Slide 4: Heme Biosynthesis (SLO1)

q.v: A 29-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital with acute onset of severe, diffuse abdominal pain, tachycardia, and motor weakness that began shortly after starting a new anticonvulsant medication. Urine collected in a specimen cup turns a dark 'port-wine' color upon standing. The physician initiates intravenous therapy with glucose and a ferric (+3) iron-containing porphyrin derivative. By what direct cellular mechanism does this specific iron-containing compound alleviate her acute attack?
o: It activates uroporphyrinogen III synthase to clear accumulated hydroxymethylbilane
It inhibits the transcription and mitochondrial transport of aminolevulinic acid synthase
It chelates excess ferrous (+2) iron in the mitochondrial matrix to halt protoporphyrin conversion
It stimulates hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase to conjugate neurotoxic porphyrinogens
It competitively blocks organic anion transporting polypeptides (OATPs) on the sinusoidal membrane
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the treatment of Acute Intermittent Porphyria with hemin, the +3 oxidation state of heme) -> Step 2 (Recognize that free heme/hemin in the cytosol inhibits aminolevulinic acid synthase transcription and transport).

r.A: Uroporphyrinogen III synthase is deficient in Congenital Erythropoietic Porphyria and is not the regulatory target of hemin therapy.
r.C: Hemin itself contains ferric (+3) iron and acts via negative feedback on ALA synthase rather than chelating mitochondrial ferrous (+2) iron.
r.D: UDP-glucuronosyltransferase conjugates bilirubin in the heme degradation pathway, not porphyrin precursors in heme synthesis.
r.E: OATPs transport bilirubin across the hepatocyte membrane and are unrelated to the feedback regulation of heme biosynthesis.

q.s: Slide 4: Heme Biosynthesis & Slide 7: Acute Intermittent Porphyria (SLO1, SLO2)

q.v: A 2-year-old child is brought to the dermatology clinic for evaluation of severe, mutilating skin blisters and scarring on sun-exposed areas that began in early infancy. Physical examination reveals conjunctival pallor, splenomegaly, and reddish-brown discoloration of the primary teeth that fluoresce brightly under ultraviolet light. Laboratory studies confirm a hemolytic anemia. A genetic defect in which of the following biochemical conversions is responsible for this patient's disorder?
o: Condensation of glycine and succinyl-CoA to aminolevulinic acid
Conversion of porphobilinogen to hydroxymethylbilane
Cyclization of hydroxymethylbilane to uroporphyrinogen III
Decarboxylation of uroporphyrinogen III to coproporphyrinogen III
Oxidation of protoporphyrinogen IX to protoporphyrin IX
q.p: Step 1 (Diagnose Congenital Erythropoietic Porphyria / Günther disease based on early-onset severe blistering photosensitivity, hemolytic anemia, and red fluorescent teeth) -> Step 2 (Identify the defective enzyme as uroporphyrinogen III synthase, which converts hydroxymethylbilane to uroporphyrinogen III).

r.A: Condensation of glycine and succinyl-CoA is catalyzed by ALA synthase, which is defective in X-linked sideroblastic anemia.
r.B: Conversion of porphobilinogen to hydroxymethylbilane is catalyzed by porphobilinogen deaminase, which is deficient in Acute Intermittent Porphyria.
r.D: Decarboxylation of uroporphyrinogen III is catalyzed by uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase, which is deficient in Porphyria Cutanea Tarda.
r.E: Oxidation of protoporphyrinogen IX is catalyzed by protoporphyrinogen oxidase, which is deficient in Variegate Porphyria.

q.s: Slide 8: CEP, PCT, VP & Slide 10-11: Porphyria Enzyme Deficiencies (SLO2)

q.v: A 34-year-old woman presents with acute abdominal pain, nausea, and progressive flaccid paralysis of her lower extremities after consuming alcohol at a wedding. On physical examination, she is also noted to have chronic fluid-filled vesicles and healed scars on the dorsum of both hands, which she states worsen every summer. Which of the following enzymes is defective in this patient?
o: Porphobilinogen deaminase
Uroporphyrinogen III synthase
Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase
Protoporphyrinogen oxidase
Ferrochelatase
q.p: Step 1 (Identify Variegate Porphyria from the mixed clinical presentation of acute neurovisceral attacks with flaccid paralysis plus chronic blistering photosensitivity) -> Step 2 (Match Variegate Porphyria to a deficiency in mitochondrial protoporphyrinogen oxidase).

r.A: Porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency causes Acute Intermittent Porphyria, which presents with neurovisceral symptoms but strictly no cutaneous photosensitivity.
r.B: Uroporphyrinogen III synthase deficiency causes Congenital Erythropoietic Porphyria, which features severe cutaneous blistering and hemolytic anemia without neurovisceral attacks.
r.C: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency causes Porphyria Cutanea Tarda, presenting with isolated chronic blistering photosensitivity and elevated liver enzymes.
r.E: Ferrochelatase deficiency causes Erythropoietic Protoporphyria, which presents with painful non-blistering photosensitivity and gallstones without neurovisceral attacks.

q.s: Slide 8: CEP, PCT, VP & Slide 10-11: Porphyria Summary Table (SLO2)

q.v: A 50-year-old man undergoes splenectomy following blunt abdominal trauma. In a healthy individual, senescent red blood cells are normally phagocytosed by macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system, where the porphyrin ring of heme is enzymatically cleaved to initiate degradation. Which of the following pairs of molecules is directly released during this initial ring-opening enzymatic reaction, prior to the action of biliverdin reductase?
o: Unconjugated bilirubin and NADP+
Biliverdin, carbon monoxide (CO), and ferrous iron (Fe2+)
Urobilinogen and stercobilin
Bilirubin diglucuronide and albumin
Protoporphyrin IX and ferric iron (Fe3+)
q.p: Step 1 (Locate the initial step of heme degradation in the reticuloendothelial system catalyzed by heme oxygenase) -> Step 2 (Identify the direct reaction products shown on the pathway diagram: biliverdin, CO, and Fe2+).

r.A: Unconjugated bilirubin and NADP+ are the products of the second step, catalyzed by biliverdin reductase using NADPH.
r.C: Urobilinogen and stercobilin are downstream intestinal metabolites formed by gut bacteria after biliary excretion of conjugated bilirubin.
r.D: Bilirubin diglucuronide is formed inside hepatocytes by UDP-glucuronosyltransferase, not in the reticuloendothelial system.
r.E: Protoporphyrin IX is a precursor in heme synthesis rather than a ring-opened degradation product.

q.s: Slide 13: Big Picture: the Porphyrin Ring of Heme is Opened for Heme Degradation (SLO3)

q.v: A 62-year-old woman is prescribed a prolonged course of broad-spectrum oral antibiotics that completely eradicate her normal intestinal bacterial flora. Assuming her hepatic conjugation and biliary tree remain completely intact, how will this bacterial depletion directly alter the downstream fate of bilirubin metabolites in her gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts?
o: Increased conversion of conjugated bilirubin to urobilinogen in the terminal ileum
Decreased fecal excretion of stercobilin and loss of the normal brown color of stool
Increased renal excretion of urobilin giving the urine a dark port-wine color
Complete cessation of MRP2-mediated transport into the biliary canaliculi
Direct accumulation of biliverdin in the systemic bloodstream
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the role of gut bacteria in converting conjugated bilirubin into urobilinogen in the intestine) -> Step 2 (Deduce that without gut bacteria, urobilinogen cannot be formed, eliminating the 80% conversion to fecal stercobilin that gives stool its brown color).

r.A: Gut bacteria are required to convert conjugated bilirubin into urobilinogen, so antibiotic eradication will decrease, not increase, urobilinogen formation.
r.C: Absence of urobilinogen decreases renal urobilin excretion (which normally gives urine a yellow color); port-wine urine is seen in Acute Intermittent Porphyria.
r.D: MRP2 transports conjugated bilirubin from hepatocytes into biliary canaliculi upstream of the gut and does not depend on gut bacteria.
r.E: Biliverdin is reduced to unconjugated bilirubin in the reticuloendothelial system long before bilirubin reaches the gut.

q.s: Slide 14: Bilirubin Enterohepatic Circulation and Excretion (SLO3)

q.v: A 30-year-old asymptomatic woman is found to have an elevated serum conjugated bilirubin level on routine blood work. Genetic sequencing reveals a loss-of-function mutation in the SLCO1B1 and SLCO1B3 genes encoding organic anion transporting polypeptides (OATP / mOAT), confirming a diagnosis of Rotor syndrome. Which of the following physiological mechanisms best explains why her defect produces a predominantly conjugated, rather than unconjugated, hyperbilirubinemia?
o: OATP is the primary canalicular pump that exports conjugated bilirubin directly into bile
Conjugated bilirubin normally cycles back into the sinusoidal blood and requires OATP for hepatocyte reuptake and retention
Mutated OATP proteins abnormally acquire UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity within the plasma
OATP deficiency stimulates MRP2 to pump unconjugated bilirubin backward into the bloodstream
Albumin irreversibly binds unconjugated bilirubin when OATP is absent, preventing its measurement in serum
q.p: Step 1 (Identify Rotor syndrome as a mutation in mOAT / OATP encoded by SLCO1B1/SLCO1B3) -> Step 2 (Apply the slide mechanism that OATP is required for the retention and reuptake of conjugated bilirubin that leaks/cycles back into the blood after conjugation).

r.A: MRP2 (ABCC), not OATP, is the canalicular transporter responsible for exporting conjugated bilirubin into the biliary canaliculi.
r.C: OATPs are membrane transport proteins and do not possess enzymatic glucuronosyltransferase activity.
r.D: MRP2 transports conjugated bilirubin out into the bile canaliculi and is defective in Dubin-Johnson syndrome.
r.E: Unconjugated bilirubin bound to albumin is readily measured as indirect bilirubin and is not masked by OATP mutations.

q.s: Slide 15: Hepatocyte Transporters & Slide 17-18: Heritable Forms of Hyperbilirubinemia (SLO3, SLO4)

q.v: A 25-year-old man is evaluated for mild, persistent scleral icterus. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates a serum total bilirubin of 4.2 mg/dL and a direct (conjugated) bilirubin of 3.6 mg/dL, with normal serum transaminases. A liver biopsy reveals gross dark pigmentation of the hepatic parenchyma. The accumulation of metabolites from which of the following substances is responsible for the characteristic gross appearance of this patient's liver?
o: Ferrous iron (Fe2+)
Uroporphyrin I
Epinephrine
Biliverdin
Stercobilin
q.p: Step 1 (Diagnose Dubin-Johnson syndrome based on isolated conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and a black liver on biopsy due to an MRP2 defect) -> Step 2 (Identify from the disorder notes that the black liver pigmentation results from epinephrine metabolites).

r.A: Iron accumulation is not the cause of the dark liver pigment in Dubin-Johnson syndrome.
r.B: Uroporphyrin I accumulates in Congenital Erythropoietic Porphyria, causing red fluorescent teeth rather than a black liver.
r.D: Biliverdin is a green pigment intermediate in macrophages and does not cause the black liver of Dubin-Johnson syndrome.
r.E: Stercobilin is an intestinal bacterial metabolite that gives feces its brown color.

q.s: Slide 17-18: Heritable Forms of Hyperbilirubinemia Table (SLO4)

q.v: A 5-day-old full-term male neonate is brought to the emergency department due to lethargy, poor feeding, and high-pitched crying. Laboratory analysis reveals a serum total bilirubin of 21 mg/dL (predominantly unconjugated). The infant subsequently develops severe neurological deficits, and neuroimaging confirms bilirubin deposition in specific brain regions. Which of the following underlying enzymatic defects, combined with transient opening of the neonatal blood-brain barrier, is responsible for this condition?
o: Absence or severe deficiency of UDP-glucuronosyltransferase
Overactivity of reticuloendothelial biliverdin reductase
Complete deficiency of canalicular MRP2 transporter
Autoimmune destruction of sinusoidal OATP transporters
Inhibition of mitochondrial ferrochelatase
q.p: Step 1 (Identify kernicterus presenting at 3-6 days postnatal with unconjugated bilirubin >= 20 mg/dL and brain staining) -> Step 2 (Link kernicterus and Crigler-Najjar Type I to a severe defect/absence of UDP-glucuronosyltransferase).

r.B: Increased biliverdin reductase activity is not the primary enzymatic defect underlying kernicterus.
r.C: MRP2 deficiency causes Dubin-Johnson syndrome, which results in benign conjugated hyperbilirubinemia rather than kernicterus.
r.D: OATP defects cause Rotor syndrome, a mild conjugated hyperbilirubinemia that does not cross the blood-brain barrier to cause kernicterus.
r.E: Ferrochelatase deficiency causes Erythropoietic Protoporphyria and does not cause severe neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

q.s: Slide 18: Heritable Hyperbilirubinemia Table & Slide 19: Kernicterus (SLO4)

q.v: A 3-day-old neonate in the intensive care unit has a baseline serum unconjugated bilirubin of 5.5 mg/dL, consistent with normal physiologic jaundice. Shortly after receiving an intravenous medication for a suspected infection, the infant's free unconjugated bilirubin levels rise sharply, placing the infant at acute risk for neurotoxicity. By what mechanism did the administered medication most likely precipitate this sudden increase in free unconjugated bilirubin?
o: Direct competitive inhibition of sinusoidal OATP1B1 uptake
Displacement of unconjugated bilirubin from plasma albumin binding sites
Induction of hepatic cytochrome P450 leading to accelerated RBC lysis
Cleavage of bilirubin diglucuronide back into unconjugated bilirubin inside the bile canaliculi
Downregulation of intracellular ligandin (GST) synthesis in hepatocytes
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize drug-induced unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia in a neonate) -> Step 2 (Identify the mechanism from Slide 20: the drug displaces bilirubin from serum albumin, leading to increased unconjugated serum bilirubin).

r.A: The lecture specifically illustrates that drug-induced unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia acts by displacing bilirubin from serum albumin rather than blocking OATP.
r.C: Hepatic cytochrome P450 induction depletes free heme in hepatocytes to trigger porphyria attacks, not red blood cell lysis.
r.D: Drugs that cause unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia in this pathway act on plasma albumin, not by deconjugating bilirubin diglucuronide in the bile.
r.E: While ligandin (GST) binds bilirubin intracellularly, the slide mechanism for drug-induced hyperbilirubinemia specifically targets extracellular serum albumin.

q.s: Slide 16: Neonatal Jaundice & Slide 20: Drug Induced Hyperbilirubinemia (SLO3, SLO4)

q.v: A 10-year-old boy is brought to his pediatrician for evaluation of chronic fatigue and pallor. Bone marrow biopsy reveals ringed sideroblasts, and genetic testing confirms an X-linked sideroblastic anemia caused by a defect in the rate-limiting enzyme of heme synthesis. Which of the following best describes the substrates and subcellular location of the reaction catalyzed by this enzyme?
o: Glycine and succinyl-CoA in the mitochondria
Glycine and acetyl-CoA in the cytoplasm
Aminolevulinic acid and iron in the mitochondria
Porphobilinogen and glycine in the cytoplasm
Protoporphyrin IX and ferrous iron in the mitochondria
q.p: Step 1 (X-linked sideroblastic anemia results from a defect in aminolevulinic acid synthase, the rate-limiting enzyme of heme synthesis) -> Step 2 (ALA synthase condenses glycine and succinyl-CoA in the mitochondria using vitamin B6 as a cofactor)

r.B: Heme synthesis uses succinyl-CoA rather than acetyl-CoA, and the initial rate-limiting reaction takes place in the mitochondria rather than the cytoplasm.
r.C: Aminolevulinic acid is the product of the first reaction in the mitochondria, whereas iron is incorporated during the final step of the pathway.
r.D: Porphobilinogen is an intermediate processed in the cytoplasm, not an initial substrate for the mitochondrial rate-limiting step.
r.E: The combination of protoporphyrin IX and ferrous iron is the final step of heme synthesis catalyzed by ferrochelatase, not the rate-limiting step.

q.s: SLO1, Slide 4: Heme Biosynthesis

q.v: Free cytosolic heme regulates its own synthesis in the liver by acting on the rate-limiting enzyme of the pathway. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this feedback regulation?
o: Allosteric activation of ferrochelatase
Inhibition of aminolevulinic acid synthase transcription and mitochondrial transport
Stimulation of porphobilinogen deaminase degradation
Competitive inhibition of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase
Activation of hepatic cytochrome P450 heme oxygenase
q.p: Step 1 (Accumulation of free heme in the hepatic cytosol signals sufficient heme levels) -> Step 2 (Free heme inhibits both the transcription and mitochondrial transport of aminolevulinic acid synthase, decreasing heme synthesis)

r.A: Ferrochelatase catalyzes the final step of heme synthesis and is inhibited by lead, not allosterically activated by free heme to regulate pathway flux.
r.C: Porphobilinogen deaminase is deficient in acute intermittent porphyria and is not the target of feedback regulation by free heme.
r.D: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase is a cytoplasmic enzyme deficient in porphyria cutanea tarda and is not regulated by free heme.
r.E: Heme regulates its anabolism by suppressing ALA synthase rather than activating cytochrome P450 degradation.

q.s: SLO1, Slide 4: Heme Biosynthesis

q.v: A 24-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with severe diffuse abdominal pain, anxiety, and tachycardia three days after starting a strict low-carbohydrate, low-calorie diet. Physical examination shows no cutaneous blisters or skin lesions, and her urine is a dark port-wine color. Laboratory analysis of her urine and plasma would most likely show elevated levels of which of the following intermediates?
o: Uroporphyrinogen III and coproporphyrinogen III
Protoporphyrin IX and ferrous iron
Aminolevulinic acid and porphobilinogen
Hydroxymethylbilane and uroporphyrinogen I
Biliverdin and unconjugated bilirubin
q.p: Step 1 (Severe abdominal pain, neuropsychiatric symptoms, port-wine urine, and lack of skin findings after fasting indicate Acute Intermittent Porphyria caused by porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency) -> Step 2 (Blockade at porphobilinogen deaminase coupled with fasting-induced ALA synthase upregulation causes upstream accumulation of aminolevulinic acid and porphobilinogen)

r.A: Uroporphyrinogen III and coproporphyrinogen III are downstream of porphobilinogen deaminase and do not accumulate in acute intermittent porphyria.
r.B: Protoporphyrin IX accumulates when ferrochelatase is deficient or inhibited, which causes erythropoietic protoporphyria or lead poisoning rather than acute intermittent porphyria.
r.D: Hydroxymethylbilane is the product of porphobilinogen deaminase, so its synthesis is decreased rather than increased in this disorder.
r.E: Biliverdin and unconjugated bilirubin are products of heme degradation, not intermediates of heme biosynthesis.

q.s: SLO2, Slide 7: Acute Intermittent Porphyria

q.v:
A 52-year-old man presents to the dermatology clinic with chronic fluid-filled blisters and scarring on the backs of his hands that worsen after sun exposure. He has no history of acute abdominal pain, motor weakness, or psychiatric symptoms. Laboratory evaluation is shown below:
Serum AST: 88 U/L
Serum ALT: 96 U/L
Urine uroporphyrin: markedly elevated
Urine porphobilinogen: normal
Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this patient?
o: Porphobilinogen deaminase
Uroporphyrinogen III synthase
Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase
Protoporphyrinogen oxidase
Ferrochelatase
q.p: Step 1 (Adult-onset chronic blistering photosensitivity with elevated liver enzymes and absence of neurovisceral attacks indicates Porphyria Cutanea Tarda) -> Step 2 (Porphyria Cutanea Tarda is caused by a deficiency in cytoplasmic uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase)

r.A: Porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency causes acute intermittent porphyria, which presents with neurovisceral attacks and no cutaneous photosensitivity.
r.B: Uroporphyrinogen III synthase deficiency causes congenital erythropoietic porphyria, which presents in early childhood with severe hemolytic anemia and reddish fluorescent teeth.
r.D: Protoporphyrinogen oxidase deficiency causes variegate porphyria, which presents with both blistering photosensitivity and acute neurovisceral attacks.
r.E: Ferrochelatase deficiency causes erythropoietic protoporphyria, which presents in childhood with painful, non-blistering photosensitivity.

q.s: SLO2, Slide 11: Porphyria Summary Table

q.v: A 9-year-old girl is brought to the clinic because she develops severe burning, stinging pain and redness on her face and arms shortly after playing outside in the sun. Physical examination of sun-exposed skin reveals mild erythema without blisters or scarring, and an abdominal ultrasound demonstrates small gallstones. A deficiency in the enzyme responsible for this patient's disorder directly prevents the incorporation of which of the following into protoporphyrin IX?
o: Succinyl-CoA
Pyridoxal phosphate
Ferrous iron (Fe2+)
Ferric iron (Fe3+)
Uridine diphosphate glucuronic acid
q.p: Step 1 (Childhood-onset painful, non-blistering photosensitivity and gallstones indicate Erythropoietic Protoporphyria caused by ferrochelatase deficiency) -> Step 2 (Ferrochelatase catalyzes the final mitochondrial step of heme synthesis by inserting ferrous iron [Fe2+] into protoporphyrin IX)

r.A: Succinyl-CoA is condensed with glycine in the first step of heme synthesis by aminolevulinic acid synthase.
r.B: Pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) is the cofactor for aminolevulinic acid synthase, not the substrate inserted into protoporphyrin IX.
r.D: Hemin contains ferric iron (+3), whereas heme synthesized by ferrochelatase incorporates ferrous iron (+2).
r.E: Uridine diphosphate glucuronic acid is used by UDP-glucuronosyltransferase to conjugate bilirubin during heme degradation.

q.s: SLO2, Slide 4 and Slide 9: Erythropoietic Protoporphyria

q.v: In the normal degradation and elimination of heme, which of the following correctly pairs the tetrapyrrole breakdown product with the compartment or excretion route where it gives rise to its characteristic color?
o: Biliverdin — excreted in feces to give stool its brown color
Unconjugated bilirubin — filtered by the kidney to give urine its yellow color
Urobilinogen — bound to albumin in the bloodstream
Stercobilin — excreted in feces to give stool its brown color
Urobilin — secreted directly by MRP2 into the biliary canaliculi
q.p: Step 1 (Conjugated bilirubin is secreted into the bile and converted by gut bacteria into urobilinogen) -> Step 2 (Approximately 80% of urobilinogen is oxidized and excreted in the feces as stercobilin, which gives stool its brown color)

r.A: Biliverdin is an intermediate formed in the reticuloendothelial system and is rapidly reduced to unconjugated bilirubin rather than excreted in feces.
r.B: Unconjugated bilirubin is water-insoluble and tightly bound to albumin in the blood, so it cannot be filtered by the kidney into the urine.
r.C: Urobilinogen is formed by bacteria in the gut lumen and undergoes enterohepatic circulation, whereas unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin in the blood.
r.E: Urobilin is oxidized from reabsorbed urobilinogen and excreted by the kidney to give urine its yellow color, whereas MRP2 secretes conjugated bilirubin into bile.

q.s: SLO3, Slide 13 and Slide 14: Heme Degradation

q.v:
A 21-year-old man presents to the student health clinic after noticing yellow discoloration of his sclerae following a two-day viral gastroenteritis during which he consumed only clear liquids. Physical examination is otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory results are shown below:
Total bilirubin: 3.1 mg/dL
Direct (conjugated) bilirubin: 0.3 mg/dL
Indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin: 2.8 mg/dL
Serum AST: 22 U/L
Serum ALT: 19 U/L
Which of the following best describes the underlying biochemical defect in this patient?
o: Complete absence of hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity
Reduction of hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity to approximately 30% of normal
Defective MRP2-mediated transport of conjugated bilirubin into biliary canaliculi
Impaired OATP-mediated hepatic reuptake of conjugated bilirubin from the blood
Drug-induced displacement of unconjugated bilirubin from serum albumin
q.p: Step 1 (Mild, intermittent unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia triggered by fasting or illness with normal liver enzymes indicates Gilbert syndrome) -> Step 2 (Gilbert syndrome is caused by a mutation in UDP-glucuronosyltransferase that reduces enzyme activity to ~30% of normal)

r.A: Complete absence of hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity causes Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I, a severe life-threatening neonatal condition.
r.C: Defective MRP2 transport causes Dubin-Johnson syndrome, which presents with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and a black liver.
r.D: Impaired OATP-mediated reuptake of conjugated bilirubin causes Rotor syndrome, which presents with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
r.E: Displacement of unconjugated bilirubin from albumin is the mechanism of drug-induced hyperbilirubinemia, not a heritable mild hyperbilirubinemia triggered by fasting.

q.s: SLO4, Slide 17 and Slide 18: Heritable Forms of Hyperbilirubinemia

q.v:
A 4-day-old full-term infant is brought to the emergency department with extreme lethargy, poor feeding, and abnormal muscle tone. The infant was born at home and received no routine postnatal follow-up. Laboratory evaluation is shown below:
Total serum bilirubin: 23.5 mg/dL
Direct (conjugated) bilirubin: 0.4 mg/dL
Indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin: 23.1 mg/dL
Genetic testing confirms a homozygous nonsense mutation resulting in complete absence of the affected hepatic enzyme. Which of the following disorders is the most likely cause of this infant's presentation?
o: Gilbert syndrome
Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I
Crigler-Najjar syndrome type II
Rotor syndrome
Dubin-Johnson syndrome
q.p: Step 1 (Severe neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia >20 mg/dL presenting at 3-6 days of life with neurologic symptoms of kernicterus indicates a severe conjugation defect) -> Step 2 (Complete absence of UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity defines Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I)

r.A: Gilbert syndrome is a mild disorder with ~30% residual UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity that does not cause severe neonatal hyperbilirubinemia or kernicterus.
r.C: Crigler-Najjar syndrome type II is an intermediate disorder in which UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity is reduced to ~10% rather than completely absent.
r.D: Rotor syndrome is caused by a defect in mOAT proteins and results in a benign conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
r.E: Dubin-Johnson syndrome is caused by a defect in the MRP2 transporter and results in conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

q.s: SLO4, Slide 18 and Slide 19: Heritable Hyperbilirubinemia and Kernicterus

q.v: A 3-day-old full-term newborn is noted to have mild yellow discoloration of the skin and sclerae during a routine nursery examination. The infant is feeding well and is otherwise healthy. Total serum bilirubin is 5.6 mg/dL (predominantly unconjugated), which resolves spontaneously by day 8 of life. Which of the following best explains this transient finding?
o: Increased red blood cell hemolysis and decreased synthesis of bilirubin diglucuronides
Complete genetic absence of hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase
Autoimmune destruction of canalicular MRP2 transporters
Inhibition of reticuloendothelial biliverdin reductase
Bacterial overgrowth in the neonatal terminal ileum and colon
q.p: Step 1 (Bilirubin peaking at 5-6 mg/dL around 72 hours of life and resolving by 7-10 days represents normal physiologic neonatal jaundice) -> Step 2 (Physiologic jaundice is caused by increased bilirubin production from RBC hemolysis combined with an immature liver that has decreased UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity and decreased synthesis of bilirubin diglucuronides)

r.B: Complete genetic absence of UDP-glucuronosyltransferase causes Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I, which leads to persistent, severe hyperbilirubinemia and kernicterus.
r.C: Defects in canalicular MRP2 transporters cause conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (Dubin-Johnson syndrome), whereas physiologic neonatal jaundice is unconjugated.
r.D: Inhibition of biliverdin reductase would prevent the formation of unconjugated bilirubin rather than cause its elevation.
r.E: Neonates have lower gut bacterial flora, and bacterial conversion of bilirubin occurs downstream of hepatic conjugation.

q.s: SLO4, Slide 16: Many Neonates Exhibit a Transient Jaundice

q.v: A 31-year-old woman with a known history of acute intermittent porphyria is hospitalized with an acute attack of severe abdominal pain and peripheral motor neuropathy. In addition to discontinuing offending medications, the physician administers intravenous glucose and hemin. Which of the following best explains the therapeutic effect of this treatment?
o: Activation of porphobilinogen deaminase to clear accumulated porphobilinogen
Induction of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes to accelerate heme turnover
Repression of hepatic aminolevulinic acid synthase to decrease synthesis of toxic intermediates
Stimulation of canalicular MRP2 transporters to increase biliary porphyrin excretion
Chelation of ferrous iron to prevent protoporphyrin IX formation
q.p: Step 1 (Acute intermittent porphyria attacks are driven by upregulation of hepatic ALA synthase behind a partial block in porphobilinogen deaminase) -> Step 2 (Glucose and hemin [Fe3+ heme] inhibit hepatic ALA synthase transcription and mitochondrial transport, halting the overproduction and accumulation of toxic upstream intermediates)

r.A: Glucose and hemin do not restore or activate the mutated porphobilinogen deaminase enzyme.
r.B: Induction of hepatic cytochrome P450 consumes free heme, which removes feedback inhibition on ALA synthase and precipitates rather than treats porphyria attacks.
r.D: MRP2 transports conjugated bilirubin into bile canaliculi and is not the target of glucose or hemin therapy in acute intermittent porphyria.
r.E: Chelating iron would reduce heme synthesis and further derepress ALA synthase, worsening the acute porphyria attack.

q.s: SLO1 & SLO2, Slide 4 and Slide 7: Acute Intermittent Porphyria

Sister chromatids separate during {{c1::anaphase}} of mitosis
add.extra: (and anaphase II of meiosis)

add.cloze: After completing meiosis I and II, a human cell is {{c1::1N, 1C}} (23 chromosomes, 23 chromatids)
add.extra: After meiosis I: 1N, 2C (23 chromosomes, 46 chromatids)

add.cloze: In meiosis I, the {{c1::separation of homologous chromosomes}} reduces the chromosome number from 2N to 1N
add.extra: Meiosis II separates sister chromatids, like mitosis

add.cloze: Isodisomy can unmask {{c1::autosomal recessive}} disorders by providing two identical copies of a mutant allele
add.extra: Isodisomy = meiosis II error; heterodisomy = meiosis I error

add.cloze: The G2/M checkpoint ensures that {{c1::DNA replication is complete}} and that {{c2::no double-stranded DNA breaks remain}}
The M-phase (spindle assembly) checkpoint confirms that {{c1::chromosomes are properly aligned}} before separation, preventing {{c2::aneuploidy}}
Cyclin–CDK pairs: early G1 = {{c1::cyclin D – CDK4/6}}; G1/S transition = {{c2::cyclin E – CDK2}}; M phase = {{c3::cyclin B – CDK1}}
add.extra: Mnemonic: "46 Dogs 2 Entertain ½ Alien (1) Baby" — CDK4/6–D, CDK2–E, CDK1/2–A (S and G2), CDK1–B

add.cloze: {{c1::Cyclin D – CDK4/6}} begins phosphorylating Rb in early G1; {{c2::cyclin E – CDK2}} hyperphosphorylates Rb so it releases E2F
add.extra: Hypophosphorylated Rb binds E2F and blocks S-phase gene transcription

add.cloze: p53 (TP53) is called the "{{c1::guardian of the genome}}" because it senses DNA damage
add.extra: Halts the cell cycle for repair (via p21), or triggers apoptosis if the damage is irreparable; mutated in ~half of cancers

add.cloze: When it detects DNA damage, p53 halts the G1/S transition by inducing transcription of {{c1::p21}}, which inhibits {{c2::CDK2}}
add.extra: Per the lecture. Some AnKing cards describe p53 as blocking CDK4; p16 is the inhibitor of CDK4/6.

add.cloze: The cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor {{c1::p16}} inhibits {{c2::CDK4/6}}, reinforcing Rb-mediated control of G1/S
add.extra: Activated by stress and DNA damage

add.cloze: {{c1::ATM}} detects double-stranded DNA breaks and coordinates the stabilization of {{c2::p53}}
add.extra: Loss of ATM → ataxia-telangiectasia
