q.v: A 42-year-old woman presents for genetic counseling regarding an increased risk of trisomic pregnancy due to advanced maternal age. The counselor explains that human oocytes remain suspended in prophase I for decades until ovulation, increasing the likelihood of chromosomal segregation errors during Meiosis I. Age-related degradation of which of the following structural components directly predisposes this patient's oocytes to nondisjunction?
o: Cohesin proteins holding sister chromatids together
E2F transcription factors bound to DNA
Cyclin D-CDK4 complexes in the cytoplasm
Barr bodies within the nuclear periphery
ATM proteins monitoring double-stranded DNA
q.p: Step 1 (Advanced maternal age increases the risk of meiotic nondisjunction and aneuploidy) -> Step 2 (This occurs because Cohesin proteins that hold sister chromatids together in prophase I start to break down over time).

r.B: E2F transcription factors regulate the expression of S-phase DNA replication proteins rather than physically holding sister chromatids together in prophase I.
r.C: Cyclin D-CDK4 complexes regulate early G1 progression by phosphorylating Rb, not by maintaining sister chromatid cohesion during meiotic arrest.
r.D: Barr bodies represent inactivated X chromosomes in somatic cells and do not maintain physical linkage between sister chromatids in prophase I.
r.E: ATM proteins detect double-stranded DNA breaks and activate p53, rather than serving as the structural glue between sister chromatids.

q.s: Slide 5: Euploidy, Non-disjunction and Aneuploidy (SLO1)

q.v: During an infertility workup, a 29-year-old man undergoes a testicular biopsy to evaluate spermatogenesis. Histological analysis reveals normal progression of germ cells through both Meiosis I and Meiosis II, resulting in mature haploid spermatids ready for differentiation. What is the expected chromosome count, chromatid count, ploidy (N), and DNA content (C) of an individual cell immediately following the completion of Meiosis II?
o: 46 chromosomes, 92 chromatids, 2N, 4C
46 chromosomes, 46 chromatids, 2N, 2C
23 chromosomes, 46 chromatids, 1N, 2C
23 chromosomes, 23 chromatids, 1N, 1C
69 chromosomes, 69 chromatids, 3N, 3C
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the cellular stage as a daughter cell that has completed Meiosis II) -> Step 2 (After sister chromatids separate in Meiosis II, the resulting cell has 1N ploidy, 1C chromatid content, 23 chromosomes, and 23 chromatids).

r.A: A state of 46 chromosomes, 92 chromatids, 2N, and 4C describes a diploid cell after DNA replication in S phase or G2 before division.
r.B: A state of 46 chromosomes, 46 chromatids, 2N, and 2C describes a diploid parent cell in G1 or a somatic daughter cell after mitosis.
r.C: A state of 23 chromosomes, 46 chromatids, 1N, and 2C describes a secondary gametocyte immediately after Meiosis I, before sister chromatids separate.
r.E: A state of 69 chromosomes (3N) represents triploidy caused by polyspermy or polar body retention, not a normal product of Meiosis II.

q.s: Slide 3: Ploidy/count (n/N), Constant (vs haploid: C), chromosomes and chromatids (SLO1)

q.v: A 16-year-old girl presents to the endocrinology clinic for evaluation of primary amenorrhea and short stature, and karyotyping confirms a 45,X (Turner syndrome) chromosomal constitution. The physician explains that although healthy 46,XX females randomly silence one X chromosome into a Barr body, having only a single X chromosome still produces clinical abnormalities. Which of the following genetic mechanisms best explains why a 45,X karyotype results in an abnormal phenotype despite normal X-inactivation in 46,XX individuals?
o: Complete absence of the 1,000 protein-encoding genes on the active X chromosome
Failure of about 20 genes on the silenced X chromosome to be expressed to match Y-chromosome homologues
Uncontrolled expression of the 10 Y-chromosome genes involved in germ cell development
Biparental inheritance of two identical X chromosomes resulting in recessive disease
Retention of a polar body during oogenesis leading to a non-viable molar pregnancy
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the condition as 45,X and recall that additional X chromosomes are normally silenced into a Barr body) -> Step 2 (About 20 genes on the silenced X chromosome escape inactivation and are expressed to match Y-chromosome homologues, which explains the phenotypes of 45,X and 47,XXY).

r.A: The first X chromosome is fully expressed in both 45,X and 46,XX individuals, so its 1,000 protein-encoding genes are not absent.
r.C: Y-chromosome genes involved in sexual differentiation and germ cell development are absent in 45,X individuals and are not the cause of X-inactivation escape phenotypes.
r.D: Inheriting two identical chromosomes from one parent describes uniparental isodisomy, whereas 45,X is a monosomy lacking a second sex chromosome.
r.E: Polar body retention causes triploidy and molar pregnancy, not the 45,X phenotype.

q.s: Slide 6: X and Y Chromosome (SLO1)

q.v: A 3-year-old boy is diagnosed with an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder after presenting with hepatomegaly and developmental delay. Genetic sequencing reveals that the child is homozygous for a rare pathogenic mutation carried only by his mother, while his father has two completely normal alleles at that locus. Further cytogenetic workup confirms that the child inherited two identical copies of the maternal chromosome and zero copies from his father due to two sequential nondisjunction events. Which of the following meiotic errors in the maternal germline directly caused this child's homozygous recessive condition?
o: Meiosis I error resulting in heterodisomy
Meiosis II error resulting in isodisomy
Polyspermy during fertilization resulting in triploidy
Mitotic nondisjunction in the paternal germline
Large chromosomal deletion detectable only by standard karyotype
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that inheriting two copies of the same chromosome from one parent causing a recessive disorder is uniparental isodisomy) -> Step 2 (Isodisomy specifically results from a Meiosis II error, whereas heterodisomy results from a Meiosis I error).

r.A: A Meiosis I error results in heterodisomy (two different homologous chromosomes from the same parent), which can cause imprinting disorders but does not duplicate a single recessive allele into homozygosity.
r.C: Polyspermy leads to triploidy and a non-viable molar pregnancy rather than uniparental disomy with a normal chromosome count.
r.D: While loss of the paternal chromosome requires a second nondisjunction event in the germ cell, the duplication of the identical maternal chromosome causing recessive disease is specifically a maternal Meiosis II error.
r.E: Uniparental isodisomy involves two intact copies of a single parental chromosome rather than a large chromosomal deletion.

q.s: Slide 7 & 8: Uniparental Disomy: Hetero and Isodisomy (SLO1)

q.v: An oncology researcher is testing a novel chemotherapeutic agent on synchronized human fibrosarcoma cells in vitro. Flow cytometry and western blot analysis show that treated cells successfully phosphorylate Rb, complete S-phase DNA synthesis, and enter G2 phase, but they fail to transition from S/G2 into M phase because a specific phase-dependent kinase complex is inhibited during G2. If the drug spares Cyclin B synthesis, which of the following Cyclin-CDK complexes is most likely being directly targeted during the S and G2 phases?
o: Cyclin D-CDK4
Cyclin D-CDK6
Cyclin E-CDK2
Cyclin A-CDK1/2
p16-CDK4
q.p: Step 1 (Localize the cell cycle arrest to the S and G2 phases after G1/S transition is already complete) -> Step 2 (Identify that Cyclin A paired with CDK1/2 is the specific complex active during the S and G2 phases).

r.A: Cyclin D-CDK4 is active during G1 and the G1 to S transition, which the treated cells have already successfully passed.
r.B: Cyclin D-CDK6 regulates G1 and the G1 to S transition by initiating Rb phosphorylation, not S and G2 phase progression.
r.C: Cyclin E-CDK2 drives the G1 to S transition and early S phase by hyperphosphorylating Rb, which was already completed in these cells.
r.E: p16 is a cyclin kinase inhibitor that blocks Cyclin D-CDK4/6 binding in G1, not an active Cyclin-CDK complex in S and G2.

q.s: Slide 13: CDK, Cyclin, Cell Cycle Phase Table (SLO2)

q.v: A cell culture is treated with a topoisomerase inhibitor that induces extensive double-stranded DNA breaks exclusively during the late stages of DNA synthesis. Microscopic observation confirms that the treated cells halt progression immediately prior to nuclear envelope breakdown and chromosome condensation. Which of the following surveillance criteria is specifically being evaluated by the checkpoint responsible for arresting these cells?
o: Whether sufficient cellular growth has occurred to initiate division
Whether sister chromatids are properly aligned along the mitotic spindle
Whether DNA is fully replicated and free of breaks before entering mitosis
Whether the contractile ring has properly assembled for cytokinesis
Whether the cell should exit G1 and enter a non-dividing G0 state
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that the cells are arresting after S phase but before mitosis, which corresponds to the G2 -> M checkpoint) -> Step 2 (The specific surveillance function of the G2 -> M checkpoint is to verify whether DNA is fully replicated and free of breaks).

r.A: Determining whether enough cellular growth has occurred is a primary surveillance question of the G1 to S checkpoint, not the G2 to M checkpoint.
r.B: Evaluating whether chromosomes are lined up properly is the function of the M-phase (spindle assembly) checkpoint.
r.D: Regulating the transition from mitosis to cell division occurs at the Mitosis to cytokinesis checkpoint after chromosome segregation.
r.E: Exiting the active cell cycle into the non-dividing G0 state occurs from G1 prior to the G1/S restriction point.

q.s: Slide 11 & 14: Cell cycle checkpoints (SLO2)

q.v: A 54-year-old man presents with a chronic cough and weight loss, and a chest CT reveals a central pulmonary mass confirmed as lung carcinoma on biopsy. His past medical history is notable for enucleation of his left eye at age 2 due to a malignant retinal tumor that originally presented with leukocoria. Which of the following genetic mechanisms best explains this patient's current adult malignancy in the context of his childhood history?
o: Inheritance of two pathogenic germline RB1 alleles that remained dormant until adulthood
Germline heterozygosity for a pathogenic RB1 allele followed by a somatic mutation in the remaining normal allele
Somatic amplification of the p16 cyclin kinase inhibitor in bronchial epithelial cells
Constitutive dephosphorylation of the Rb protein causing permanent sequestration of E2F
Inherited deficiency in mismatch repair genes MSH1/6 leading to hereditary retinoblastoma
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize childhood leukocoria/retinoblastoma and adult lung, prostate, or breast cancer as Hereditary Retinoblastoma cancer predisposition syndrome) -> Step 2 (This autosomal dominant syndrome involves inheriting one heterozygous pathogenic RB1 allele with a high risk of the normal RB1 allele becoming mutated somatically via the 2-Hit Hypothesis).

r.A: Inheriting two pathogenic RB1 alleles in the germline is embryonic lethal and cannot occur in a viable patient.
r.C: Amplification of p16 would inhibit Cyclin D-CDK4/6 and suppress tumor growth rather than predispose to lung carcinoma.
r.D: Constitutive dephosphorylation of Rb would keep Rb bound to E2F and halt the cell cycle in G1, preventing tumor proliferation.
r.E: Mutations in MSH1/6, MLH1, and PMS2 cause Lynch syndrome (HNPCC), whereas Hereditary Retinoblastoma is caused by RB1 mutations.

q.s: Slide 16 & 17: Hereditary Retinoblastoma and 2-Hit Hypothesis (SLO3)

q.v: Molecular profiling of a resected colon adenocarcinoma reveals a homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the TP53 gene, which occurs in approximately half of all human cancers. In a healthy colonocyte exposed to mutagenic stress, the normal protein product of this gene prevents S-phase entry by inducing a cyclin kinase inhibitor that blocks CDK2. If a pharmacological agent were designed to bypass the lost TP53 pathway by mimicking a different endogenous inhibitor that blocks Cyclin D-CDK4/6 binding, which of the following proteins would this drug be mimicking?
o: E2F
CDK1
BRCA2
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that p53 normally induces p21 to inhibit Cyclin E-CDK2, and look for the alternative endogenous CKI that blocks Cyclin D-CDK4/6 binding) -> Step 2 (Identify p16 as the specific cyclin kinase inhibitor that blocks Cyclin D-CDK4/6 binding).

r.A: p21 is the cyclin kinase inhibitor directly induced by p53 that inhibits Cyclin E-CDK2, rather than blocking Cyclin D-CDK4/6 binding.
r.C: E2F is a transcription factor that promotes S-phase replication factor expression once released from Rb, not a cyclin kinase inhibitor.
r.D: CDK1 is a cyclin-dependent kinase that pairs with Cyclin A and Cyclin B to drive S, G2, and M phases, not an inhibitor of CDK4/6.
r.E: BRCA2 is a DNA repair protein involved in homologous recombination of double-stranded breaks, not a cyclin kinase inhibitor.

q.s: Slide 18: P53 is the guardian of the genome! (SLO3)

q.v: A 35-year-old woman with a strong family history of ovarian cancer is found to carry a pathogenic germline mutation in BRCA2. Her oncologist explains that when her ovarian epithelial cells sustain double-stranded DNA breaks during G2 phase, they cannot utilize high-fidelity homologous recombination. Consequently, her cells are forced to rely exclusively on an alternative double-stranded break repair pathway that results in which of the following molecular outcomes?
o: High-fidelity repair using the intact sister chromatid as a donor DNA template
Rapid end-joining that introduces nucleotide deletions or nucleotide additions
Direct reversal of the break by stabilizing the p16-Cyclin D complex
Immediate arrest at the M-phase spindle assembly checkpoint without DNA modification
Complete failure to detect the double-stranded break due to loss of ATM kinase
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that BRCA1/2 mutations limit homologous recombination, leaving only Nonhomologous End Joining [NHEJ] available for double-stranded break repair) -> Step 2 (NHEJ is a quick, error-prone pathway that causes disrupted DNA via nucleotide deletion or nucleotide addition).

r.A: Using a sister chromatid as a donor DNA template in G2/M describes homologous recombination (HDR/HR), which is impaired in BRCA2 mutants.
r.C: p16 is a G1 cyclin kinase inhibitor and does not directly reverse double-stranded DNA breaks.
r.D: The M-phase checkpoint monitors chromosome alignment on the mitotic spindle, whereas NHEJ actively modifies and rejoins broken DNA ends.
r.E: Detection of double-stranded DNA breaks is mediated by the ATM protein (mutated in ataxia telangiectasia), which remains intact in isolated BRCA2 deficiency.

q.s: Slide 20 & 21: NHEJ vs HDR and BRCA mutations (SLO4)

q.v: A 6-year-old girl is evaluated in the neurology clinic for progressive difficulty walking and slurred speech, and physical examination reveals prominent, dilated capillary blood vessels over her cheeks and conjunctivae. Laboratory studies of her cultured fibroblasts show extreme sensitivity to ionizing radiation, with cells failing to halt DNA synthesis after sustaining double-stranded DNA breaks. Defective activation of which of the following immediate downstream targets is directly responsible for these cells failing to trigger senescence, apoptosis, or checkpoint arrest?
o: Cohesin
Rb
Cyclin B
BRCA1
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize the clinical presentation and radiation sensitivity as Ataxia Telangiectasia caused by loss of the ATM protein that detects double-stranded DNA damage) -> Step 2 (ATM/ATR activation normally phosphorylates and activates p53 to trigger DNA repair, checkpoint arrest, apoptosis, or senescence).

r.A: Cohesin holds sister chromatids together during prophase I of meiosis and is not the downstream signaling target of ATM.
r.B: Phosphorylation of Rb by CDK4/6 and CDK2 promotes cell cycle progression into S phase, whereas ATM signaling halts the cell cycle.
r.D: Cyclin B activates CDK1 to drive mitosis, whereas ATM phosphorylates p53 to arrest the cell cycle in response to DNA damage.
r.E: While BRCA1 participates in homologous recombination repair, the slide pathway specifically demonstrates that ATM/ATR activation directly phosphorylates p53 to coordinate DNA repair, checkpoint arrest, apoptosis, and senescence.

q.s: Slide 22: ATM protein detects double stranded DNA damage (SLO4)

q.v:
A 26-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with severe vaginal bleeding and pelvic cramping at 10 weeks gestation. Uterine evacuation is performed for a suspected non-viable molar pregnancy. Cytogenetic evaluation of the evacuated conceptus reveals the following:
  Chromosome count: 69 chromosomes
  Ploidy status: 3N (triploid)
  Maternal-to-paternal chromosome ratio: 2:1
Which of the following mechanisms best explains the genetic findings in this tissue?
o: Meiosis I nondisjunction
Meiosis II nondisjunction
Mitotic nondisjunction
Polar body retention
Uniparental isodisomy
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize 69 chromosomes / 3N with a 2:1 maternal-to-paternal ratio in a molar pregnancy as triploidy) -> Step 2 (Identify polar body retention or polyspermy as the specific causes of triploidy taught on the slides)

r.A: Meiosis I nondisjunction results in aneuploidy (such as trisomy or monosomy) or heterodisomy, rather than an extra complete set of chromosomes.
r.B: Meiosis II nondisjunction leads to aneuploidy of a single chromosome or uniparental isodisomy, not triploidy.
r.C: Mitotic nondisjunction after fertilization produces mosaic aneuploidy for an individual chromosome rather than a uniform 3N karyotype.
r.E: Uniparental isodisomy involves inheriting two identical copies of a single chromosome from one parent while maintaining a normal diploid (2N, 46 chromosomes) count.

q.s: Slide 4, Euploidy, Non-disjunction and Aneuploidy (SLO1)

q.v:
A 5-year-old boy is evaluated by a medical geneticist for an imprinting disorder. His parents are healthy and have no family history of genetic conditions. Chromosomal microarray and parental genotyping of the child's DNA demonstrate the following:
  Total chromosome number: 46,XY
  Chromosome 15 origin: 2 maternal copies, 0 paternal copies
  Maternal chromosome 15 alleles: heterozygous (both maternal homologs present)
Which of the following meiotic or mitotic errors is the primary origin of this patient's chromosomal abnormality?
o: Meiosis I error
Meiosis II error
Mitotic anaphase error
Polyspermy
Silencing escape
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the inheritance of two different homologous chromosomes from the same parent as uniparental heterodisomy) -> Step 2 (Link heterodisomy to a Meiosis I error)

r.B: A Meiosis II error results in uniparental isodisomy, in which the child inherits two identical sister chromatids (homozygous alleles) from one parent.
r.C: A mitotic anaphase error leads to somatic mosaicism rather than constitutional uniparental heterodisomy from gamete formation.
r.D: Polyspermy results in triploidy (69 chromosomes) and a non-viable molar pregnancy rather than a diploid (46,XY) karyotype.
r.E: Silencing escape refers to the expression of genes on the inactivated X chromosome (Barr body) and does not cause uniparental disomy.

q.s: Slide 7, Uniparental Disomy: Hetero and Isodisomy (SLO1)

q.v: A 22-year-old man presents to the reproductive medicine clinic for evaluation of infertility and gynecomastia. Peripheral blood karyotyping reveals a 47,XXY chromosomal constitution, and a buccal smear demonstrates a single dark-staining Barr body within the squamous epithelial nuclei. Despite random silencing of the extra X chromosome, the patient exhibits phenotypic differences compared to a 46,XY male. Approximately how many genes on the silenced X chromosome remain expressed to match the expression of homologous genes on the Y chromosome?
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize 47,XXY with a Barr body as having a silenced extra X chromosome that undergoes partial silencing escape) -> Step 2 (Recall that about 20 genes on the silenced X chromosome are expressed to match homologous Y chromosome genes)

r.A: About 10 genes on the Y chromosome are involved in sexual differentiation and germ cell development.
r.C: About 30 is the total number of genes located on the entire Y chromosome.
r.D: Forty-six is the normal diploid chromosome number (2N) in a euploid human somatic cell.
r.E: Approximately 1,000 is the total number of protein-encoding genes located on the X chromosome.

q.s: Slide 6, X and Y (SLO1)

q.v: A 58-year-old woman is treated with paclitaxel for metastatic breast carcinoma, a chemotherapeutic agent that interferes with mitotic spindle function and prevents chromosomes from lining up properly on the metaphase plate. Which of the following checkpoints is primarily responsible for halting the cell cycle in response to this defect?
o: G1/S checkpoint
G2/M checkpoint
M-phase checkpoint
Mitosis to cytokinesis checkpoint
G0 restriction point
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that failure of chromosomes to line up properly on the spindle is monitored during mitosis) -> Step 2 (Identify the M-phase checkpoint as the surveillance mechanism that verifies proper chromosome alignment)

r.A: The G1/S checkpoint evaluates whether the cell has achieved sufficient growth and whether pre-replication DNA damage is present.
r.B: The G2/M checkpoint verifies that DNA is fully replicated and free of double-stranded breaks prior to mitotic entry.
r.D: The mitosis to cytokinesis checkpoint regulates final cell division after chromosome alignment and segregation have already occurred.
r.E: G0 is a quiescent cellular state for cells that have exited the cell cycle rather than a spindle alignment checkpoint.

q.s: Slide 11, Cell cycle is tightly regulated by checkpoints (SLO2)

q.v: Which of the following cyclin-CDK complexes is primarily responsible for regulating cell cycle progression through both the S phase and the G2 phase?
o: Cyclin D - CDK4/6
Cyclin E - CDK2
Cyclin A - CDK1/2
Cyclin B - CDK1
Cyclin D - CDK2
q.p: Step 1 (Recall the phase-specific pairing of cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases across the cell cycle) -> Step 2 (Match S and G2 phases to Cyclin A paired with CDK1/2)

r.A: The Cyclin D - CDK4/6 complex regulates progression through G1 and the early G1 to S transition.
r.B: The Cyclin E - CDK2 complex regulates the G1 to S transition and initiation of S phase, rather than G2.
r.D: The Cyclin B - CDK1 complex specifically drives progression through the M phase (mitosis).
r.E: Cyclin D pairs with CDK4 and CDK6 in early G1, whereas CDK2 pairs with Cyclin E and Cyclin A.

q.s: Slide 13, CDK / Cyclin / Cell Cycle Phase Table (SLO2)

q.v: During the G1 to S transition, which of the following complexes directly hyperphosphorylates the retinoblastoma (Rb) protein to cause its dissociation from the E2F transcription factor?
o: Cyclin D - CDK4/6
Cyclin E - CDK2
Cyclin A - CDK1
Cyclin B - CDK1
p16 - CDK4
q.p: Step 1 (Distinguish initial phosphorylation of Rb by CDK4/6 from hyperphosphorylation of Rb) -> Step 2 (Identify Cyclin E - CDK2 as the complex that hyperphosphorylates Rb to fully release E2F)

r.A: Cyclin D - CDK4/6 initiates the early phosphorylation of Rb in G1, whereas CDK2 is required to hyperphosphorylate Rb.
r.C: Cyclin A - CDK1 is active later in the cell cycle during S and G2 phases after E2F has already been released.
r.D: Cyclin B - CDK1 regulates the M phase and is not involved in the G1/S phosphorylation of Rb.
r.E: p16 is a cyclin-kinase inhibitor that blocks Cyclin D - CDK4/6 binding rather than phosphorylating Rb.

q.s: Slide 15 and Slide 19, G1 -> S transition and SLO3 Review (SLO3)

q.v: A 14-month-old girl is brought to the pediatrician after her mother noticed a white reflection in the child's left pupil in recent family photographs. Ophthalmologic examination confirms leukocoria and reveals a large intraocular retinal mass. Genetic testing of peripheral blood leukocytes identifies a germline mutation in one allele of the RB1 gene. Which of the following best describes the inheritance pattern of this patient's cancer predisposition syndrome and the consequence of inheriting two pathogenic RB1 alleles at conception?
o: Autosomal dominant / embryonic lethal
Autosomal dominant / congenital bilateral tumors
Autosomal recessive / embryonic lethal
Autosomal recessive / congenital bilateral tumors
X-linked recessive / embryonic lethal
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize leukocoria and a retinal mass in a child with a heterozygous germline RB1 mutation as hereditary retinoblastoma) -> Step 2 (Identify the inheritance pattern as autosomal dominant and homozygous germline RB1 mutation as embryonic lethal)

r.B: Inheriting two pathogenic RB1 alleles at conception is embryonic lethal rather than viable with congenital tumors.
r.C: Hereditary retinoblastoma predisposition follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern because inheriting a single mutant allele confers high risk of a somatic second hit.
r.D: Hereditary retinoblastoma is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, and homozygosity for two pathogenic alleles is embryonic lethal.
r.E: The RB1 gene is located on an autosome and follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern rather than X-linked recessive.

q.s: Slide 16, Hereditary Retinoblastoma (SLO3)

q.v: A 48-year-old man presents to the dermatology clinic with a Pigmented skin lesion on his back that has recently increased in size. Excisional biopsy confirms malignant melanoma, and molecular profiling of the tumor reveals a homozygous deletion of the gene encoding the p16 protein. Loss of p16 function promotes tumorigenesis by failing to block which of the following molecular events?
o: Binding of Cyclin D to CDK4/6
Binding of E2F to DNA promoters
Phosphorylation of p53 by ATM
Degradation of Cyclin B by CDK1
Inhibition of CDK2 by p21
q.p: Step 1 (Identify p16 as a cyclin-kinase inhibitor that regulates the G1/S transition) -> Step 2 (Recall that p16 specifically blocks Cyclin D - CDK4/6 binding)

r.B: Rb directly binds E2F to block transcription, whereas p16 acts upstream by inhibiting the Cyclin D - CDK4/6 complex.
r.C: ATM phosphorylates and activates p53 in response to double-stranded DNA breaks independently of p16.
r.D: Cyclin B and CDK1 regulate mitosis, whereas p16 specifically targets the G1 phase kinases CDK4 and CDK6.
r.E: p21 is a separate cyclin-kinase inhibitor induced by p53 that inhibits CDK2, not the target of p16.

q.s: Slide 18, P53 is the guardian of the genome! (SLO3)

q.v: A 41-year-old woman with a history of early-onset breast cancer undergoes prophylactic oophorectomy after genetic testing reveals a pathogenic germline mutation in BRCA1. In her tumor cells, double-stranded DNA breaks cannot be repaired via homologous recombination and are instead repaired by an alternative pathway. Which of the following best characterizes this alternative DNA repair mechanism?
o: Quick and results in nucleotide deletions or additions
Quick and requires a sister chromatid template
Slow and restricted exclusively to the G2/M phase
High-fidelity and active only during the S phase
High-fidelity and requires donor DNA strands
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that BRCA1 mutation impairs homologous recombination, leaving only nonhomologous end joining [NHEJ] available for double-stranded break repair) -> Step 2 (Identify NHEJ as quick and error-prone, causing nucleotide deletions or additions)

r.B: Requiring a sister chromatid template is a feature of homologous recombination (HDR), not nonhomologous end joining.
r.C: Being restricted to the G2/M phase is characteristic of accurate homologous recombination, whereas NHEJ is active throughout the cell cycle.
r.D: High-fidelity repair during S and G2 phases describes homologous recombination rather than NHEJ.
r.E: Requiring donor DNA strands to achieve accurate repair describes homologous recombination (HDR), which is lost in BRCA1-deficient cells.

q.s: Slide 20 and Slide 21, DNA is very susceptible to damage during replication / BRCA mutations (SLO4)

q.v: A 34-year-old man is accidentally exposed to ionizing radiation at a nuclear facility, inducing numerous double-stranded DNA breaks in his hematopoietic stem cells. To prevent these damaged cells from replicating their DNA, a specific sensor protein detects the double-stranded breaks and phosphorylates p53, which subsequently induces a cyclin-kinase inhibitor to halt the cell cycle. Which of the following correctly identifies the DNA damage sensor protein and the terminal target inhibited by this pathway?
o: ATM / CDK2
ATM / CDK1
BRCA1 / CDK4/6
Rb / E2F
p16 / CDK2
q.p: Step 1 (Identify ATM as the sensor protein that detects double-stranded DNA damage and phosphorylates p53) -> Step 2 (Trace activated p53 to the production of p21, a CKI that specifically inhibits CDK2)

r.B: ATM is the correct double-stranded break sensor, but p53-induced p21 specifically inhibits CDK2 at the G1/S transition rather than CDK1.
r.C: BRCA1 mediates homologous recombination repair, and the p53-p21 pathway inhibits CDK2 rather than CDK4/6.
r.D: Rb binds E2F to prevent S-phase transcription under basal conditions, but Rb is not the sensor of double-stranded DNA breaks.
r.E: p16 is a cyclin-kinase inhibitor that blocks Cyclin D - CDK4/6 binding and does not sense double-stranded DNA breaks.

q.s: Slide 18 and Slide 22, P53 is the guardian of the genome! / ATM protein detects double stranded DNA damage (SLO3, SLO4)

add.cloze: {{c1::Unequal crossing over}} during meiosis typically results in the addition or loss of only part of a chromosome
add.extra: Contrast nondisjunction, which adds or loses a whole chromosome (aneuploidy)

add.cloze: Chromosome banding is the pattern of alternating dark and light regions, {{c1::heterochromatin}} (dark: AT-rich, gene-poor) and {{c2::euchromatin}} (light: GC-rich, gene-rich), used as landmarks to identify chromosomes
add.extra: G-banding of metaphase chromosomes

add.cloze: The lower limit of resolution of a standard genome-wide karyotype is about {{c1::5–10 Mb}}
add.extra: FISH ~70 kb–1 Mb (targeted); chromosomal microarray >5 kb–200 kb

add.cloze: A key advantage of karyotyping over chromosomal microarray is that it can detect {{c1::balanced chromosomal rearrangements}}
add.extra: e.g., balanced translocations and inversions

add.cloze: A major limitation of FISH is that it measures only {{c1::one or two targets at a time}}, and you must {{c2::know the target to look for}}
add.extra: Karyotype and CMA are genome-wide

add.cloze: Chromosomal microarray cannot detect balanced translocations because they cause {{c1::no net gain or loss of DNA}}
add.extra: CMA detects copy-number changes and regions of homozygosity (UPD), not position

add.cloze: In ISCN nomenclature, the first number (e.g., 46 or 47) is the {{c1::total number of chromosomes}}, and a + or − before a chromosome number means {{c2::gain or loss of that whole chromosome}}
add.extra: e.g., 47,XX,+21 = female with trisomy 21

add.cloze: A balanced Robertsonian translocation carrier has a total of {{c1::45}} chromosomes
add.extra: e.g., 45,XY,t(13;14)(q10;q10); phenotypically normal

add.cloze: Robertsonian translocations are considered balanced even though the short arms are lost, because the p arms of acrocentric chromosomes {{c1::carry no unique genes}}
add.extra: They carry ribosomal DNA genes, present in multiple copies on the other acrocentric chromosomes

add.cloze: The viable outcomes for offspring of a t(14;21) Robertsonian carrier are {{c1::a normal (euploid) karyotype}}, {{c2::a balanced carrier}}, or {{c3::Down syndrome (translocation trisomy 21)}}
add.extra: ~4% of Down syndrome is due to an unbalanced Robertsonian translocation

q.v: A 64-year-old woman undergoes surgical resection of a solid tumor, and the pathology specimen is processed SOLELY as formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue without preserving any fresh cells. The oncology team orders a comprehensive cytogenetic panel to evaluate for copy number variants and structural rearrangements. Which of the following laboratory procedures will fail on this specimen because its required cell-cycle arrest step cannot be performed?
o: Blocking spindle formation with colchicine to observe chromosomes at their most condensed state
Hybridizing fluorescently labeled DNA probes to denatured single-stranded target DNA
Digesting extracted genomic DNA with restriction enzymes followed by adapter ligation
Labeling ultra-long single DNA strands at specific hexamer sequences to map structural orientation
Assessing relative allelic ratios across the genome using single nucleotide polymorphism probes
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that FFPE tissue contains fixed, non-viable cells that cannot be cultured to enter mitosis/metaphase, which is required for karyotyping) -> Step 2 (Connect karyotyping to its specific laboratory mechanism of using colchicine to block spindle formation and arrest cells in metaphase).

r.B: Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) can be performed directly on interphase nuclei in fixed FFPE tissue without requiring cell culture or mitotic arrest.
r.C: Restriction enzyme digestion and adapter ligation are steps in chromosomal microarray (CMA), which utilizes extracted DNA from any cell cycle phase and is compatible with FFPE tissue.
r.D: Labeling ultra-long DNA strands describes optical genome mapping (OGM), which uses extracted high-molecular-weight DNA rather than metaphase-arrested cells.
r.E: Assessing allelic ratios via SNP probes is part of chromosomal microarray (CMA), which can be performed on bulk DNA extracted from fixed FFPE specimens.

q.s: Slides 6, 7, 8, 10, and 11: Cell Cycle and Chromosome Analysis, Cytogenetics Sample Types, Comparison of Cytogenetic Methods, Karyotyping Process

q.v: A 2-year-old boy with failure to thrive and multiple congenital malformations undergoes peripheral blood venous sampling for a standard G-banded chromosome study. After culturing the lymphocytes for 3 days with phytohemagglutinin and arresting them in metaphase, the laboratory digests the chromosomes with trypsin and stains them with Giemsa. A submicroscopic alteration is suspected within one of the resulting light-staining bands. Which of the following molecular characteristics best describes the chromosomal region within this light band?
o: Condensed heterochromatin with a low density of functional genes
AT-rich nucleotide sequences that replicate late in the cell cycle
Euchromatin that is GC-rich and contains a high density of genes
Tandemly repeated ribosomal DNA sequences located on acrocentric p arms
Primary constrictions serving as the attachment site for the mitotic spindle
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that trypsin digestion and Giemsa staining create G-banding patterns consisting of dark and light bands) -> Step 2 (Determine the molecular composition of the light-staining bands, which represent euchromatin that is GC-rich and gene-rich).

r.A: Heterochromatin that is gene-poor stains as dark bands rather than light bands in G-banded karyotyping.
r.B: AT-rich nucleotide regions correspond to dark-staining heterochromatin bands rather than light-staining euchromatin bands.
r.D: Genes for ribosomal DNA are specifically located on the redundant p arms of acrocentric chromosomes rather than defining light G-bands generally.
r.E: The primary constriction where the spindle apparatus attaches is the centromere, not the euchromatic light bands created by Giemsa staining.

q.s: Slides 11 and 12: Karyotyping Process, Chromosome Identification

q.v: A 4-year-old girl with developmental delay and dysmorphic features undergoes high-resolution whole-genome assessment via a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) chromosomal microarray. Across a 1.5-Mb segment on the long arm of chromosome 7, the genotype distribution plot displays four distinct horizontal allelic tracks corresponding to calculated (A minus B) y-axis values of 1.5, 0.5, -0.5, and -1.5. Which of the following genetic abnormalities is present within this specific chromosomal region?
o: A hemizygous microdeletion leaving a single allele copy
A normal diploid complement with balanced heterozygosity
Copy-neutral uniparental isodisomy with absence of heterozygosity
A chromosomal duplication resulting in three allele copies
A balanced reciprocal translocation with no net gain or loss of DNA
q.p: Step 1 (Analyze the SNP microarray allelic track pattern showing 4 tracks with y-axis values of 1.5, 0.5, -0.5, and -1.5, which correspond to the genotypes AAA, AAB, ABB, and BBB) -> Step 2 (Deduce that the presence of 3 alleles and 4 tracks indicates a regional chromosomal duplication).

r.A: A deletion leaves only 1 allele and generates 2 tracks on the SNP array at y-axis values of 0.5 (A) and -0.5 (B).
r.B: A normal diploid region has 2 alleles and generates 3 tracks corresponding to AA (1), AB (0), and BB (-1).
r.C: Uniparental isodisomy or absence of heterozygosity lacks AB heterozygotes, whereas 4 tracks specifically indicate the presence of three allele copies (duplication).
r.E: Chromosomal microarray cannot detect balanced reciprocal translocations, which would show a normal diploid 3-track pattern.

q.s: Slides 22, 24, and 25: Chromosomal Microarray, SNP CMA Genotyping

q.v: A 55-year-old man being evaluated for a hematologic malignancy has bone marrow aspirate submitted for cytogenetic analysis. The final laboratory report includes the following International System for Human Cytogenomic Nomenclature (ISCN) string: 47~51,X,-Y,del(3)(p12),+8[cp10]/46,XY[10].nuc ish(D17Z1x3)[105/200]. Based on this nomenclature, what does the bracketed designation [cp10] specifically communicate to the clinician?
o: A balanced translocation breakpoint located at band 10 of the short arm of chromosome C
The reference human genome build utilized to map nucleotide coordinates of the deletion
A composite karyotype of 10 cancer cells sharing the listed chromosomal abnormalities
Interphase fluorescence in situ hybridization showing probe separation in 10 percent of cells
A constitutional mosaic clone ruled out at a 95 percent confidence level across 10 metaphases
q.p: Step 1 (Locate the symbol [cp10] within the ISCN nomenclature string from a cancer specimen) -> Step 2 (Interpret [cp10] according to ISCN rules as a composite karyotype used in cancer, where the number of cells sharing the abnormalities is specified in brackets).

r.A: Chromosome bands are specified within parentheses after the abnormality type, such as (p12), rather than inside square brackets with 'cp'.
r.B: Reference genome builds are indicated in brackets as [hg19] or [GRCh38] when nucleotide coordinates are used in microarray nomenclature.
r.D: Interphase FISH is denoted by '.nuc ish' and break-apart probe separation is denoted by 'sep', whereas [105/200] indicates the cell count for the FISH result.
r.E: Standard chromosome studies require 20 cells to rule out 14% mosaicism at a 95% confidence level, and normal versus abnormal clones are separated by a slash mark (/).

q.s: Slide 30: Cytogenetic Nomenclature

q.v: A 26-year-old primigravida undergoes a fetal ultrasound at 16 weeks of gestation that reveals severe fetal growth restriction and an abnormally small, non-cystic placenta. Amniocentesis is performed, and chromosome analysis of cultured amniocytes demonstrates a 69,XXX karyotype. Which of the following reproductive mechanisms is the most likely cause of this fetal presentation?
o: Fertilization of a haploid ovum by two separate haploid sperm
Fertilization of an empty ovum by a single sperm that subsequently duplicated its genome
Failure of meiosis I or cytokinesis resulting in a diploid egg fertilized by a haploid sperm
Failure of cytoplasmic division after S-phase DNA replication in the first mitotic division
Post-zygotic fusion of two diploid blastomeres during preimplantation development
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the fetus as having triploidy [69,XXX] accompanied by a small placenta and severe fetal growth restriction, which defines digynic triploidy of maternal origin) -> Step 2 (Connect digynic triploidy to its cellular mechanism: meiosis I or cytokinesis failure producing a diploid egg, or retention of the 2nd polar body, fertilized by a haploid sperm).

r.A: Dispermy (fertilization by two sperm) causes diandric triploidy, which presents with a large cystic placenta and partial hydatidiform mole rather than a small placenta.
r.B: Fertilization of an empty ovum by one sperm with subsequent duplication results in a diploid (46,XX) monospermic complete hydatidiform mole, not triploidy.
r.D: Failure of cytokinesis after the first S-phase in a fertilized egg results in a single cell containing 92 chromosomes (tetraploidy), not 69 chromosomes.
r.E: Fusion of two diploid blastomeres in preimplantation development is a mechanism for tetraploidy (4n), not digynic triploidy.

q.s: Slides 37, 38, and 39: Mechanism for triploidy, Mechanism for molar pregnancy, Mechanism for tetraploidy

q.v: A 29-year-old woman experiences a first-trimester spontaneous abortion, and products of conception are sent for cytogenetic evaluation. Karyotyping reveals 92,XXXX in all analyzed cells. A research study investigating the cellular origin of this abnormality finds that the fertilized zygote repeated DNA replication without ever entering mitosis or undergoing cell division. Which of the following terms best describes this specific cellular mechanism?
o: Anaphase I meiotic nondisjunction
Endoreduplication
Adjacent-2 quadrivalent segregation
Pericentric chromosomal inversion
Dispermic fertilization
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that 92,XXXX represents tetraploidy [4 copies of each chromosome] and note the specific mechanism described: repeating DNA replication without entering mitosis or cell division) -> Step 2 (Identify this exact mechanism as endoreduplication).

r.A: Meiotic nondisjunction is the unequal separation of chromosomes during meiosis I or II, leading to aneusomy (such as trisomy or monosomy) rather than tetraploidy.
r.C: Adjacent-2 segregation occurs during meiosis I in carriers of reciprocal translocations, leading to unbalanced gametes with partial trisomy and partial monosomy.
r.D: Pericentric inversion is a balanced structural rearrangement involving both chromosome arms and the centromere, with no change in chromosome ploidy.
r.E: Dispermic fertilization of a haploid egg results in diandric triploidy (69 chromosomes), whereas polyspermy causing tetraploidy would require fertilization by 3 sperm.

q.s: Slides 31, 39, and 40: Abnormalities of chromosome number, Mechanism for tetraploidy, What does this look like?

q.v: A phenotypically normal 31-year-old man undergoes peripheral blood karyotyping after his wife experiences two consecutive spontaneous abortions. His karyogram reveals a balanced reciprocal translocation between two nonhomologous chromosomes, and he is counseled regarding the risk of producing unbalanced gametes. During meiosis I, the four involved chromosomes align to form a quadrivalent structure that subsequently undergoes Adjacent-2 segregation. Which of the following chromosomal combinations is segregated together into a single daughter cell during this specific division?
o: Two normal nonhomologous chromosomes without any translocated segments
Two derivative chromosomes that together contain a complete, balanced set of genetic material
One normal chromosome and one nonhomologous derivative chromosome with non-homologous centromeres
Two homologous centromeres consisting of one normal chromosome and its corresponding derivative chromosome
A fused acrocentric chromosome paired with loss of redundant ribosomal DNA short arms
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the meiotic configuration as a quadrivalent formed by two normal and two derivative chromosomes in a reciprocal translocation carrier undergoing Adjacent-2 segregation) -> Step 2 (Determine from the quadrivalent segregation diagram that Adjacent-2 separates homologous centromeres together into the same gamete—one normal chromosome and its homologous derivative chromosome—producing an unbalanced gamete).

r.A: Segregation of the two normal chromosomes into one gamete (and the two balanced derivatives into the other) describes alternate segregation, which yields balanced gametes.
r.B: Segregation of both reciprocal derivative chromosomes together into one daughter cell occurs during alternate segregation, resulting in a balanced carrier gamete.
r.C: Segregation of one normal chromosome with the nonhomologous derivative chromosome (non-homologous centromeres) defines Adjacent-1 segregation, not Adjacent-2.
r.E: Fusion of acrocentric chromosomes with loss of short-arm ribosomal DNA describes the formation of a Robertsonian translocation, not meiotic quadrivalent segregation.

q.s: Slides 45, 46, 47, 48, and 49: Reciprocal translocations

q.v: A 28-year-old man and his partner present for preconception genetic counseling because his brother has Down syndrome. Peripheral blood chromosome analysis is performed on the patient and returns a karyotype of 45,XY,t(14;21)(q10;q10). Despite having only 45 chromosomes, the patient is completely healthy and phenotypically normal. Why does the loss of chromosomal material during the formation of this rearrangement fail to cause clinical abnormalities in this patient?
o: The missing genetic material is compensated by uniparental disomy of the remaining homolog
The breakpoint occurs exclusively within AT-rich centromeric heterochromatin
The lost short arms contain only redundant ribosomal DNA genes present on other acrocentric chromosomes
The inverted segment is paracentric and does not disrupt the primary constriction
The deleted region is submicroscopic and located in a gene-poor subtelomeric band
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize 45,XY,t(14;21)(q10;q10) as a balanced Robertsonian translocation involving two acrocentric chromosomes, 14 and 21, resulting in a total count of 45 chromosomes) -> Step 2 (Explain why it is phenotypically normal/balanced: only the p arms are lost, which contain genes for ribosomal DNA that are redundant with multiple copies on other acrocentric chromosomes).

r.A: Robertsonian translocation carriers do not have uniparental disomy; they retain one normal copy of each involved long arm plus the fused derivative chromosome.
r.B: While the fusion occurs near the centromeric q10 region, physical genetic material is actually lost from the short (p) arms, not just rearranged within heterochromatin.
r.D: Paracentric inversions occur within a single chromosome arm without losing material or changing chromosome number, unlike a Robertsonian fusion.
r.E: The entire p arms of both acrocentric chromosomes are lost during fusion, which is tolerated because their ribosomal DNA is redundant, not because it is a subtelomeric microdeletion.

q.s: Slides 53, 54, and 55: Robertsonian translocations

q.v: A 58-year-old man presents with fatigue and leukocytosis, and a bone marrow evaluation shows 100% cellularity with marked myeloid hyperplasia. Dual-fusion fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) performed on a peripheral blood smear using green probes for chromosome 22q11.2 and orange probes for chromosome 9q34 demonstrates two yellow fusion signals, one green signal, and one orange signal in 191 of 200 interphase nuclei. Targeted oral therapy is initiated based on this cytogenetic finding. What is the direct molecular mechanism of the drug used to treat this patient's disorder?
o: Restoration of lost TP53 tumor suppressor function caused by a 17p13 deletion
Degradation of the PML::RARA fusion protein resulting from a t(15;17) translocation
Inhibition of tyrosine kinase activity by blocking ATP binding to the BCR-ABL fusion protein
Downregulation of Cyclin D1 overexpression driven by an IGH::CCND1 rearrangement
Prevention of hyperdiploid chromosome gains involving chromosomes 4, 10, and 17
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the patient's condition as chronic myeloid leukemia [CML] with the t(9;22)(q34;q11.2) Philadelphia chromosome creating the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene, confirmed by dual-fusion FISH) -> Step 2 (Identify the mechanism of targeted therapy [imatinib/TKI]: inhibiting the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase fusion protein by blocking ATP binding so it cannot phosphorylate its substrate).

r.A: Deletion of 17p13 causes loss of the TP53 tumor suppressor gene in many cancers, which is distinct from the t(9;22) translocation in CML.
r.B: The PML::RARA fusion gene arises from t(15;17)(q22;q21) in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), not t(9;22) in CML.
r.D: IGH::CCND1 fusion leading to Cyclin D1 positivity is seen in plasma cell malignancies like multiple myeloma (and mantle cell), not CML.
r.E: Hyperdiploidy involving gains of chromosomes X, 4, 6, 10, 14, 17, and 18 is a favorable prognostic finding in pediatric B-cell precursor ALL, not the target of CML therapy.

q.s: Slides 58, 59, 60, 67, and 68: Cytogenetics in cancer, CML t(9;22) implications for therapy, Case 2 – Chronic myeloid leukemia

q.v: A 66-year-old man with anemia and monoclonal gammopathy undergoes a bone marrow biopsy that reveals 90% cellularity composed of Cyclin D1-positive plasma cells. An interphase fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) panel shows an IGH::CCND1 fusion in 36% of cells and an ATM gain in 35% of cells, yet a standard 20-cell G-banded karyotype from the same bone marrow aspirate is reported as a normal male karyotype: 46,XY,inv(9)(p12q13)[20]. Which of the following best explains why the standard chromosome analysis failed to detect the abnormalities seen on the FISH panel?
o: The t(11;14) rearrangement is a pericentric inversion that does not alter Giemsa banding patterns
Malignant plasma cells are terminally differentiated B-cells that do not actively divide in culture to reach metaphase
Standard G-banded karyotyping only evaluates bulk extracted DNA and cannot detect mosaic clones below 50 percent
The IGH and CCND1 probes cross-hybridize with acrocentric centromeres during interphase
Colchicine selectively lyses malignant myeloid blasts while sparing normal T lymphocytes
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize the discrepancy in Case 5 [Multiple Myeloma]: interphase FISH detected ~40% abnormal cells with IGH::CCND1 fusion and hyperdiploidy, whereas the G-banded karyotype was normal) -> Step 2 (Apply the biological principle that karyotyping requires dividing metaphase cells, and malignant plasma cells are terminally differentiated B-cells that do not actively divide, meaning the karyotype only analyzed normal dividing marrow cells).

r.A: The inv(9)(p12q13) seen on the karyogram is a normal constitutional variant, whereas the missed myeloma abnormality is a translocation/gain in non-dividing plasma cells.
r.C: Karyotyping is a single-cell analysis (not bulk DNA like CMA) with a sensitivity of 10-15% (rules out 14% mosaicism in 20 cells), so 36-40% abnormal cells would easily be detected if they divided.
r.D: Acrocentric centromere cross-hybridization is a property of centromeric probes on chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21, and 22, not locus-specific IGH (14q32) and CCND1 (11q13) probes.
r.E: Multiple myeloma is a malignancy of plasma cells (B-cells), and colchicine arrests dividing cells in metaphase rather than lysing blasts.

q.s: Slides 77, 78, 81, and 82: Case 5 – Multiple myeloma, Questions for Case 5

q.v: A 24-year-old primigravida undergoes a routine ultrasound at 15 weeks of gestation that reveals an enlarged, cystic placenta, ventriculomegaly, and holoprosencephaly. Amniocentesis is performed, and chromosome analysis of the cultured amniocytes demonstrates a 69,XXY karyotype. Which of the following mechanisms is the most likely cause of this fetal chromosomal abnormality?
o: Fertilization of a haploid ovum by two sperm
Retention of the second polar body during maternal meiosis II
Failure of cytokinesis following the first zygotic S-phase
Fertilization of an empty ovum by one sperm with subsequent genome duplication
Failure of homologous chromosomes to separate during maternal meiosis I
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize 69,XXY with a large cystic placenta as a partial hydatidiform mole caused by diandric triploidy) -> Step 2 (Identify the primary mechanism of diandric triploidy as dispermy, or fertilization of a haploid egg by two sperm)

r.B: Retention of the second polar body causes digynic triploidy, which presents with a small, non-cystic placenta and severe fetal growth restriction.
r.C: Failure of cytokinesis following the first zygotic S-phase results in tetraploidy (92 chromosomes) rather than triploidy.
r.D: Fertilization of an empty ovum by one sperm followed by duplication of the paternal genome produces a monospermic complete hydatidiform mole with a 46,XX karyotype.
r.E: Failure of homologous chromosomes to separate during maternal meiosis I results in trisomy or monosomy of a single chromosome (aneusomy) rather than a full extra set of chromosomes.

q.s: SLO 1 / Slides 37-38, 74-76: Mechanism for triploidy and Case 4 - Prenatal Triploidy

q.v: A 30-year-old woman experiences a first-trimester spontaneous abortion, and ultrasound imaging shows a complete hydatidiform mole with no fetal tissue and a 15-25% risk for invasive gestational trophoblastic disease. Cytogenetic analysis of the evacuated tissue reveals a 46,XX karyotype composed entirely of paternal chromosomes. Which of the following mechanisms accounts for the majority of cases of this specific condition?
o: Fertilization of an empty ovum by two haploid sperm
Fertilization of an empty ovum by one sperm followed by duplication
Fertilization of a haploid ovum by two haploid sperm
Meiosis I failure resulting in a diploid ovum fertilized by a haploid sperm
Mitotic nondisjunction in the early post-zygotic embryo
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize a 46,XX complete hydatidiform mole) -> Step 2 (Identify the most common mechanism as monospermic fertilization of an empty ovum followed by duplication of the sperm genome)

r.A: Dispermic fertilization of an empty ovum accounts for only 10-15% of complete hydatidiform moles and can result in either 46,XX or 46,XY.
r.C: Fertilization of a normal haploid ovum by two sperm results in a dispermic partial mole with a triploid (69,XXX, 69,XXY, or 69,XYY) karyotype.
r.D: Meiosis I failure in the oocyte followed by fertilization by a haploid sperm results in digynic triploidy (69 chromosomes) with a small placenta.
r.E: Mitotic nondisjunction in the early embryo leads to chromosomal mosaicism rather than a purely androgenetic diploid complete mole.

q.s: SLO 1 / Slide 38: Mechanism for molar pregnancy

q.v: A 36-year-old woman at 11 weeks of gestation undergoes chorionic villus sampling (CVS) because her husband is a known carrier of a cryptic balanced translocation, t(1;22)(p36.3;q13.3). Standard G-banded karyotyping and chromosomal microarray (CMA) performed on the fetal sample both return normal 46,XX results. However, metaphase fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) using subtelomeric probes for 1p and 22q demonstrates that the fetus carries the paternal balanced translocation. Which of the following meiotic segregation patterns in the father gave rise to the gamete involved in this conception?
o: Alternate segregation
Adjacent-1 segregation
Adjacent-2 segregation
Meiosis I nondisjunction
Meiosis II nondisjunction
q.p: Step 1 (Determine that the fetus inherited the balanced form of a reciprocal translocation from a carrier parent) -> Step 2 (Identify alternate segregation of the meiotic quadrivalent as the pattern that produces balanced gametes)

r.B: Adjacent-1 segregation involves the separation of nonhomologous centromeres and always produces unbalanced gametes with partial trisomy and partial monosomy.
r.C: Adjacent-2 segregation involves the separation of homologous centromeres into the same daughter cell and always produces unbalanced gametes.
r.D: Meiosis I nondisjunction refers to the failure of homologous chromosomes to separate, leading to whole-chromosome aneusomy.
r.E: Meiosis II nondisjunction refers to the failure of sister chromatids to separate during the second meiotic division, leading to whole-chromosome aneusomy.

q.s: SLO 1 / Slides 46-49, 62-66: Reciprocal translocations and Case 1 - Prenatal Cryptic Translocation

q.v: A 3-year-old boy with developmental delay and no known family history of genetic disorders undergoes diagnostic evaluation. Which of the following cytogenetic techniques has the unique advantage of detecting uniparental disomy and regions of absence of heterozygosity across the genome without requiring viable dividing cells?
o: G-banded karyotyping
Interphase fluorescence in situ hybridization
Metaphase fluorescence in situ hybridization
Single nucleotide polymorphism chromosomal microarray
Optical genome mapping
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the need to detect absence of heterozygosity/uniparental disomy on extracted DNA from non-dividing cells) -> Step 2 (Select SNP chromosomal microarray, which uses allelic ratios to detect LOH/AOH and UPD)

r.A: G-banded karyotyping requires viable dividing cells arrested in metaphase and cannot detect copy-neutral absence of heterozygosity or uniparental disomy.
r.B: Interphase FISH uses targeted fluorescent DNA probes to assess specific copy number or structural variants and cannot detect genome-wide absence of heterozygosity.
r.C: Metaphase FISH requires dividing cells and targeted probes, and it cannot assess single nucleotide polymorphism allele patterns for uniparental disomy.
r.E: Optical genome mapping uses ultra-long DNA strands to resolve structural variants and translocations, but it cannot detect single nucleotide variants or absence of heterozygosity.

q.s: SLO 2 / Slides 10, 22-23, 27: Comparison of Cytogenetic Methods, Chromosomal Microarray, and Optical Genome Mapping

q.v:
A 19-year-old man presents to the emergency department with fatigue, easy bruising, and petechiae. Laboratory studies show pancytopenia, severe neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia. A bone marrow biopsy is 100% cellular and predominantly occupied by sheets of atypical promyelocytes and blasts. Interphase fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is performed on the bone marrow aspirate and yields the following result:
  nuc ish (PML,RARA)x3(PML con RARAx1)[178/200]
Follow-up G-banded chromosome analysis reveals 46,XY,t(15;16;17)(q24;q24;q21)[20]. If a chromosomal microarray (CMA) were performed on this bone marrow specimen, which of the following results would most likely be expected?
o: Deletion of 15q24 and duplication of 17q21
Normal male result with no copy number gains or losses
Trisomy of chromosomes 15, 16, and 17
Loss of heterozygosity across the entire long arm of chromosome 16
Amplification of the PML::RARA fusion gene with three extra copies
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that the patient has acute promyelocytic leukemia caused by a balanced three-way translocation t(15;16;17)) -> Step 2 (Predict that CMA will show a normal male result because balanced translocations involve no net gain or loss of DNA)

r.A: The notation x3 in dual-fusion FISH indicates that one allele of each gene was split by the translocation break, not that a true copy number duplication or deletion occurred.
r.C: The patient has a balanced rearrangement among chromosomes 15, 16, and 17 rather than whole-chromosome trisomies.
r.D: Balanced reciprocal translocations involve exchange of segments between nonhomologous chromosomes and do not cause loss of heterozygosity.
r.E: The x3 signal count in dual-fusion FISH reflects one intact probe and two separated probe pieces from the broken allele, not gene amplification.

q.s: SLO 2 / Slides 70-73: Case 3 - Acute promyelocytic leukemia

q.v:
A newborn boy is admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit due to intrauterine growth restriction, hypotonia, and respiratory distress. Physical examination reveals wide-spaced eyes, an absent nasal bone, large anterior and posterior fontanels, hypospadias, and a patent ductus arteriosus. Peripheral blood cytogenetic testing is ordered, and the final report states:
  46,XY,add(4)(p15.2).ish del(4)(p16.3)(WHS-)
Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to determine whether this infant's condition was inherited from a carrier parent?
o: Single nucleotide polymorphism chromosomal microarray on both parents
Standard G-banded karyotyping on peripheral blood from both parents
Interphase FISH for the 22q11.2 region on both parents
Whole-exome sequencing of the infant and both parents
Repeat peripheral blood karyotyping on the infant at one year of age
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that add(4)(p15.2) with deletion of 4p16.3 in Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome indicates an unbalanced translocation likely inherited from a parent with a balanced translocation) -> Step 2 (Select parental chromosome analysis/karyotyping to detect a balanced translocation in a carrier parent)

r.A: Chromosomal microarray cannot detect balanced chromosomal rearrangements, so it would miss a balanced translocation in a phenotypically normal carrier parent.
r.C: The 22q11.2 probe tests for DiGeorge/velocardiofacial syndrome, whereas this infant has Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome involving chromosome 4p.
r.D: Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome with additional chromosomal material on 4p is a structural chromosomal abnormality rather than a single-gene point mutation.
r.E: Repeating the infant's karyotype will not change his constitutional chromosome complement or determine parental carrier status.

q.s: SLO 3 / Slides 83-87: Case 6 - Wolf Hirschhorn syndrome

q.v: Which of the following structural chromosomal abnormalities is considered balanced and results in a normal phenotype in the carrier, even though it involves both the short (p) and long (q) arms and includes the centromere?
o: Paracentric inversion
Pericentric inversion
Robertsonian translocation
Isochromosome formation
Terminal microdeletion
q.p: Step 1 (Identify a balanced structural abnormality within a single chromosome that involves both p and q arms and contains the centromere) -> Step 2 (Match this definition to a pericentric inversion)

r.A: A paracentric inversion is a balanced rearrangement that occurs entirely within one chromosome arm and does not involve the centromere.
r.C: A Robertsonian translocation involves the fusion of the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes with loss of their short (p) arms.
r.D: An isochromosome (noted as i in nomenclature) is an unbalanced structural abnormality with loss of one arm and duplication of the other.
r.E: A terminal microdeletion involves missing genetic material and is therefore an unbalanced structural abnormality.

q.s: SLO 3 / Slide 57: Chromosome inversions

q.v: A 61-year-old man presents with fatigue, night sweats, and splenomegaly. A bone marrow evaluation reveals 100% cellularity with marked myeloid hyperplasia, and cytogenetic analysis shows 46,XY,t(9;22)(q34;q11.2)[20]. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of the targeted therapy indicated for this patient's condition?
o: Binds to the PML-RARA fusion protein and induces promyelocyte differentiation
Inhibits the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase by blocking the ATP binding site
Restores wild-type TP53 tumor suppressor function in 17p13-deleted cells
Blocks microtubule polymerization to arrest leukemic cells in metaphase
Induces degradation of Cyclin D1 in cells carrying the IGH-CCND1 fusion
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize chronic myeloid leukemia with the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22)(q34;q11.2), which creates the BCR::ABL fusion gene) -> Step 2 (Identify the mechanism of imatinib as a tyrosine kinase inhibitor that targets the BCR-ABL fusion protein and blocks ATP binding)

r.A: The PML::RARA fusion results from t(15;17)(q22;q21) in acute promyelocytic leukemia rather than t(9;22) in chronic myeloid leukemia.
r.C: Deletion of 17p13 causes loss of the TP53 tumor suppressor gene in various cancers, which is distinct from the t(9;22) translocation.
r.D: Blocking spindle microtubule formation to arrest cells in metaphase is the laboratory function of colchicine during the karyotyping process, not targeted CML therapy.
r.E: The IGH::CCND1 fusion is seen in multiple myeloma and mantle cell lymphoma rather than chronic myeloid leukemia.

q.s: SLO 3 / Slides 58-60, 67: Cytogenetics in cancer and CML t(9;22) implications for therapy

q.v: Which of the following International System for Human Cytogenomic Nomenclature (ISCN) strings describes a bone marrow specimen with a composite karyotype shared across 10 cells, a normal male clone in 10 cells, and an interphase FISH study showing three copies of the D17Z1 locus?
o: 46,XY,t(9;22)(q34;q11.2)[20].nuc ish (ASS1x2,ABL1x3,BCRx3)(ABL1 con BCRx2)[191/200]
46,XX.ish t(1;22)(1pSubtel-,22qSubtel+;1pSubtel+,22qSubtel-)
q.p: Step 1 (Match the required elements to ISCN symbols: [cp10] for a 10-cell composite karyotype, / for separating distinct clones, and .nuc ish (D17Z1x3) for interphase FISH showing 3 copies of D17Z1) -> Step 2 (Select the matching ISCN nomenclature string)

r.A: This nomenclature string describes an unbalanced Robertsonian translocation resulting in trisomy 13 in a female with a single cell line.
r.B: This nomenclature string denotes a chromosomal microarray result based on reference genome build GRCh38 showing a single-copy deletion on chromosome 11q.
r.D: This nomenclature string describes a single clone with t(9;22) in 20 cells followed by dual-fusion interphase FISH for BCR and ABL1.
r.E: This nomenclature string describes a normal female karyotype followed by metaphase FISH (.ish) showing a cryptic subtelomeric translocation between chromosomes 1 and 22.

q.s: SLO 4 / Slide 30: Cytogenetic Nomenclature

q.v:
A 4-year-old boy is diagnosed with B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). Cytogenetic analysis of his bone marrow aspirate reveals the following result:
  53,XY,+X,+4,+6,+10,+14,+17,+18[18]/46,XY[2]
Based on this cytogenetic finding, which of the following best describes the clinical implication for this patient?
o: High risk for progression to choriocarcinoma
Favorable prognosis associated with hyperdiploidy
Resistance to all standard chemotherapy due to TP53 loss
Requirement for parental karyotyping to rule out a balanced carrier
Diagnosis of constitutional trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome)
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret the ISCN karyotype as an acquired hyperdiploid clone with gain of chromosomes X, 4, 6, 10, 14, 17, and 18 alongside a normal 46,XY cell line in pediatric B-cell ALL) -> Step 2 (Associate hyperdiploidy of these specific chromosomes in pediatric B-cell ALL with a favorable prognosis)

r.A: An elevated risk for choriocarcinoma is associated with complete hydatidiform molar pregnancies, not pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
r.C: Loss of the TP53 tumor suppressor gene is caused by deletion of the short arm of chromosome 17, del(17)(p13), whereas this patient has a whole-chromosome gain (+17).
r.D: The presence of a normal 46,XY cell line and multiple whole-chromosome gains in bone marrow indicates an acquired somatic cancer abnormality rather than an inherited translocation.
r.E: Although +18 is present in the leukemic clone, the normal 46,XY cell line confirms that thetrisomies are somatic changes in the leukemia rather than constitutional Edwards syndrome.

q.s: SLO 4 / Slides 30, 58: Cytogenetic Nomenclature and Cytogenetics in cancer
