q.v: A 26-year-old medical student participates in a metabolic study evaluating fuel utilization during a prolonged fast. Sixteen hours after his last meal, ingested glucose has been completely cleared and his hepatic glycogen stores are rapidly depleting. As his liver transitions to synthesizing new glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors to support his brain and erythrocytes, the breakdown of stored triacylglycerols in adipose tissue increases markedly. In addition to free fatty acids being oxidized to generate the ATP required for this process, which of the following triacylglycerol-derived molecules feeds directly into the gluconeogenic pathway as a carbon substrate?
o: Acetyl-CoA
Glycerol
Leucine
Lysine
Malate
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that triacylglycerol breakdown during fasting yields free fatty acids and glycerol) -> Step 2 (Determine that glycerol feeds directly into the gluconeogenic pathway as a substrate, whereas free fatty acids only provide ATP)

r.A: Acetyl-CoA is generated from free fatty acid breakdown to enter the TCA cycle and provide energy, and it allosterically activates pyruvate carboxylase rather than serving as a direct carbon substrate for glucose synthesis.
r.C: Leucine is a strictly ketogenic amino acid derived from protein breakdown and cannot be used as a substrate for gluconeogenesis.
r.D: Lysine is a strictly ketogenic amino acid derived from protein breakdown and cannot be used to synthesize new glucose.
r.E: Malate is a shuttle intermediate used to transport oxaloacetate out of the mitochondria into the cytosol rather than a product of triacylglycerol breakdown.

q.s: Slide 5: Gluconeogenesis (inputs) Overview; Slide 6: Summary: Substrates for Gluconeogenesis

q.v: A 42-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue and paresthesias after adhering to a strict vegan diet without supplementation for several years. Laboratory studies confirm a severe vitamin B12 deficiency. Because vitamin B12 is required to convert specific amino acid carbon skeletons into succinyl-CoA for entry into the citric acid cycle, this patient has an impaired ability to utilize which of the following groups of amino acids for gluconeogenesis during a fast?
o: Tryptophan, isoleucine, phenylalanine, tyrosine
Leucine and lysine
Valine, isoleucine, threonine, methionine
Alanine, lactate, glycerol
Phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the acronym for amino acids requiring vitamin B12 to form succinyl-CoA: VITM) -> Step 2 (Match the 1-letter amino acid codes V, I, T, M to valine, isoleucine, threonine, and methionine)

r.A: Tryptophan, isoleucine, phenylalanine, and tyrosine (along with threonine) represent the WIFTY acronym for amino acids that are both glucogenic and ketogenic, not the specific group requiring vitamin B12 to form succinyl-CoA.
r.B: Leucine and lysine (LK) are exclusively ketogenic amino acids and cannot enter the gluconeogenic pathway even when vitamin B12 levels are normal.
r.D: Lactate and glycerol are non-amino acid gluconeogenic precursors that enter via pyruvate and the triose phosphate stage, respectively, independent of vitamin B12.
r.E: Phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan are aromatic amino acids from the WIFTY group that are both glucogenic and ketogenic, rather than the VITM group requiring vitamin B12.

q.s: Slide 7: SLO1 Review (My AA acronyms: -> Succinyl CoA VITM needs vitamin B12)

q.v: A hepatocyte is actively synthesizing glucose from lactate delivered via the Cori cycle during an overnight fast. After lactate is converted to pyruvate in the cytoplasm, pyruvate enters the mitochondria and is carboxylated to oxaloacetate by pyruvate carboxylase. Because the inner mitochondrial membrane is impermeable to oxaloacetate, it must be converted into an intermediate via the malate shuttle to exit into the cytosol. What is the immediate enzymatic reaction that occurs once this shuttle intermediate enters the cytosol to allow gluconeogenesis to continue?
o: Reduction of oxaloacetate using NADH
Re-oxidation of malate to oxaloacetate generating NADH
Decarboxylation of malate directly to phosphoenolpyruvate using ATP
Cleavage of glucose-6-phosphate in the endoplasmic reticulum
Carboxylation of pyruvate to oxaloacetate using ATP
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that mitochondrial oxaloacetate is reduced to malate to cross into the cytosol via the malate shuttle) -> Step 2 (Determine that once in the cytosol, malate is re-oxidized to oxaloacetate, reducing NAD+ to NADH, before PEP carboxykinase converts it to PEP)

r.A: Reduction of oxaloacetate to malate using NADH occurs inside the mitochondria prior to transport, not after entering the cytosol.
r.C: Malate is not directly decarboxylated to phosphoenolpyruvate; it must first be re-oxidized to oxaloacetate, which is then converted to phosphoenolpyruvate using GTP.
r.D: Cleavage of glucose-6-phosphate by glucose-6-phosphatase occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum at the final step of gluconeogenesis, not immediately following mitochondrial transport.
r.E: Carboxylation of pyruvate to oxaloacetate occurs inside the mitochondria via pyruvate carboxylase, not in the cytosol.

q.s: Slide 10: Malate Shuttle for oxaloacetate transport; Slide 11: Malate Shuttle

q.v: A researcher is studying the energetic efficiency of hepatic carbohydrate metabolism in isolated hepatocytes. She traces the complete conversion of two molecules of pyruvate into one molecule of free glucose via the gluconeogenic pathway, bypassing the three irreversible steps of glycolysis. How many total high-energy phosphate equivalents (ATP/GTP) and reducing equivalents (NADH) are consumed to build one molecule of glucose from pyruvate, and what is the primary metabolic source of this energy during fasting?
o: 2 ATP and 2 NADH; derived from anaerobic glycolysis
4 ATP and 1 NADH; derived from glycogenolysis
6 ATP and 2 NADH; derived from fatty acid breakdown to acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle
6 ATP and 0 NADH; derived from the pentose phosphate pathway
2 ATP and 6 NADH; derived from the Cori cycle
q.p: Step 1 (Determine the stoichiometric energy cost of building one glucose molecule in gluconeogenesis) -> Step 2 (Identify that 6 ATP and 2 NADH are required, and this energy comes from fatty acids being broken down to acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle)

r.A: Two ATP and 2 NADH represent the net yield of glycolysis rather than the energetic cost of building a glucose molecule via gluconeogenesis.
r.B: Building a molecule of glucose requires 6 ATP equivalents and 2 NADH, and glycogenolysis does not supply the primary ATP for hepatic gluconeogenesis.
r.D: Gluconeogenesis requires 2 molecules of NADH in addition to 6 ATP, and the pentose phosphate pathway is not the primary energy source during fasting.
r.E: The stoichiometry of 2 ATP and 6 NADH is inverted, and the Cori cycle delivers lactate as a carbon substrate rather than serving as the hepatic ATP source.

q.s: Slide 8: Bypassing Glycolysis Enzymes; Slide 9: Gluconeogenesis (key enzymes)

q.v: A 19-year-old woman is evaluated after fasting for 20 hours prior to an elective procedure. Her plasma glucagon levels are significantly elevated while insulin levels are suppressed. In her hepatocytes, glucagon signaling activates FBPase2, leading to a marked change in the intracellular concentration of a key allosteric regulator. How does the glucagon-induced change in this regulator simultaneously coordinate the rates of glycolysis and gluconeogenesis?
o: Increases fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, which inhibits PFK-1 and activates fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase
Decreases fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, which removes activation of PFK-1 and relieves inhibition of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase
Increases AMP, which activates pyruvate carboxylase and inhibits pyruvate kinase
Decreases acetyl-CoA, which activates PEP carboxykinase and inhibits hexokinase
Increases citrate, which inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and activates PFK-1
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that glucagon activates FBPase2, which decreases intracellular fructose-2,6-bisphosphate levels) -> Step 2 (Deduce that lower fructose-2,6-bisphosphate removes allosteric activation of PFK-1 and relieves allosteric inhibition of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase)

r.A: Glucagon decreases rather than increases fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is an activator of PFK-1 and an inhibitor of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase.
r.C: Elevated AMP indicates a low-energy state that inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (gluconeogenesis) and activates PFK-1 and pyruvate kinase (glycolysis).
r.D: Fatty acid oxidation during fasting increases acetyl-CoA, which allosterically activates pyruvate carboxylase and inhibits pyruvate kinase.
r.E: Citrate inhibits PFK-1 rather than activating it, and it is not the hormone-regulated bisphosphate controlled by FBPase2.

q.s: Slide 13: Gluconeogenesis Regulation; Slide 14: Insulin vs Glucagon Regulation Diagram

q.v: During a sprint, a 22-year-old athlete experiences a rapid surge in circulating epinephrine. Both his hepatocytes and skeletal muscle cells respond to epinephrine by increasing glycogen breakdown, yet his liver exports glucose into the blood while his skeletal muscle rapidly consumes glucose-6-phosphate via glycolysis. Beyond the absence of glucose-6-phosphatase in muscle, which of the following tissue-specific differences explains why epinephrine promotes glycolysis in skeletal muscle while glucagon and epinephrine inhibit glycolysis in the liver?
o: Skeletal muscle cells lack the glucagon receptor and express a PFK2 isoform that is activated by phosphorylation
Skeletal muscle cells express a hexokinase isoform that is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate
Hepatocytes lack protein kinase A and rely exclusively on protein phosphatase 1 to regulate PFK2
Skeletal muscle glycogen phosphorylase produces free glucose directly instead of glucose-1-phosphate
Epinephrine activates protein phosphatase 1 in skeletal muscle to dephosphorylate glycogen synthase
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the divergent glycolytic response to epinephrine/cAMP signaling in skeletal muscle versus liver) -> Step 2 (Recognize that muscle cells lack the glucagon receptor and their PFK2 isoform is less sensitive or activated by phosphorylation, promoting glycolysis in response to epinephrine)

r.B: Hexokinase is allosterically inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate, whereas liver glucokinase is not; this does not explain epinephrine-mediated activation of muscle glycolysis.
r.C: Hepatocytes utilize Gs, adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, and protein kinase A (PKA) to mediate glucagon and norepinephrine signaling.
r.D: Glycogen phosphorylase in both liver and muscle cleaves alpha-1,4 linkages to yield glucose-1-phosphate, not free glucose.
r.E: Epinephrine acts via cAMP and PKA to phosphorylate and activate glycogen phosphorylase (via phosphorylase kinase) while phosphorylating and inhibiting glycogen synthase; insulin activates protein phosphatase 1.

q.s: Slide 22: Regulation of glycogen synthase and phosphorylase (Note box)

q.v: Following a carbohydrate-rich meal, a 30-year-old man has elevated plasma insulin levels, stimulating glycogenesis in his hepatocytes and skeletal muscle. Glucose enters the cells, is phosphorylated to glucose-6-phosphate, and is subsequently converted to glucose-1-phosphate and then UDP-glucose. As the glycogen polymer is synthesized from a core protein primer, how do the enzymes of glycogenesis construct the normal branched structure of the molecule?
o: Debranching enzyme forms alpha-1,4 linkages on glycogenin while glycogen phosphorylase adds alpha-1,6 branches
Glycogenin elongates the main chain via alpha-1,6 linkages while glycogen synthase creates periodic alpha-1,4 branch points
Glycogen synthase elongates the chain with alpha-1,4 linkages from the glycogenin primer while branching enzyme creates periodic alpha-1,6 linkages
Phosphoglucomutase links UDP-glucose units via alpha-1,4 bonds while UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase creates alpha-1,6 branches
Glycogen synthase cleaves four terminal glucose residues and reattaches three of them via an alpha-1,6 linkage
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the enzymes and substrates involved in glycogen synthesis: glycogenin, glycogen synthase, and branching enzyme) -> Step 2 (Determine that glycogen synthase elongates the chain with alpha-1,4 linkages while branching enzyme introduces periodic alpha-1,6 linkages that can be further elongated)

r.A: Debranching enzyme and glycogen phosphorylase are catabolic enzymes of glycogenolysis, not anabolic enzymes of glycogenesis.
r.B: Main chains are linked by alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds and branch points are linked by alpha-1,6 glycosidic bonds, not vice versa.
r.D: Phosphoglucomutase interconverts glucose-6-phosphate and glucose-1-phosphate, and UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase forms UDP-glucose; neither directly polymerizes the glycogen chain.
r.E: Removing three of four remaining glucose residues near a branch point and transferring them is the mechanism of debranching enzyme during glycogenolysis.

q.s: Slide 18: Glycogen; Slide 19: Glycogenesis

q.v: Biochemical analysis of hepatic glycogen breakdown is performed on tissue samples during early fasting. Glycogen phosphorylase, utilizing its required cofactor, cleaves sequential alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds along an outer branch of glycogen to release glucose-1-phosphate until it halts four glucose residues away from an alpha-1,6 branch point. What cofactor is required by glycogen phosphorylase, and how does the debranching enzyme process the remaining four glucose residues so degradation can continue?
o: Vitamin B12; it hydrolyzes all four remaining glucose residues directly into free glucose
Vitamin B6 (PLP); it transfers a strand of three glucoses to the end of another branch via an alpha-1,4 linkage and hydrolyzes the single remaining alpha-1,6 glucose
Biotin; it converts the remaining four glucose residues directly into UDP-glucose
Vitamin B6 (PLP); it cleaves the alpha-1,6 bond first so the four-glucose chain is released intact as maltose
Thiamine pyrophosphate; it phosphorylates the alpha-1,6 branch point to release four molecules of glucose-6-phosphate
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that glycogen phosphorylase requires vitamin B6/PLP and stops when 4 glucoses remain at a branch) -> Step 2 (Determine that debranching enzyme removes 3 of the 4 glucoses, adds them to another branch via an alpha-1,4 linkage, and hydrolyzes the 1 remaining glucose)

r.A: Vitamin B12 is required for converting VITM amino acids to succinyl-CoA, and debranching enzyme only hydrolyzes the single glucose residue at the alpha-1,6 linkage after transferring the other three.
r.C: Biotin is not the cofactor for glycogen phosphorylase, and UDP-glucose is an intermediate of glycogenesis rather than glycogenolysis.
r.D: Although vitamin B6 (PLP) is the correct cofactor, debranching enzyme first transfers a strand of three glucoses via an alpha-1,4 linkage before hydrolyzing the single remaining glucose.
r.E: Glycogen phosphorylase requires B6/PLP, and debranching enzyme releases free unphosphorylated glucose via hydrolysis of the final residue, not glucose-6-phosphate.

q.s: Slide 21: Glycogenolysis

q.v: Two pediatric patients are evaluated in a metabolic clinic for hepatomegaly and fasting hypoglycemia. Patient A has a deficiency in glucose-6-phosphatase (Von Gierke disease), whereas Patient B has a deficiency in glycogen debranching enzyme (Cori disease). Although both disorders impair glycogenolysis, Patient A suffers from much more severe fasting hypoglycemia accompanied by marked lactic acidosis, hyperlipidemia, and hyperuricemia, while Patient B has milder hypoglycemia and normal serum lactate levels. Which of the following best explains why Patient B is spared from severe lactic acidosis and experiences milder hypoglycemia compared to Patient A?
o: Patient B can still synthesize glucose via gluconeogenesis and release glucose-1-phosphate from outer glycogen branches, whereas Patient A blocks the final step of both gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis
Patient B has a compensatory upregulation of lysosomal alpha-1,4-glucosidase that exports free glucose from muscle into the blood
Patient A accumulates abnormal glycogen with long unbranched chains that cause liver cirrhosis, whereas Patient B has completely normal glycogen structure
Patient B lacks hepatic hexokinase, preventing glucose-6-phosphate from entering glycolysis to form pyruvate and lactate
Patient A can only utilize fatty acids for gluconeogenesis, whereas Patient B can convert leucine and lysine into glucose
q.p: Step 1 (Compare the enzymatic blocks in Von Gierke disease [glucose-6-phosphatase] versus Cori disease [debranching enzyme]) -> Step 2 (Deduce that glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency blocks the final step of both gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, trapping G6P and shunting it into glycolysis/lactate, PPP/uric acid, and lipids, whereas Cori disease leaves gluconeogenesis intact)

r.B: Lysosomal alpha-1,4-glucosidase (mutated in Pompe disease) prevents lysosomal glycogen accumulation in muscle and does not compensate for hepatic debranching enzyme deficiency.
r.C: Long chains with few branches causing cirrhosis are characteristic of Andersen disease (Type IV, branching enzyme deficiency), while Cori disease produces short outer branches and Von Gierke has normal glycogen structure.
r.D: Both patients have intact glycolytic enzymes; Patient A develops lactic acidosis because trapped glucose-6-phosphate is forced down glycolysis into pyruvate and lactate.
r.E: Neither patient can convert fatty acids, leucine, or lysine into glucose, as these cannot serve as net carbon substrates for gluconeogenesis.

q.s: Slide 24: Glycogen Storage disease type I; Slide 26: Cori (III) and Andersen (IV); Slide 27: Von Gierke Disease vs Cori Disease

q.v: A 6-year-old boy is evaluated for asymptomatic hepatomegaly noted on a routine physical examination. Laboratory evaluation after an overnight fast reveals mild ketotic hypoglycemia, normal serum lactate, and normal uric acid levels. Liver biopsy demonstrates increased amounts of structurally normal glycogen, and enzymatic assay confirms a deficiency in the hepatic isoform of glycogen phosphorylase. The physician reassures the parents that this is a relatively benign condition that adults often grow out of. Which glycogen storage disease does this patient have, and how does it differ from a deficiency in the skeletal muscle isoform of the same enzyme?
o: Pompe disease; the muscle isoform deficiency causes fatal infantile cardiomyopathy due to lysosomal inclusion bodies
Andersen disease; the muscle isoform deficiency causes severe hepatic cirrhosis and early death
Hers disease; the muscle isoform deficiency (McArdle disease) presents in adolescence with exercise-induced muscle cramps, tea-colored urine, and a pathognomonic 'second wind' phenomenon
GSD Type 0; the muscle isoform deficiency results in a complete absence of glycogen stores and severe fasting ketosis
Von Gierke disease; the muscle isoform deficiency causes glucose-6-translocase dysfunction and nephromegaly
q.p: Step 1 (Identify hepatic glycogen phosphorylase deficiency presenting with hepatomegaly, mild ketotic hypoglycemia, and normal glycogen structure as Hers disease, Type VI) -> Step 2 (Contrast this with the muscle isoform mutation, McArdle disease [Type V], which causes adolescent exercise intolerance, rhabdomyolysis/tea-colored urine, and the 'second wind' phenomenon)

r.A: Pompe disease (Type II) is caused by a mutation in lysosomal alpha-1,4-glucosidase (alpha-1,6-glucosidase), not glycogen phosphorylase.
r.B: Andersen disease (Type IV) is caused by branching enzyme deficiency resulting in abnormal glycogen with few branches, not hepatic glycogen phosphorylase deficiency.
r.D: GSD Type 0 is caused by glycogen synthase deficiency, which results in an absence of glycogen rather than normal glycogen stores.
r.E: Von Gierke disease (Type I) is caused by glucose-6-phosphatase (1A) or glucose-6-translocase (1B) deficiency and causes severe hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis.

q.s: Slide 28: McArdle (V) and Hers (VI); Slide 29: Glycogen storage diseases table

q.v: A 34-year-old man participates in a fasting study and has not eaten for 36 hours. During this time, hormone-sensitive lipase breaks down triacylglycerols in his adipose tissue into free fatty acids and glycerol to support hepatic glucose production. Which of the following best describes the respective roles of these two lipid breakdown products in hepatic gluconeogenesis?
o: Free fatty acids enter the Cori cycle; glycerol allosterically activates pyruvate kinase
Free fatty acids are converted to oxaloacetate; glycerol provides NADH via beta-oxidation
Free fatty acids provide ATP via beta-oxidation; glycerol serves directly as a carbon substrate
Free fatty acids are converted to pyruvate; glycerol allosterically activates fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase
Free fatty acids serve directly as a carbon substrate; glycerol provides ATP via the TCA cycle
q.p: Step 1 (Triacylglycerol breakdown yields free fatty acids and glycerol) -> Step 2 (Free fatty acid breakdown produces ATP required for gluconeogenesis while glycerol feeds directly into gluconeogenesis as a substrate)

r.A: Lactate, rather than free fatty acids, is the muscle-derived intermediate that participates in the Cori cycle, and pyruvate kinase is a glycolytic enzyme bypassed during gluconeogenesis.
r.B: Free fatty acids are broken down to acetyl-CoA, which cannot be used for net oxaloacetate synthesis, and beta-oxidation oxidizes fatty acids rather than glycerol.
r.D: Mammals cannot convert free fatty acids into pyruvate, and glycerol enters the pathway as a phosphorylated intermediate rather than acting as an allosteric regulator.
r.E: This option reverses the roles of the two molecules: glycerol provides the carbon skeleton for glucose synthesis, whereas fatty acid breakdown supplies the ATP needed to drive the pathway.

q.s: SLO 1, Slide 5: Gluconeogenesis (inputs) Overview

q.v: During gluconeogenesis, three irreversible steps of glycolysis must be circumvented by four specialized bypass enzymes located in different cellular compartments. Which of the following gluconeogenic bypass enzymes is located in the endoplasmic reticulum and requires a specific translocase for its substrate to enter?
o: Pyruvate carboxylase
Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase
Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase
Glucose-6-phosphatase
Glycogen phosphorylase
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the four bypass enzymes of gluconeogenesis) -> Step 2 (Localize glucose-6-phosphatase to the endoplasmic reticulum where it requires glucose-6-translocase to transport glucose-6-phosphate)

r.A: Pyruvate carboxylase is located in the mitochondria, where it catalyzes the carboxylation of pyruvate to oxaloacetate.
r.B: Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase functions in the cytoplasm to convert re-oxidized oxaloacetate into phosphoenolpyruvate.
r.C: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase is a cytoplasmic enzyme that bypasses phosphofructokinase-1 by dephosphorylating fructose-1,6-bisphosphate.
r.E: Glycogen phosphorylase is the rate-limiting cytoplasmic enzyme of glycogenolysis and is not one of the four gluconeogenic bypass enzymes.

q.s: SLO 2, Slide 8: Bypassing Glycolysis Enzymes and Slide 24: Glycogen Storage disease type I

q.v: Which of the following allosteric regulators simultaneously stimulates phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) in glycolysis and inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase in gluconeogenesis?
o: Acetyl-CoA
Citrate
ATP
Alanine
Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the reciprocal regulatory step between PFK-1 and FBPase-1) -> Step 2 (Determine that fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and AMP activate PFK-1 while inhibiting FBPase-1)

r.A: Acetyl-CoA is an allosteric activator of pyruvate carboxylase in gluconeogenesis and an inhibitor of pyruvate kinase in glycolysis.
r.B: Citrate is an allosteric inhibitor of phosphofructokinase-1 that signals a high-energy state, rather than an activator of glycolysis.
r.C: ATP allosterically inhibits both phosphofructokinase-1 and pyruvate kinase in glycolysis when cellular energy levels are high.
r.D: Alanine is an allosteric inhibitor of pyruvate kinase in glycolysis and serves as a glucogenic amino acid substrate for gluconeogenesis.

q.s: SLO 3, Slide 14: Gluconeogenesis Regulation

q.v:
A researcher isolates hepatocytes to study the allosteric regulation of carbohydrate metabolism under varying cellular energy states. She adds different metabolic intermediates to the cell lysates and measures the resulting activity of key glycolytic and gluconeogenic enzymes:
  Enzyme X: inhibited by ATP, citrate, and glucagon signaling; activated by AMP
  Enzyme Y: inhibited by ATP, acetyl-CoA, and alanine; activated by fructose-2,6-bisphosphate
  Enzyme Z: activated by acetyl-CoA; stimulated by glucagon signaling
Which of the following correctly identifies Enzymes X, Y, and Z?
o: Hexokinase / Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase / PEP carboxykinase
Phosphofructokinase-1 / Pyruvate kinase / Pyruvate carboxylase
Pyruvate kinase / Phosphofructokinase-1 / Glucose-6-phosphatase
Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase / Hexokinase / Pyruvate carboxylase
Pyruvate carboxylase / Pyruvate kinase / Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase
q.p: Step 1 (Match the allosteric inhibitor profiles of ATP/citrate to PFK-1 and ATP/acetyl-CoA/alanine to pyruvate kinase) -> Step 2 (Match acetyl-CoA activation to pyruvate carboxylase)

r.A: Hexokinase is inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate rather than citrate, and PEP carboxykinase is not directly allosterically activated by acetyl-CoA.
r.C: Pyruvate kinase is inhibited by alanine and acetyl-CoA rather than citrate, and glucose-6-phosphatase is not allosterically activated by acetyl-CoA.
r.D: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase is inhibited, not activated, by AMP, and hexokinase is not regulated by alanine or fructose-2,6-bisphosphate.
r.E: Pyruvate carboxylase requires ATP and is activated by acetyl-CoA, whereas fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase is inhibited by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate.

q.s: SLO 3, Slide 13 and Slide 14: Gluconeogenesis Regulation

q.v: A 28-year-old woman consumes a high-carbohydrate meal, causing a rapid rise in her plasma insulin-to-glucagon ratio. In her hepatocytes, insulin binds to its receptor and activates protein kinase B (AKT), which subsequently stimulates a specific intracellular enzyme to reciprocally regulate glycogen synthase and glycogen phosphorylase. Which of the following enzymes directly removes phosphate groups to activate glycogen synthase and inhibit glycogen phosphorylase in this state?
o: Protein kinase A
Adenylyl cyclase
Protein phosphatase 1
Phosphorylase kinase
UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase
q.p: Step 1 (Insulin binds its receptor and activates AKT in the hepatocyte) -> Step 2 (AKT activates protein phosphatase 1, which dephosphorylates to activate glycogen synthase and inhibit glycogen phosphorylase)

r.A: Protein kinase A is activated by cAMP in response to glucagon or epinephrine and phosphorylates glycogen synthase to inhibit it.
r.B: Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP into cAMP following G-protein activation by glucagon or norepinephrine receptors.
r.D: Phosphorylase kinase is stimulated via the cAMP cascade to phosphorylate and activate glycogen phosphorylase during fasting or exercise.
r.E: UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase converts glucose-1-phosphate into UDP-glucose for chain elongation rather than regulating enzyme phosphorylation states.

q.s: SLO 4, Slide 20: Glycogenesis/Glycogenolysis and Slide 22: Regulation of glycogen synthase and phosphorylase

q.v: Which of the following cofactors is required by glycogen phosphorylase to cleave alpha-1,4 glycosidic linkages during glycogenolysis?
o: Cobalamin (Vitamin B12)
Pyridoxal phosphate (Vitamin B6)
Biotin (Vitamin B7)
Thiamine pyrophosphate (Vitamin B1)
Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (Vitamin B3)
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the reaction catalyzed by glycogen phosphorylase: cleavage of alpha-1,4 bonds to yield glucose-1-phosphate) -> Step 2 (Recall that glycogen phosphorylase requires vitamin B6 / PLP as its essential cofactor)

r.A: Vitamin B12 is required for the conversion of propionyl-CoA (from valine, isoleucine, threonine, and methionine) to succinyl-CoA, not for glycogen phosphorylase.
r.C: Biotin is typically used in carboxylation reactions and is not the cofactor for glycogen phosphorylase.
r.D: Thiamine pyrophosphate is not involved in the phosphorolytic cleavage of alpha-1,4 linkages in glycogen.
r.E: NADH/NAD+ is used by the malate shuttle and lactate dehydrogenase, whereas glycogen phosphorylase requires pyridoxal phosphate (B6/PLP).

q.s: SLO 4, Slide 21: Glycogenolysis

q.v:
A 5-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department after experiencing a generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. Her parents state that she recently began sleeping through the night and missed her usual midnight feeding. Physical examination reveals hepatomegaly and renomegaly. Laboratory studies show:
  Serum glucose: 28 mg/dL
  Serum lactate: elevated
  Serum triglycerides: elevated
  Serum uric acid: elevated
The physician recommends initiating nighttime feedings with uncooked cornstarch. A deficiency in which of the following proteins would produce a clinical and biochemical presentation identical to glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency in this patient?
o: Glucose-6-translocase
Lysosomal alpha-1,4-glucosidase
Glycogen debranching enzyme
Glycogen branching enzyme
Hepatic glycogen phosphorylase
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize Von Gierke disease / GSD Type I from severe fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia, and renomegaly treated with cornstarch) -> Step 2 (Identify that GSD Type IB is caused by a mutation in glucose-6-translocase, which blocks the same final step of gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis as G6Pase deficiency)

r.B: Lysosomal alpha-1,4-glucosidase deficiency causes Pompe disease (Type II), which presents with hypotonia and cardiomegaly without severe fasting lactic acidosis.
r.C: Glycogen debranching enzyme deficiency causes Cori disease (Type III), which presents with milder hypoglycemia, normal serum lactate, and no renal involvement.
r.D: Glycogen branching enzyme deficiency causes Andersen disease (Type IV), which leads to hepatic cirrhosis and early death from abnormal glycogen chains.
r.E: Hepatic glycogen phosphorylase deficiency causes Hers disease (Type VI), a benign condition presenting with hepatomegaly and mild ketotic hypoglycemia without lactic acidosis.

q.s: SLO 5, Slide 3: Von Gierke Disease and Slide 24: Glycogen Storage disease type I

q.v: A 4-month-old boy is admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit for progressive respiratory distress, poor feeding, and generalized weakness. Physical examination reveals profound hypotonia and a displaced apical impulse. A chest radiograph demonstrates massive cardiomegaly. Laboratory studies show normal blood glucose and normal serum lactate levels. A skeletal muscle biopsy stained with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) reveals large intracellular inclusion bodies filled with normal-structured glycogen. Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of muscle damage in this patient's disorder?
o: Inability to generate glucose-1-phosphate for anaerobic glycolysis during muscle contraction
Accumulation of toxic glycogen molecules with abnormally long, unbranched outer chains
Disruption of myofibrils by lysosomal buildup of undegraded glycogen rather than energy deficiency
Diversion of trapped glucose-6-phosphate into the pentose phosphate pathway and fatty acid synthesis
Depletion of hepatic glycogen stores leading to systemic energy starvation of cardiac muscle
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize Pompe disease / GSD Type II from infantile hypotonia, cardiomegaly, and PAS-positive glycogen inclusion bodies) -> Step 2 (Identify that cellular damage results from lysosomal buildup of glycogen due to alpha-1,4-glucosidase mutation, not from energy deficiency)

r.A: Failure to generate glucose-1-phosphate from muscle glycogen during exercise describes McArdle disease (Type V), which presents in adolescence with cramps and myoglobinuria.
r.B: Accumulation of abnormal glycogen with long outer chains and few branches describes Andersen disease (Type IV), which triggers an inflammatory response and cirrhosis in the liver.
r.D: Shunting of trapped glucose-6-phosphate into glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway, and lipid synthesis occurs in the liver in Von Gierke disease (Type I).
r.E: Depletion of hepatic glycogen stores due to defective synthesis occurs in glycogen synthase deficiency (Type 0), which causes fasting ketotic hypoglycemia rather than cardiomegaly.

q.s: SLO 5, Slide 25: Pompe Disease (Type II)

q.v: A 10-month-old girl is evaluated by a pediatric gastroenterologist for failure to thrive, progressive abdominal distension, and jaundice. Physical examination reveals firm hepatosplenomegaly and ascites. Liver biopsy histology demonstrates diffuse hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis, along with accumulated glycogen particles that have very few branch points and abnormally long outer chains. Despite supportive care, the patient's liver failure worsens. Which of the following is the most definitive treatment for this patient's underlying condition?
o: Nighttime uncooked cornstarch feedings
Intravenous enzyme replacement therapy
Avoidance of strenuous anaerobic exercise
Liver transplantation
Oral pyridoxine (vitamin B6) supplementation
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize Andersen disease / GSD Type IV from infantile cirrhosis and abnormal glycogen with few branches and long chains due to branching enzyme mutation) -> Step 2 (Identify that management requires diet, supportive care, and liver transplantation)

r.A: Nighttime uncooked cornstarch feedings are used to prevent severe fasting hypoglycemia in Von Gierke disease (Type I), not to reverse cirrhosis in Andersen disease.
r.B: Enzyme replacement therapy is a key treatment for Pompe disease (Type II) to clear lysosomal glycogen accumulation in muscle.
r.C: Modifying exercise intensity to reach a 'second wind' is used to manage muscle cramps and myoglobinuria in McArdle disease (Type V).
r.E: Pyridoxine is the cofactor for glycogen phosphorylase, whereas this patient has a deficiency in glycogen branching enzyme.

q.s: SLO 5, Slide 26: Cori (III) and Andersen (IV)

q.v:
A 14-year-old girl presents to the clinic with painful muscle cramps and stiffness that occur shortly after she begins running during track practice. She notes that if she slows down and rests briefly when the pain starts, she can resume running without discomfort, a phenomenon her coach calls a 'second wind.' Yesterday, after pushing through the initial pain during a sprint, she noticed her urine was dark brown and tea-colored. A diagnostic workup is performed and compared against other glycogen storage disorders:
  Serum glucose (fasting): 85 mg/dL (normal)
  Serum lactate (fasting): normal
  Serum creatine kinase (post-exercise): markedly elevated
  Muscle biopsy glycogen structure: normal α-1,4 and α-1,6 branching
Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this patient?
o: Glycogen synthase
Glucose-6-phosphatase
Glycogen debranching enzyme
Muscle glycogen phosphorylase
Hepatic glycogen phosphorylase
q.p: Step 1 (Interpret the clinical and lab data: adolescent onset, exercise cramps, second wind phenomenon, tea-colored urine/myoglobinuria, elevated CK, normal fasting glucose/lactate, and normal glycogen structure indicate McArdle disease / GSD Type V) -> Step 2 (Identify the deficient enzyme as muscle glycogen phosphorylase / myophosphorylase)

r.A: Glycogen synthase deficiency (Type 0) results in an absence of stored glycogen and presents with fasting hypoglycemia and ketosis.
r.B: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (Type I) affects the liver and kidney, presenting in infancy with severe fasting hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis.
r.C: Glycogen debranching enzyme deficiency (Type III) results in abnormal glycogen with short outer branches (limit dextrins) and causes fasting hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly.
r.E: Hepatic glycogen phosphorylase deficiency (Type VI) affects only the liver isoform, causing hepatomegaly and mild ketotic hypoglycemia rather than exercise-induced myoglobinuria.

q.s: SLO 5, Slide 28: McArdle (V) and Hers (VI) and Slide 29: Glycogen storage diseases

add.cloze: Transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair differs from global genome NER by focusing on DNA lesions that {{c1::block RNA polymerase}} in actively transcribed genes
add.extra: Global genome NER scans the whole genome; both remove bulky, helix-distorting lesions such as pyrimidine dimers

add.cloze: The ATM protein (mutated in ataxia-telangiectasia) is a {{c1::kinase}} that {{c2::senses double-strand breaks}} and orchestrates their repair
add.extra: Activates p53 and cell-cycle checkpoints; loss → ataxia, telangiectasias, immunodeficiency, lymphoma/leukemia

add.cloze: A characteristic physical finding in males with Fragile X syndrome after puberty is {{c1::macroorchidism}}
add.extra: Also long face, large jaw, large everted ears, mitral valve prolapse, autism; CGG repeat in FMR1

add.cloze: Fragile X premutation carriers may later develop {{c1::fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS)}}, with intention tremor and ataxia
add.extra: Female premutation carriers are also at risk of primary ovarian insufficiency

add.cloze: Huntington disease is caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene; CAG encodes {{c1::glutamine}}
add.extra: Polyglutamine expansion; autosomal dominant with anticipation (paternal transmission)

add.cloze: Myotonia in myotonic dystrophy is {{c1::difficulty relaxing muscles after contraction}}
add.extra: Classic example: inability to release a handshake or grip. CTG repeat in DMPK.

add.cloze: {{c1::Homologous recombination}} misdirected by misaligned low-copy repeats causes {{c2::interstitial deletion (microdeletion) syndromes}}
add.extra: Examples: 22q11 deletion syndrome, Williams syndrome (7q11.23), Prader-Willi/Angelman (15q11-13), cri-du-chat (5p)

q.v: A researcher is studying the baseline fidelity of genomic replication in proliferating mammalian cells. During DNA synthesis, the replicative enzyme misincorporates a nucleotide approximately once every 100,000 bases, yet ~99% of these errors are immediately resolved before the replication fork advances. Which of the following enzymatic activities is directly responsible for correcting this initial subset of errors?
o: 5' to 3' endonuclease cleavage
3' to 5' proofreading exonuclease
N-glycosidic bond hydrolysis
ATP-dependent helicase unwinding
3' phosphodiester bond lyase
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that DNA polymerase corrects ~99% of its 1 in 10^5 replication errors immediately via proofreading) -> Step 2 (Determine that the specific enzymatic mechanism of DNA polymerase proofreading is 3' to 5' exonuclease activity).

r.A: Endonuclease cleavage at the 5' phosphodiester bond is performed by AP endonuclease during base excision repair, not by DNA polymerase during replication.
r.C: Hydrolysis of the N-glycosidic bond is catalyzed by DNA glycosylases to initiate base excision repair of modified bases.
r.D: Helicase unwinding is utilized during nucleotide excision repair to release a 27-29 nucleotide damaged oligomer, not for polymerase proofreading.
r.E: Cleavage of the 3' phosphodiester bond to remove a sugar is performed by AP lyase during base excision repair.

q.s: Slide 6: Causes of Mutations & Slide 7: Replication Errors

q.v: A molecular biologist isolates a mutant cell line that exhibits a 1,000-fold increase in spontaneous point mutations following cellular division. Biochemical assays reveal that the replicative DNA polymerase has normal 3' to 5' exonuclease activity, but the cells fail to resolve rare mispaired bases (such as an A~G pair) before the next round of DNA synthesis. If left uncorrected prior to the subsequent replication cycle, what is the immediate fate of this mispaired lesion?
o: It causes permanent arrest of the RNA polymerase transcription complex
It spontaneously converts into an apurinic site via purine loss
It becomes fixed as a stabilized mutation in one of the daughter duplexes
It induces covalent cross-linking between adjacent pyrimidine bases
It triggers recombinase-mediated chromosomal translocation
q.p: Step 1 (Identify a replication error that escapes proofreading and creates a mismatched base pair, such as A~G) -> Step 2 (Conclude that if left uncorrected through the next round of replication, the mismatch is fixed/stabilized as a permanent mutation in one daughter duplex).

r.A: Replication mismatches do not block transcription; rather, cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and abasic sites block replication and transcription.
r.B: Apurinic sites arise from spontaneous depurination of adenine or guanine, not from uncorrected replication mismatches.
r.D: Covalent cross-linking between adjacent pyrimidines (cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers) is caused by ultraviolet radiation damage.
r.E: Recombinase-mediated events are involved in site-specific recombination, whereas uncorrected mismatches simply fix as point mutations in one daughter duplex during replication.

q.s: Slide 7: Replication Errors

q.v: In a laboratory experiment investigating spontaneous endogenous DNA damage, human fibroblasts are cultured under normal physiological conditions without exogenous mutagens. Mass spectrometry of the cellular DNA reveals the spontaneous hydrolytic loss of amino groups from purine residues, specifically converting adenine into a modified base. During the next round of DNA replication, how will this newly formed base alter hydrogen bonding?
o: It mimics thymine and forms two hydrogen bonds with adenine
It mimics guanine and forms two hydrogen bonds with cytosine
It covalently dimerizes with an adjacent pyrimidine on the same strand
It pairs with thymine to create an O6-methyl-guanine:thymine mismatch
It creates an abasic site that completely blocks DNA polymerase progression
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that spontaneous deamination of adenine produces hypoxanthine [Hx]) -> Step 2 (Determine that hypoxanthine alters normal hydrogen bonding by binding to cytosine with two hydrogen bonds).

r.A: Uracil, which arises from the spontaneous deamination of cytosine, mimics thymine and binds with adenine.
r.C: Dimerization of adjacent pyrimidines to form cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers is induced by UV radiation, not purine deamination.
r.D: O6-methyl-guanine pairing with thymine is caused by exogenous alkylating agents such as dietary N-nitroso compounds.
r.E: Abasic sites that block replication result from spontaneous depurination (loss of the entire purine base), whereas deamination leaves the hypoxanthine base intact.

q.s: Slide 9 & Slide 10: Chemical Modification of DNA - Spontaneous Deamination

q.v: A 52-year-old man presents for a routine health maintenance exam. He reports a diet heavily reliant on cured and processed meats, including daily consumption of bacon and hot dogs. His physician counsels him that preservatives in these foods contain N-nitroso compounds that act as chemical mutagens. Which of the following specific DNA lesions and subsequent replication errors is directly induced by these dietary agents?
o: Deamination of guanine to xanthine, which subsequently base pairs with thymine
Loss of up to 10,000 purines per cell per day, resulting in an apurinic site
Formation of O6-methylguanine, which base pairs with thymine during replication
Oxidation of guanine by reactive oxygen species, leading to a 27-nucleotide excision
Covalent binding of bulky adducts that interrupt hydrogen bonding and cause lung cancer
q.p: Step 1 (Associate dietary bacon and hot dogs with N-nitroso compounds, which act as DNA alkylating agents) -> Step 2 (Identify that alkylating agents methylate guanine to O6-methyl G, which mispairs with thymine during DNA replication and leads to a G-C to A-T mutation).

r.A: Deamination of guanine to xanthine is a spontaneous chemical modification, not a methylation event caused by N-nitroso alkylating agents.
r.B: The loss of 2,000 to 10,000 purines per cell per day describes spontaneous depurination, not alkylation.
r.D: The excision of a 27-29 nucleotide oligomer is characteristic of nucleotide excision repair of bulky adducts, whereas methylated bases are repaired by base excision repair.
r.E: Bulky adducts that distort the helix and lead to lung cancer are characteristic of oxidized benzo[a]pyrene from cigarette smoke.

q.s: Slide 12 & Slide 13: Chemical Modification of DNA - Alkylating Agents

q.v: A microbiology researcher is characterizing the mismatch repair pathway in Escherichia coli. She isolates a bacterial strain that successfully recognizes helix distortions caused by non-Watson-Crick base pairing after replication, but fails to incise the newly synthesized strand to initiate excision. Genetic sequencing confirms normal MutS and MutL proteins, but reveals a loss-of-function mutation in MutH. Which of the following molecular features normally enables the defective protein in this strain to distinguish the parental strand from the daughter strand?
o: Presence of mCpG islands exclusively on the newly synthesized strand
Methylation of the adenine residue within a 5'-GATC-3' sequence on the parental strand
Absence of a damaged or chemically modified base at the mismatch site
Cleavage of the N-glycosidic bond at an unmethylated cytosine residue
Recognition of a 12-to-13 nucleotide oligomer flanked by Uvr proteins
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that in E. coli mismatch repair, MutH is the endonuclease that nicks the daughter DNA strand) -> Step 2 (Recognize that MutH distinguishes the strands by binding to 5'-GATC-3' sites where the 'A' is methylated on the parental strand, while the new GATC remains unmethylated for several minutes after replication).

r.A: Methylated CpG (mCpG) is a proposed, unclear mechanism for strand recognition in the human mismatch repair system, which lacks MutH and GATC methylation.
r.C: While it is true that a mismatch lacks a damaged or modified base and is recognized by helix distortion, this is the role of MutS, not how MutH distinguishes the parental strand.
r.D: Cleavage of the N-glycosidic bond is performed by DNA glycosylase during base excision repair, not by MutH.
r.E: Recognition and excision of a 12-13 nucleotide oligomer by Uvr proteins describes nucleotide excision repair in E. coli.

q.s: Slide 16: Mismatch Repair, Slide 17: Mismatch Repair in E. coli, & Slide 18: Human Mismatch Repair System

q.v: A biochemist is studying the enzymatic repair of spontaneous cytosine deamination in human cell extracts. She observes that a specific glycosylase successfully cleaves the bond between the uracil base and the deoxyribose sugar, generating an abasic site. She then adds AP endonuclease, which makes an incision at the 5'-phosphodiester bond. Before DNA polymerase can insert the single replacement nucleotide, which of the following enzymatic steps must immediately occur?
o: DNA ligase must seal the nick in the sugar-phosphate backbone
AP lyase must remove the remaining sugar group by cutting the 3'-phosphodiester bond
Helicase must unwind and release a 27-to-29 nucleotide damaged segment
Excinuclease must make a secondary incision 3' to the abasic lesion
MutL homologs must link the glycosylase to the incised phosphodiester backbone
q.p: Step 1 (Trace the steps of Base Excision Repair following glycosylase cleavage and AP endonuclease 5'-phosphodiester bond incision) -> Step 2 (Determine that the immediate next step prior to DNA polymerase gap-filling is AP lyase cutting the 3'-phosphodiester bond to remove the sugar).

r.A: DNA ligase seals the nick as the final step of base excision repair, only after DNA polymerase has filled the single nucleotide gap.
r.C: Helicase release of a 27-29 nucleotide oligomer occurs in human nucleotide excision repair, not base excision repair.
r.D: Excinucleases making 5' and 3' incisions around a lesion is a mechanism of nucleotide excision repair.
r.E: MutL homologs (MLH and PMS proteins) function in human mismatch repair, not base excision repair.

q.s: Slide 20: Base Excision Repair & Slide 21: Base Excision Repair Steps

q.v: A 62-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history is diagnosed with primary lung carcinoma. Molecular analysis of his bronchial epithelial tissue demonstrates widespread covalent DNA adducts formed by oxidized benzo[a]pyrene, which interrupt normal hydrogen bonding and severely distort the DNA double helix. In healthy human cells, after XP proteins recognize this helix-distorting lesion and excinucleases cleave the backbone on both sides, what is the specific size and mechanism of fragment removal?
o: A single abasic sugar is removed by the 3' cleavage activity of AP lyase
A 12-to-13 nucleotide oligomer is unwound and released by Uvr proteins
A 27-to-29 nucleotide oligomer is released by the action of DNA helicase
A methylated 5'-GATC-3' segment is nicked and degraded by MutH
A 200-base-pair variable region is excised and joined by RAG recombinase
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that oxidized benzo[a]pyrene from cigarette smoke creates bulky, helix-distorting adducts repaired by human Nucleotide Excision Repair [NER]) -> Step 2 (Recall that following XP recognition and excinuclease cleavage in humans, DNA helicase releases a damaged oligomer of 27-29 nucleotides).

r.A: Removal of a single abasic sugar by AP lyase occurs during base excision repair of single base lesions, not bulky benzo[a]pyrene adducts.
r.B: Release of a 12-13 nucleotide oligomer involving Uvr proteins describes nucleotide excision repair in E. coli, whereas human NER excises a 27-29 nucleotide oligomer.
r.D: Methylated 5'-GATC-3' recognition by MutH is specific to E. coli mismatch repair.
r.E: Excision and joining of variable regions by RAG recombinase describes site-specific V(D)J recombination of immunoglobulin genes.

q.s: Slide 22: Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER), Slide 23: Nucleotide Excision Repair Steps, & Slide 24: Clinical Correlation

q.v: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the pediatric clinic due to severe photosensitivity, extensive freckling on sun-exposed skin, and multiple early-onset cutaneous malignancies. The physician also notes progressive neurological abnormalities on physical examination. Cultured skin fibroblasts from this patient fail to repair ultraviolet-induced cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers. Which of the following best describes the inheritance pattern and primary molecular defect underlying this patient's disorder?
o: Autosomal dominant mutation in MutS and MutL homologs
Autosomal recessive mutation in nucleotide excision repair proteins
Autosomal dominant defect in base excision repair glycosylases
Autosomal recessive deficiency in Rec-catalyzed homologous recombination
X-linked mutation in RAG site-specific recombinases
q.p: Step 1 (Diagnose the patient with Xeroderma Pigmentosum based on extreme sunlight sensitivity, freckling, early skin cancer, neurological abnormalities, and inability to repair UV-induced pyrimidine dimers) -> Step 2 (Identify that Xeroderma Pigmentosum is an autosomal recessive disease caused by mutations in nucleotide excision repair proteins).

r.A: Autosomal dominant mutations in MutS and MutL homologs cause Hereditary Nonpolyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC), a defect in mismatch repair.
r.C: Defects in base excision repair glycosylases affect single base mutations (deamination, depurination, alkylation), not UV-induced cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers.
r.D: Rec proteins catalyze homologous recombination between DNAs with high sequence identity, which is not the defective pathway in Xeroderma Pigmentosum.
r.E: RAG recombinases catalyze site-specific V(D)J recombination for antibody diversity, not nucleotide excision repair.

q.s: Slide 3 & Slide 25: Xeroderma Pigmentosum, Slide 14: Radiation Damage

q.v: During the maturation of human B lymphocytes, the genomic locus encoding the kappa light chain variable (V) region undergoes programmed somatic rearrangement to generate a vast repertoire of over 200 distinct antibody regions. A researcher investigating this process isolates the enzyme responsible for joining the separated DNA segments. Which of the following sequence requirements and catalytic proteins accurately characterizes this specific type of DNA recombination?
o: Requires extensive sequence identity across homologous chromosomes and is catalyzed by Rec proteins
Requires a specific sequence at the ends of a mobile element but no specific sequence in the recipient DNA, catalyzed by transposase
Requires short, specific DNA sequences present on both participating DNA segments and is catalyzed by RAG recombinase
Requires hemi-methylated 5'-GATC-3' sequences on the parental template and is catalyzed by MSH and MLH homologs
Requires adjacent pyrimidine dimers to initiate strand invasion and is catalyzed by XP excinucleases
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that V(D)J recombination of the human kappa light chain V region to generate antibody diversity is an example of site-specific recombination) -> Step 2 (Recall that site-specific recombination joins two DNA segments that both contain short, specific DNA sequences, and in immunoglobulin genes, this is catalyzed by the recombinase RAG).

r.A: Recombination between DNAs with high sequence identity catalyzed by Rec proteins describes homologous recombination, such as crossing-over during meiosis.
r.B: Requiring specific sequences only at the ends of the moving DNA segment and not in the recipient DNA describes transposition catalyzed by transposases.
r.D: MSH and MLH proteins are human mismatch repair homologs, and humans do not use 5'-GATC-3' methylation.
r.E: XP proteins and excinucleases repair pyrimidine dimers via nucleotide excision repair, not DNA recombination.

q.s: Slide 28: Types of DNA Recombination, Slide 30: Site-Specific Recombination, & Slide 31: Recombination of Immunoglobulin Genes

q.v: A 31-year-old man presents with opportunistic infections and is diagnosed with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) secondary to human immunodeficiency virus-1 (HIV-1) infection. The pathogenesis of his chronic infection relies on the permanent integration of the viral DNA genome into the host T-lymphocyte genome. This viral integration event occurs via the same fundamental molecular mechanism that mediates which of the following processes?
o: Crossing-over between homologous eukaryotic chromosomes during meiosis
Spread of penicillin and tetracycline resistance genes from bacterial plasmids
Generation of human kappa light chain diversity via V(D)J joining
Accumulation of replication errors in hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer
Removal of spontaneous uracil residues arising from cytosine deamination
q.p: Step 1 (Identify from the lecture clinical correlation that integration of the human HIV-1 virus into the human genome occurs through a 'transposition' mechanism) -> Step 2 (Connect this to the companion clinical correlation showing that transposition also mediates the spread of antibiotic resistance [such as penicillin or tetracycline] from bacterial plasmids).

r.A: Crossing-over between eukaryotic chromosomes during meiosis occurs via homologous recombination, not transposition.
r.C: Generation of kappa light chain antibody diversity via V(D)J joining occurs through site-specific recombination catalyzed by RAG.
r.D: Hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC) results from defective mismatch repair due to mutations in Mut homologs, not transposition.
r.E: Removal of uracil from cytosine deamination is carried out by the base excision repair pathway.

q.s: Slide 32: Transposition & Slide 33: Clinical Correlation

q.v: A 28-year-old man enrolled in a nutritional study consumes a diet heavily supplemented with high-fructose corn syrup (HFCS) for 4 weeks. Repeat laboratory testing demonstrates a marked elevation in serum triglyceride and lipid levels compared to baseline, and an endoscopic small-bowel biopsy reveals noticeably elongated intestinal villi. Which of the following intracellular changes within the intestinal villus cells directly promotes the survival of hypoxic cells to drive this structural adaptation?
o: Accumulation of fructose-1-phosphate favoring the monomeric form of pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2)
Activation of the PKM2 tetramer by elevated galactose-1-phosphate
Inhibition of ketohexokinase (KHK) by excess cytoplasmic citrate
Direct conversion of fructose to glucose-6-phosphate at the apical brush border
Depletion of intracellular NADPH due to rapid reduction of fructose by aldose reductase
q.p: Step 1 (High dietary HFCS enters enterocytes via GLUT5 and is phosphorylated by KHK to fructose-1-phosphate) -> Step 2 (Fructose-1-phosphate promotes the PKM2 monomer over the PKM2 tetramer, activating pathways that aid the survival of hypoxic villus cells, leading to villi lengthening and increased nutrient uptake/blood lipid levels).

r.B: Fructose-1-phosphate transitions PKM2 toward its monomeric state rather than activating the tetrameric form, and galactose-1-phosphate is not involved in this pathway.
r.C: Ketohexokinase (KHK) actively phosphorylates fructose to fructose-1-phosphate in the villus cell rather than being inhibited by citrate.
r.D: In enterocytes, fructose is phosphorylated to fructose-1-phosphate by KHK rather than being directly converted to glucose-6-phosphate at the apical membrane.
r.E: Aldose reductase reduces glucose or galactose into sugar alcohols using NADPH, whereas intestinal villi lengthening is driven by KHK-mediated fructose-1-phosphate formation.

q.s: Slide 4: SLO 1 - Possible mechanism linking fructose consumption to increased nutrient uptake

q.v: A healthy 22-year-old woman consumes a small serving of fruit containing a low, moderate dose of fructose. Later that evening, she consumes a 64-ounce soda containing a very large dose of fructose. Compared to the low dose of fructose, which of the following best describes the fate and downstream lipid packaging of the high dose of fructose?
o: It is completely metabolized into glucose within enterocytes and exported via SGLT1
It overflows from the intestine to the liver via the portal blood, where excess carbons can be packaged into B100-VLDL
It is trapped inside intestinal enterocytes due to saturation of basolateral GLUT2 transporters
It bypasses intestinal GLUT5 transporters and is absorbed exclusively in the colon as short-chain fatty acids
It is preferentially converted into chylomicrons by hepatocytes after uptake via SGLT1
q.p: Step 1 (Moderate doses of fructose are mostly metabolized by intestinal enterocytes, whereas high doses exceed enterocyte capacity and overflow to the liver and colon) -> Step 2 (Hepatocytes take up the excess fructose via GLUT5 and GLUT2 and, if used to produce fat, package it into B100-VLDL rather than enterocyte-derived chylomicrons).

r.A: Low doses of fructose are metabolized by the intestine, whereas high doses overwhelm enterocyte metabolism and overflow to the liver and colon; additionally, SGLT1 transports glucose and galactose, not fructose.
r.C: During high-dose fructose consumption, excess fructose exits across the basal membrane into the capillary vessel and overflows to the liver and colon rather than becoming trapped.
r.D: High doses of fructose still utilize apical GLUT5 in enterocytes before overflowing to the capillary blood, liver, and colon.
r.E: Chylomicrons are produced by enterocytes, whereas the liver produces B100-VLDL following fructose uptake via GLUT5 and GLUT2.

q.s: Slide 5: SLO 1 - Low doses vs. High doses of fructose metabolism

q.v: An 8-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department with lethargy, vomiting, and diaphoresis two hours after being fed a commercial baby food sweetened with sorbitol. Physical examination shows jaundice and hepatomegaly. Laboratory evaluation reveals severe hypoglycemia, lactic acidemia, hyperuricemia, and normal serum ketone levels. Deficiency of the enzyme responsible for this infant's condition directly prevents the cleavage of a phosphorylated intermediate into which of the following pairs of molecules?
o: UDP-glucose and glucose-1-phosphate
Dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) and glyceraldehyde
Fructose-6-phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate
Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and pyruvate
Acetaldehyde and acetic acid
q.p: Step 1 (Clinical presentation of hypoglycemia, lactic acidemia, hyperuricemia, and normal ketones after sorbitol/fructose ingestion indicates Hereditary Fructose Intolerance caused by Aldolase B deficiency) -> Step 2 (Aldolase B normally cleaves fructose-1-phosphate into dihydroxyacetone phosphate [DHAP] and glyceraldehyde).

r.A: UDP-glucose and glucose-1-phosphate are intermediates in the galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT) pathway, which is defective in classic galactosemia.
r.C: Fructose-6-phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate are upstream glycolytic intermediates bypassed during hepatic fructose metabolism.
r.D: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate is formed downstream from glyceraldehyde and DHAP, rather than being cleaved directly from fructose-1-phosphate along with pyruvate.
r.E: Acetaldehyde and acetic acid are intermediates of ethanol metabolism, not fructose metabolism.

q.s: Slide 6 & Slide 18: SLO 1 - Fructose Metabolism Disorders (Hereditary Fructose Intolerance)

q.v: A 40-year-old man consumes a diet extremely high in sucrose and high-fructose corn syrup. Unlike hepatic glucose metabolism, which is tightly controlled by feedback inhibition at its rate-limiting steps, hepatic fructose metabolism enters glycolysis unchecked and floods the citric acid cycle. Which of the following intermediates is exported in excess from the mitochondria to the cytoplasm to serve as the direct precursor for acetyl-CoA and subsequent triacylglycerol (TAG) synthesis?
o: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate
Fructose-1-phosphate
Citrate
Dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP)
Galactitol
q.p: Step 1 (Fructose metabolism bypasses the highly regulated steps of glycolysis—glucokinase/hexokinase and PFK-1—entering as DHAP and glyceraldehyde to form glyceraldehyde-3-P, pyruvate, and mitochondrial acetyl-CoA) -> Step 2 (Excess citrate from the citric acid cycle is exported to the cytoplasm, where it is converted back to acetyl-CoA to synthesize fatty acids and TAG).

r.A: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate is a cytoplasmic glycolytic intermediate that is bypassed by fructose-1-phosphate cleavage, not exported from the citric acid cycle.
r.B: Fructose-1-phosphate is formed in the cytoplasm by fructokinase and cleaved by aldolase B; it does not exit the mitochondria to form acetyl-CoA.
r.D: DHAP is a cytoplasmic cleavage product of fructose-1-phosphate that enters glycolysis, not a citric acid cycle intermediate exported to form cytoplasmic acetyl-CoA.
r.E: Galactitol is an osmotically active sugar alcohol formed from galactose by aldose reductase, unrelated to hepatic fatty acid synthesis.

q.s: Slide 4 & Slide 6: SLO 1 - Fructose Metabolism Disorders (Glycolysis bypass and excess citrate export)

q.v: A 24-year-old man from Northern Europe and his 24-year-old friend from East Asia both consume a large milkshake. Two hours later, one man remains completely asymptomatic, while the other develops severe abdominal cramps, bloating, flatulence, and watery diarrhea. Which of the following evolutionary genetic mechanisms best explains why the asymptomatic individual is able to tolerate this meal in adulthood?
o: Upregulation of basolateral GLUT5 transporters in the colon
Independent acquisition of mutations that maintain lactase expression after infancy
Constitutive suppression of intestinal SGLT1 cotransporters
Increased expression of hepatic galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT)
Adaptive deficiency of fructokinase (KHK) in small intestinal enterocytes
q.p: Step 1 (Adult-type lactose intolerance results from the normal reduction in lactase expression after infancy, causing unabsorbed lactose to induce osmotic water retention and bacterial fermentation) -> Step 2 (Some human populations independently acquired mutations that maintain lactase expression later in life, preventing symptoms after dairy intake).

r.A: GLUT5 is a fructose transporter, whereas lactose digestion requires brush-border lactase to cleave lactose into glucose and galactose.
r.C: SGLT1 is required for the apical absorption of galactose and glucose; suppressing it would worsen carbohydrate malabsorption rather than allow dairy tolerance.
r.D: GALT metabolizes galactose-1-phosphate intracellularly after absorption and has no role in cleaving luminal lactose in the intestine.
r.E: Fructokinase deficiency causes essential fructosuria and does not enable the digestion of dietary lactose.

q.s: Slide 8 & Slide 18: SLO 2 - Galactose Metabolism (Lactose Intolerance)

q.v: A 5-day-old breastfed neonate is admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit with vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, and failure to thrive. Ophthalmologic exam reveals bilateral lens opacities, and blood cultures grow Escherichia coli. Laboratory studies show hypoglycemia with normal serum ketone levels. A deficiency in the culprit enzyme blocks the conversion of galactose-1-phosphate into glucose-1-phosphate, a reaction that normally requires the recycling of UDP-galactose back into UDP-glucose via which of the following enzymes?
o: Aldose reductase
Galactokinase
4-Epimerase
Sorbitol dehydrogenase
Aldolase B
q.p: Step 1 (Neonatal vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, cataracts, and E. coli sepsis in a breastfed infant indicate Classic Galactosemia due to galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase [GALT] deficiency) -> Step 2 (In the normal GALT pathway, galactose-1-phosphate reacts with UDP-glucose to form glucose-1-phosphate and UDP-galactose, which is regenerated into UDP-glucose by 4-epimerase).

r.A: Aldose reductase converts excess unphosphorylated galactose into galactitol, which causes cataracts, rather than interconverting UDP-galactose and UDP-glucose.
r.B: Galactokinase catalyzes the initial ATP-dependent phosphorylation of galactose to galactose-1-phosphate.
r.D: Sorbitol dehydrogenase converts sorbitol to fructose in the polyol pathway and plays no role in galactose metabolism.
r.E: Aldolase B cleaves fructose-1-phosphate into DHAP and glyceraldehyde in fructose metabolism.

q.s: Slide 8 & Slide 18: SLO 2 - Galactose Metabolism (Classic Galactosemia pathway)

q.v: A 62-year-old woman with a 15-year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus undergoes a physiological study comparing intracellular metabolites across different tissues. Biopsies of her peripheral nerves and renal cortex demonstrate markedly elevated intracellular sorbitol concentrations and cellular swelling, whereas analysis of seminal vesicle tissue shows active conversion of glucose to sorbitol without toxic sorbitol accumulation. Which of the following best explains why seminal vesicles are spared from the osmotic swelling observed in her nerves and kidneys?
o: Seminal vesicles require insulin for glucose entry across the plasma membrane
Seminal vesicles lack aldose reductase and cannot reduce glucose
Seminal vesicles express sorbitol dehydrogenase, which oxidizes sorbitol to fructose using NAD+
Seminal vesicles rapidly phosphorylate sorbitol into sorbitol-1-phosphate via fructokinase
Seminal vesicles export sorbitol into the bloodstream via high-capacity GLUT2 transporters
q.p: Step 1 (In hyperglycemia, glucose enters insulin-independent tissues and is converted to sorbitol by aldose reductase using NADPH) -> Step 2 (Whereas lens, nerve, retina, and kidney cells have low or absent sorbitol dehydrogenase [SD] leading to osmotic sorbitol accumulation, seminal vesicles possess SD, which uses NAD+ to convert sorbitol into fructose).

r.A: Seminal vesicles actively take up glucose and convert it to sorbitol and fructose to fuel sperm, rather than blocking glucose entry.
r.B: Seminal vesicles do possess aldose reductase to convert glucose into sorbitol as the first step in producing fructose.
r.D: Sorbitol is oxidized to fructose by sorbitol dehydrogenase, not phosphorylated by fructokinase.
r.E: Sorbitol does not pass freely out of cells; seminal vesicles prevent accumulation by oxidizing it to fructose via sorbitol dehydrogenase.

q.s: Slide 10 & Slide 11: SLO 3 - Effect of Hyperglycemia on Sorbitol Metabolism

q.v: In an experimental model of diabetic retinopathy and cataract formation, retinal and lens cells are incubated in a medium containing high concentrations of glucose. Intracellular tracking reveals a rapid influx of glucose without insulin stimulation, followed by the accumulation of an osmotically active molecule that cannot pass freely out of the cells, resulting in cellular influx of water. The enzymatic reaction that directly synthesizes this osmotically active molecule requires an adequate intracellular supply of which of the following cofactors?
o: NAD+
NADH + H+
ATP
NADPH + H+
UDP-glucose
q.p: Step 1 (In the lens and retina during hyperglycemia, insulin-independent glucose entry leads to sorbitol production via aldose reductase, causing osmotic water influx) -> Step 2 (The conversion of glucose to sorbitol by aldose reductase requires adequate supplies of NADPH + H+, which is oxidized to NADP+).

r.A: NAD+ is the cofactor required by sorbitol dehydrogenase to convert sorbitol to fructose, not by aldose reductase to synthesize sorbitol.
r.B: NADH + H+ is the product formed when sorbitol dehydrogenase oxidizes sorbitol to fructose.
r.C: ATP is required by kinases such as fructokinase and galactokinase, whereas aldose reductase utilizes NADPH + H+.
r.E: UDP-glucose is a nucleotide sugar cofactor used by galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase in galactose metabolism.

q.s: Slide 10, Slide 11, & Slide 12: SLO 3 - Effect of Hyperglycemia on Sorbitol Metabolism

q.v: A 26-year-old man experiences intense facial flushing, tachycardia, and nausea shortly after drinking a single glass of wine. A similar reaction occurs in a 50-year-old man who drinks beer while taking disulfiram for alcohol use disorder. Both individuals are experiencing the accumulation of a toxic, highly reactive electrophile due to reduced activity of an enzyme that is partially deficient in up to 35–40% of certain global populations. Which of the following reactions is directly catalyzed by the affected enzyme?
o: Conversion of ethanol to acetaldehyde coupled with the reduction of NAD+
Conversion of acetaldehyde to acetate coupled with the reduction of NAD+
Conversion of acetic acid to acetyl-CoA coupled with the hydrolysis of ATP
Conversion of glycolic acid to glyoxylic acid using thiamine
Conversion of formic acid to carbon dioxide and water using folate
q.p: Step 1 (Both disulfiram treatment and the common genetic deficiency present in 35-40% of some populations impair aldehyde dehydrogenase, causing toxic acetaldehyde accumulation) -> Step 2 (Aldehyde dehydrogenase catalyzes the oxidation of acetaldehyde to acetate while reducing NAD+ to NADH + H+).

r.A: The conversion of ethanol to acetaldehyde is catalyzed by alcohol dehydrogenase (AldH), which is upstream of the enzyme inhibited by disulfiram.
r.C: The activation of acetic acid to acetyl-CoA occurs downstream of aldehyde dehydrogenase.
r.D: The metabolism of glycolic acid involves ethylene glycol detoxification pathways, not the oxidation of acetaldehyde by aldehyde dehydrogenase.
r.E: The folate-dependent conversion of formic acid to CO2 and H2O is the final detoxification step of methanol metabolism.

q.s: Slide 13 & Slide 14: SLO 4 - Ethanol Metabolism and Aldehyde Dehydrogenase

q.v: A 38-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after intentionally ingesting automotive antifreeze (ethylene glycol). Before alcohol dehydrogenase inhibition can be initiated, a portion of the ethylene glycol is oxidized by alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase into glycolic acid, which is subsequently converted to glyoxylic acid. To shunt glyoxylic acid away from forming renal-toxic oxalic acid and instead promote its conversion into non-toxic metabolites such as glycine and alpha-hydroxy-beta-ketoadipate, which of the following pairs of vitamin cofactors is directly involved in this downstream detoxification pathway?
o: Folate and cobalamin
Thiamine and pyridoxine
Niacin and riboflavin
Biotin and pantothenic acid
Ascorbic acid and vitamin K
q.p: Step 1 (Ethylene glycol is metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase to glycolic acid and glyoxylic acid, which can form toxic oxalic acid) -> Step 2 (As shown in the ethylene glycol detoxification pathway, thiamine promotes the conversion of glycolic/glyoxylic intermediates to alpha-hydroxy-beta-ketoadipate, and pyridoxine promotes the conversion of glyoxylic acid to glycine).

r.A: Folate is used to detoxify formic acid into CO2 and H2O during methanol poisoning, not ethylene glycol poisoning.
r.C: Niacin (precursor to NAD+) drives the initial oxidation of ethylene glycol into toxic intermediates via alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenases rather than shunting glyoxylic acid to glycine.
r.D: Biotin and pantothenic acid are not the vitamin cofactors utilized in the detoxification of glycolic and glyoxylic acid.
r.E: Ascorbic acid and vitamin K are not involved in the enzymatic shunting of glycolic acid or glyoxylic acid.

q.s: Slide 14: SLO 4 - Ethanol, methanol and ethylene glycol metabolism

add.cloze: MALT samples antigens from {{c1::mucosal surfaces}}; unlike a lymph node, it lies {{c2::directly beneath the epithelium and lacks a complete capsule and afferent lymphatics}}
add.extra: Antigen crosses specialized epithelium (M cells) to follicles beneath the mucosa. Peyer patches are most prominent in the ileum; plasma cells support mucosal IgA responses.

add.cloze: Lymph flows through a lymph node: afferent lymphatic → {{c1::subcapsular sinus}} → {{c2::cortical (trabecular) sinuses}} → {{c3::medullary sinuses}} → efferent lymphatic
add.extra: Afferents enter the convex surface; the efferent exits at the hilum, where blood vessels and high endothelial venules enter. APCs sample the lymph along the route.

add.cloze: Splenic {{c2::white pulp}} performs {{c1::immune surveillance of blood-borne antigens}}
add.extra: White pulp = PALS (T cells around a central arteriole) + follicles (B cells). Red pulp = cords of Billroth + sinusoids: RBC quality control.

myLectures.note: Fuerst, Tue Nov 3. Cards picked to match the slides, checked against your 28 Lipoproteins cards (see lipoproteins_card_check.csv). Picks limited to what the slides discuss; B&B lipid-drug details the lecture doesn't cover (fibrates, niacin, ezetimibe, statin dosing/guidelines, dyslipidemia types I, III, IV) were left out. Adds 10 cloze notes (deck: Fuerst - Lipoproteins). B&B has no cards on Tangier disease, Lp(a) or saturated fat and LDL clearance.

add.cloze: Apo{{c1::E}} mediates hepatic uptake of chylomicron remnants by {{c2::receptor-mediated endocytosis}}
add.extra: Remnant receptors on the liver include the LDL receptor. Chylomicrons get ApoE (and ApoC-II) from HDL in the blood.

add.cloze: The primary structural apolipoprotein required for synthesis and secretion of VLDL by the liver is {{c1::ApoB-100}}
add.extra: The ApoB gene encodes both B-48 (intestine, chylomicrons) and B-100 (liver, VLDL/IDL/LDL); RNA editing in enterocytes creates a stop codon → shorter B-48.

add.cloze: Statins {{c1::competitively}} inhibit HMG-CoA reductase
add.extra: Lowering hepatocyte cholesterol then increases LDL receptor expression and LDL clearance.

add.cloze: Familial hypercholesterolemia (type IIa) is caused by mutations in the {{c1::LDL receptor}} pathway (most in the LDL-binding domain). Normally, after LDL is delivered to the endosome, the LDL receptor is {{c2::recycled back to the plasma membrane}}
add.extra: LDLR life cycle: synthesis → transport → LDL binding → clustering in clathrin-coated pits → recycling; mutations can hit any step.

add.cloze: When intracellular cholesterol is high: {{c1::ACAT is activated}} to store cholesterol as esters, and {{c2::HMG-CoA reductase activity and LDL receptor synthesis}} are downregulated
add.extra: Mevalonate also feeds back to inhibit HMG-CoA reductase.

add.cloze: A lipoprotein has a hydrophobic core of {{c1::triglycerides and cholesteryl esters}} and an amphipathic outer monolayer of {{c2::phospholipids and unesterified cholesterol}} (plus apolipoproteins)
Glycerol released from chylomicron triglycerides is converted to glycerol 3-phosphate in the liver by {{c1::glycerol kinase}}
add.extra: Adipocytes lack glycerol kinase, so glycerol goes to the liver (e.g., for gluconeogenesis).

add.cloze: Deficiency of Apo{{c1::C-II}} (or of lipoprotein lipase) prevents clearance of triglycerides in lipoproteins from the blood → hypertriglyceridemia
add.extra: ApoC-II is the cofactor that activates LPL on capillary endothelium (bound to heparan sulfate proteoglycan).

add.cloze: De novo cholesterol synthesis is activated in the {{c1::well-fed state, when insulin signaling dominates}}
The amino acid {{c1::leucine}} can serve as a precursor for the HMG-CoA reductase pathway
add.extra: Leucine is purely ketogenic; its breakdown yields acetyl-CoA and HMG-CoA.

myLectures.name: Lipid Metabolism
myLectures.note: Fuerst, Tue Nov 3. Cards picked to match the slides, checked against your 28 Lipid Metabolism cards (see lipid_metabolism_card_check.csv). Picks limited to what the slides discuss; related B&B cards the lecture doesn't cover (primary carnitine deficiency, MCAD inheritance/treatment, ketone urine tests, aspirin dosing/toxicity, PGs in the kidney/uterus/ductus, celecoxib sulfa) were left out. Adds 7 cloze notes (deck: Fuerst - Lipid Metabolism).

add.cloze: Glucagon and epinephrine activate hormone-sensitive lipase through {{c1::cAMP → protein kinase A phosphorylation}}
add.extra: Counterregulatory hormones: epinephrine, glucagon, cortisol, GH. Cortisol and GH act by a different, slower mechanism. Insulin opposes HSL.

add.cloze: Free fatty acids released from adipose tissue travel in the blood bound to {{c1::albumin}}
add.extra: Glycerol leaves the adipocyte through an aquaporin and goes to the liver for gluconeogenesis.

add.cloze: {{c1::HMG-CoA synthase}} is the rate-limiting enzyme of ketone body synthesis; ketone and cholesterol synthesis share the intermediate {{c2::HMG-CoA}}
add.extra: Mitochondrial HMG-CoA → ketones; cytosolic HMG-CoA → mevalonate (HMG-CoA reductase) → cholesterol.

add.cloze: The liver cannot use the ketone bodies it makes because it lacks {{c1::succinyl-CoA transferase (SCOT, thiophorase)}}
add.extra: SCOT transfers CoA from succinyl-CoA to acetoacetate in extrahepatic tissues. SCOT deficiency → ketoacidosis during fasting.

add.cloze: {{c1::Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC)}} is the rate-limiting enzyme of de novo fatty acid synthesis; it is activated by {{c2::insulin}} (and citrate) and inhibited by {{c3::glucagon, via cAMP-driven phosphorylation}}
add.extra: ACC needs biotin and ATP. Its product malonyl-CoA blocks CPT-I, so fatty acids are not oxidized while being made.

add.cloze: The glycerol backbone for both triglyceride and phospholipid synthesis comes from {{c1::glycerol-3-phosphate}}
add.extra: G3P comes from glucose metabolism (DHAP). Phosphatidic acid → DAG → TAG or phosphatidylcholine.

add.cloze: Phospholipase A2 is activated by a rise in cytosolic {{c1::Ca2+}}
add.extra: Receptor → G protein → PLC → IP3 → Ca2+ release from ER → PLA2 releases arachidonic acid from C-2 of membrane phospholipids. Cortisol (glucocorticoids) inhibit PLA2.
