myLectures.deck: Weinberg - The Science of the Mediterranean Diet

add.cloze: The Mediterranean diet is roughly {{c1::20% protein, 45% carbohydrate and 35% fat}}; its main plant-based proteins are {{c2::beans, peas and lentils}}
add.extra: Other components: whole grains, fresh vegetables, fruit, fish and shellfish, cheese and yogurt, olive oil and olives, nuts and seeds, moderate red wine.

add.cloze: PREDIMED compared a low-fat control diet with two Mediterranean diet arms: one supplemented with {{c1::extra virgin olive oil}} and one with {{c2::mixed tree nuts}}; a significant reduction in cardiovascular events appeared after only {{c3::1 year}}
add.extra: PREDIMED, N Engl J Med 2018 (primary prevention). Med Diet benefits were first described by Ancel Keys in the Seven Countries Study (1957).

add.cloze: The CORDIOPREV trial (2022) found a 26% reduction in major cardiovascular events with the Mediterranean diet in people with {{c1::established cardiovascular disease}} (secondary prevention)
Plant isomers of cholesterol are called {{c1::phytosterols}}. β-sitosterol {{c2::competes with cholesterol for the NPC1L1 transporter}}, competitively inhibiting intestinal cholesterol absorption
add.extra: Cholesterol absorption ~50% vs β-sitosterol <1%: NPC1L1 takes up all sterols, and ABC-G5/G8 selectively pumps phytosterols back out of the enterocyte.

add.cloze: Less dietary cholesterol reaching the liver (in chylomicrons) leads to upregulation of hepatic {{c1::LDL receptors}}, lowering plasma LDL
add.extra: More phytosterols + less dietary cholesterol lowers plasma LDL by ~30% (lecture).

add.cloze: Adding plant sterols to margarine can lower LDL by about {{c1::15%}}

DHA makes up about {{c1::50%}} of retinal phospholipids (and ~30% of brain phospholipids); increased {{c2::fish intake (DHA/EPA)}} is linked to neuroprotection and neonatal visual and brain development
add.extra: ALA (18:3 ω-3) is the essential precursor of the longer ω-3s; EPA (20:5) is a prostanoid precursor; DHA is 22:6.

add.cloze: Omega-3 fatty acids compete with {{c1::arachidonic acid}} (ω-6) for cyclooxygenase; shifting prostanoid synthesis toward ω-3 derivatives reduces {{c2::inflammation}}
add.extra: ω-6 (arachidonic acid) → inflammatory prostanoids; ω-3 (EPA, DHA) → non-inflammatory prostanoids.

add.cloze: The antiarrhythmic effect of omega-3 fatty acids is attributed to {{c1::stabilization of the cardiac membrane}}
add.extra: Other ω-3 cardiovascular effects: ↓ VLDL synthesis and plasma TGs, ↓ blood pressure, ↓ platelet aggregation.

add.cloze: Replacing saturated fat with monounsaturated fat {{c1::decreases}} the LDL/HDL ratio; MUFAs are better than PUFAs for vascular health because they {{c2::resist free-radical lipoxidation}}
add.extra: SFA: ↓ LDL uptake (LDL receptors) and ↑ VLDL secretion → ↑ plasma LDL. MUFA: ↑ LDL uptake and ↓ VLDL secretion → ↓ LDL and TG. Oleic acid = 18:1.

add.cloze: Antioxidant sources in the Mediterranean diet: extra virgin olive oil → {{c1::polyphenols}}; red wine → {{c2::resveratrol}}; leafy greens (kale, spinach) → {{c3::vitamin E and carotenoids}}. These phytochemical antioxidants prevent the formation of {{c4::atherogenic advanced oxidation products}}
add.extra: Antioxidants arrest the free-radical peroxidation chain reaction of unsaturated fatty acids in membranes and limit the inflammatory response to oxidative damage. Others: flavonoids, vitamin C, β-carotene, lycopene.

myLectures.name: Introduction to Immunology
myLectures.note: New lecture (Mullins, Mon Nov 2). Cards picked to match the slides, checked against your 40 Intro to Immunology cards (see intro_immunology_card_check.csv). This lecture is mostly framework (danger model, the five stages, localization), which B&B doesn't teach as such, so 14 cloze notes come from your cards (deck: Mullins - Introduction to Immunology). Picks include what the picture-only slides show (innate cell types and complement, HLA-A/B/C vs DP/DQ/DR, beta2-microglobulin, invariant chain/MHC II loading, Langerhans cells carrying antigen to naive T cells, plasma cells in bone marrow). Left out: TLR4/CD14, MHC I on all nucleated cells, perforin/granzyme, Th subsets beyond Th1, IgG in the secondary response.

add.cloze: The central tension an effective immune system must manage: {{c1::eliminate threats while limiting unacceptable injury to host tissues}}
add.extra: Lecture: an effective system must be powerful, targeted, localized and self-limited. The same mechanisms that protect can cause collateral injury, autoimmunity, allergy or immunopathology.

add.cloze: Defining immunity only as recognition of non-self is limited: foreignness alone does not decide whether a response is needed; {{c1::danger, tissue injury and context}} also shape activation. Besides microbes, dangers include {{c2::tissue injury, irritants/toxins, cellular stress, and cancers (from infection or mutation)}}
add.extra: Lecture framing: "strangers" vs "dangers".

add.cloze: Stages of an immune response: (1) Detect: {{c1::barriers fail; innate sensors recognize microbial patterns or tissue injury}}. (2) Rapid local response: {{c2::pre-formed innate cells and molecules recognize and try to contain the danger}}. (3) Decide + amplify: {{c3::costimulation and cytokines determine whether rare antigen-specific lymphocytes activate and expand}}. (4) Localize + eliminate: {{c4::effectors reach the relevant tissue and remove the threat while limiting damage}}. (5) Resolve + remember: {{c5::the response contracts and selected lymphocytes persist as memory}}
add.extra: Stages 1-2 are innate; 3-5 are adaptive. Fire analogy: fire door (barrier), smoke detector (sensor), sprinkler (innate), fire department (adaptive).

add.cloze: Examples of innate barriers: {{c1::skin, mucociliary escalator, saliva, urinary mucous membranes, tears, and stomach acid}}
add.extra: Barriers prevent colonization and invasion from becoming disease.

add.cloze: Pattern-recognition receptors detect {{c1::conserved microbial structures and products}} and also {{c2::altered self, cellular stress and damage-associated signals}}; this is why a sterile needle puncture can still cause inflammation
add.extra: After bacteria enter a dirty cut, innate cells detect both microbial patterns and tissue-damage signals. In a sterile injury, damaged host cells release danger signals that activate innate cells without microbes.

add.cloze: Innate effectors are {{c1::already available}}, so innate immunity responds in minutes to hours; on first exposure adaptive immunity takes {{c2::days}} because {{c3::rare antigen-specific clones must be activated and expanded}}
On repeat exposure (e.g., after vaccination or infection), adaptive responses are {{c1::faster and larger}} because of memory, whereas innate responses are {{c2::broadly similar}}
add.extra: Lecture: primary vs memory responses, "why to get your flu shot".

add.cloze: An antigen is {{c1::a molecular structure specifically bound by an antibody/B-cell receptor, or recognized by a T-cell receptor as peptide-HLA}}. Antigen alone does not activate adaptive immunity: {{c2::antigen + danger = adaptive activation}}, because danger signals activate APCs and induce costimulation
add.extra: Antigen provides specificity; danger provides context.

add.cloze: HLA stands for {{c1::human leukocyte antigen}}, the human form of the {{c2::major histocompatibility complex (MHC)}}
add.extra: HLA molecules bind peptide fragments and display them for T cells: "Here's what I found. Should we respond?"

add.cloze: Signal 3 in naive T-cell activation is {{c1::cytokines}}, which shape clonal expansion and functional differentiation
add.extra: Signal 1: TCR recognizes peptide-HLA. Signal 2: costimulation (APC encountered danger and is licensed). Without signal 2 → anergy.

add.cloze: Clonal {{c1::selection}}: antigen activates lymphocytes bearing pre-existing receptors of the right specificity (antigen does not design the receptor). Clonal {{c2::expansion}}: the activated lymphocyte proliferates into many effector cells, some of which persist as memory
The adaptive effector that most directly eliminates a virus-infected host cell is {{c1::a CD8 cytotoxic T lymphocyte}} recognizing viral peptide presented by {{c2::HLA class I}}
add.extra: CD4 T cells see HLA class II and coordinate other leukocytes.

add.cloze: Humoral immunity (plasma cells secreting antibody) is best suited to {{c1::extracellular targets and toxins}}
add.extra: Antibodies recruit complement and Fc-receptor-bearing cells. Cell-mediated immunity: T cells recognize peptide-HLA on cells.

add.cloze: Localization: antigen is captured in tissue → carried to the {{c1::draining lymph node}} → specific lymphocytes activate and expand → enter the blood → {{c2::home back to the infected tissue}}. This matters because effectors must reach {{c3::the correct tissue to eliminate the threat while limiting systemic damage}}
add.extra: Tissue → lymph node → circulation → tissue.

myLectures.name: Danger Signals and Antigens
myLectures.note: Mullins, Tue Nov 3 (slides are titled 'Danger Signal and Antigens'). Cards picked to match the slides and their figures, checked against your 34 cards (see danger_signals_card_check.csv). PAMP/PRR, innate-vs-adaptive and TCR cards are already in Introduction to Immunology, so they aren't repeated here. Adds 9 cloze notes (deck: Mullins - Danger Signals and Antigens). Left out: Gram stain and cell-wall details, prion disease, specific viruses, endotoxin structure, haptens/epitopes.

add.cloze: A {{c1::pathogen}} is an agent capable of causing disease in a susceptible host, whereas {{c2::microorganism (microbe)}} is a broad term for microscopic biological entities that does not imply disease
add.extra: Not every microbe causes disease, and not every infectious agent is cellular.

add.cloze: Infectious-agent classes: prokaryotic = bacteria; eukaryotic = {{c1::fungi, protozoa and helminths}}; non-cellular = {{c2::viruses and prions}}. Viruses replicate {{c3::using host-cell machinery}}; prions are {{c4::infectious misfolded proteins}}
add.extra: Prokaryotes: no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles, cell wall present, binary fission. Eukaryotes: nucleus and organelles, cell division / complex life cycles.

add.cloze: Whether infection produces disease depends on {{c1::agent}} factors, {{c2::host}} factors and {{c3::contextual}} factors
add.extra: Agent: virulence factors, inoculum, tissue tropism, replication strategy. Host: barrier integrity, immune status, age, genetics, prior immunity. Context: portal of entry, tissue environment, microbiota, exposure conditions.

add.cloze: PAMP sources: unmethylated CpG DNA comes from {{c1::bacteria and some viruses}}; double-stranded RNA from {{c2::viral replication}}; fungal glycans (mannans, β-glucans) from {{c3::fungal cell walls}}
add.extra: Other PAMPs: LPS (Gram-negative outer membrane, TLR4), peptidoglycan (Gram-positive, TLR2), flagellin (bacterial flagella, TLR5).

add.cloze: Three advantages of recognizing conserved microbial patterns: {{c1::efficiency}} (a limited receptor set surveys many pathogens), {{c2::speed}} (immediate response) and {{c3::reliability}} (essential microbial structures are hard to discard)

An immunologic antigen is {{c1::a molecular structure recognized specifically by the adaptive immune system}}; pathogen-derived antigens include {{c2::proteins/peptides, polysaccharides, lipids and other complex molecules}}
add.extra: Antigens are both inducers and targets of adaptive responses. A capsid antigen from one virus generally differs from the matching antigen of a related virus.

add.cloze: A B cell recognizes {{c1::intact (native) antigen}} directly through its {{c2::B-cell receptor (membrane-bound antibody)}}
add.extra: T cells recognize only short peptides (~8-20 amino acids) bound to HLA (MHC) on antigen-presenting cells.

add.cloze: PRRs are {{c1::germline-encoded and pattern-focused}}, whereas BCRs and TCRs are {{c2::highly diverse and antigen-specific}}

Innate PAMP recognition answers "{{c1::Is a microbe present?}}"; adaptive antigen recognition answers "{{c2::Which specific target is present?}}". A PAMP is not the same as an antigen: PAMPs are {{c3::conserved patterns recognized by innate PRRs}}, antigens are {{c4::specific structures recognized by B- or T-cell receptors}}
add.extra: PAMPs are shared across many microbes; antigens are often unique to a pathogen or strain. Lecture: "All PAMPs are antigens, but not all antigens are PAMPs."

myLectures.name: Pharmacokinetics
myLectures.note: Beardsley, Wed Nov 4. Cards picked to match the slides and the PK practice problems, checked against your 48 Pharmacokinetics cards (see pharmacokinetics_card_check.csv). Ion-trapping cards are already in pH, Acid-Base and Buffers. Left out: renal clearance (renal block), antiarrhythmic/glaucoma/clinical-trial 'phase' cards, prodrug examples the lecture doesn't name, NAT2 acetylators. Adds 21 cloze notes (deck: Beardsley - Pharmacokinetics), including your calculation cards.

add.cloze: Pharmacokinetics is {{c1::absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion (ADME)}} of drugs: how the body affects the drug
add.extra: Pharmacodynamics is how the drug affects the body.

add.cloze: The {{c1::uncharged (non-ionized)}} form of a drug crosses membranes by passive diffusion more readily. Most absorption of both weak acids and weak bases still occurs in the {{c2::small intestine}}, because its {{c3::very large surface area and more permeable membranes}} compensate even for ionized drug
add.extra: Weak acids are un-ionized in acidic environments; weak bases are ionized there. At pH = pKa, ionized = un-ionized.

add.cloze: Bioavailability (F) is {{c1::the fraction of unchanged drug that reaches the systemic circulation}}; for IV administration F = {{c2::1 (100%)}}
add.extra: F = AUC oral / AUC IV (equal doses). Typical F: IM/SC 75-100%, oral 5-<100%, rectal 30-<100%, transdermal 80-100%.

add.cloze: Morphine needs a much larger oral than IV dose because {{c1::extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism}} leaves an oral bioavailability of only about {{c2::30%}}
add.extra: First-pass loss: P-glycoprotein pumping back into the gut lumen, gut-wall enzymes, liver enzymes, biliary excretion. Propranolol is the lecture example of a big oral-vs-IV difference.

add.cloze: Grapefruit juice {{c1::inhibits intestinal CYP enzymes (CYP3A4) and P-glycoprotein}}, {{c2::increasing}} the oral bioavailability of many drugs (e.g., atorvastatin)
add.extra: Active components: furanocoumarins.

add.cloze: Serum drug levels should be drawn {{c1::after the distribution phase}} (after the initial rapid fall in plasma concentration)
add.extra: Levels drawn during distribution overestimate concentration and throw off Vd and clearance calculations. Most IV drugs are also given slowly so the early peak isn't toxic.

add.cloze: For a highly albumin-bound drug, low serum albumin {{c1::increases}} the Vd. Digoxin has a very high Vd because of {{c2::extensive binding to cardiac and skeletal muscle}}
add.extra: Tissue binding/distribution raises Vd; plasma protein binding lowers it.

add.cloze: Steady state is reached when {{c1::the rate of drug administration equals the rate of elimination}}. Average Css = {{c2::(F × dose) / (CL × dosing interval)}}; for a constant IV infusion, Css = {{c3::infusion rate / CL}}
add.extra: Equivalent: maintenance dose = (Css × CL × τ) / F.

add.cloze: Reduced renal or hepatic function {{c1::lowers clearance and raises Css}} at the same dosing rate, so if clearance falls 50% the maintenance dose should be {{c2::cut by 50%}}. Because half-life lengthens, the time to reach steady state {{c3::increases}}
add.extra: The loading dose is unchanged; only the maintenance dose depends on elimination.

add.cloze: Phase II metabolism is {{c1::conjugation}} (glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation, methylation, glycine or glutathione conjugation). A prodrug is {{c2::an inactive compound activated by metabolism}}. A CYP inhibitor {{c3::raises levels and toxicity of an active drug}} but lowers the active metabolite of a prodrug
add.extra: Phase I: oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis (CYP450). Example: etravirine (CYP2C19 inhibitor) decreases clopidogrel activation; cobicistat (CYP3A4 inhibitor) raises atorvastatin.

add.cloze: With zero-order (capacity-limited) elimination, as serum concentration rises {{c1::the elimination rate plateaus, so the drug accumulates rapidly and causes toxicity}}
add.extra: Lecture: a 40% dose increase is fine for valproate (first order) but dangerous for phenytoin (capacity-limited).

add.cloze: A larger Vd {{c1::lengthens}} the half-life, because t½ = {{c2::0.7 × Vd / CL}}
add.extra: More drug in tissues returns to plasma slowly.

add.cloze: A loading dose is given to {{c1::reach the target plasma concentration quickly}}; it {{c2::does not change}} the time to reach steady state, which depends only on half-life
add.extra: Loading dose = (Cp × Vd) / F. "Filling the tank" doesn't depend on how fast it drains.

add.cloze: The maintenance dose is determined by {{c1::clearance}}: MD = {{c2::(Css × CL × τ) / F}}. If oral F = 0.5, the oral dose must be {{c3::doubled}} vs IV. As the dosing interval lengthens, the dose per interval must {{c4::increase}} to keep the same average Css
add.extra: Lecture form: MD rate = (Cp × CL) / f. Dividing a daily dose more often reduces peak-trough variability.

add.cloze: A 100 mg IV bolus gives C0 = 2 mg/L, so Vd = {{c1::50 L}}
add.extra: Vd = dose / C0.

add.cloze: Oral loading dose with Vd = 40 L, target 2 mg/L and F = 0.5: {{c1::160 mg}}
Maintenance dose per 12 h with Css = 2 mg/L, CL = 4 L/hr and F = 0.5: {{c1::192 mg}}
A constant IV infusion of 12 mg/hr with CL = 6 L/hr gives Css = {{c1::2 mg/L}}
add.extra: Css = infusion rate / CL.

add.cloze: With Vd = 42 L and CL = 6 L/hr, t½ ≈ {{c1::4.9 hours}}
add.extra: t½ = 0.7 × Vd / CL = 0.7 × 42 / 6. (Vd/CL alone = 7 h is the mean residence time, not the half-life.)

add.cloze: If clearance falls by 50% and the infusion rate is unchanged, the steady-state concentration {{c1::doubles}}
add.extra: Css = infusion rate / CL.

add.cloze: A drug with t½ = 7 h is ~97% eliminated about {{c1::35 hours}} after stopping

myLectures.name: Innate Immunity
myLectures.note: Mullins, Wed Nov 4. Cards picked to match the slides and figures, checked against your 35 Innate Immunity cards (see innate_immunity_card_check.csv). Adds 21 short one-word cloze notes (deck: Mullins - Innate Immunity). Already in other lectures: PAMP/PRR, dendritic cells and anergy (Intro to Immunology), LPS cytokines (Danger Signals), NADPH oxidase/MPO (TCA, Bioenergetics). Left out: complement regulators (DAF, C1-INH, PNH), complement in SLE/GN, LAD cord separation/inheritance, CGD and Chediak-Higashi, Th subsets.

add.cloze: Innate immunity buys {{c1::time}} until adaptive immunity responds
add.extra: It also limits spread and shapes adaptive immunity.

add.cloze: Too little innate activation permits microbial {{c1::spread}}; too much causes tissue {{c2::injury}}
Innate defense layers: barriers, resident {{c1::sentinels}}, recruited cells, soluble mediators, and {{c2::resolution}}
Epithelial barriers work by mechanical removal, chemical inhibition, and resident {{c1::microbiota}}
Burns, indwelling devices, and mucosal injury raise infection risk by breaking {{c1::barriers}}
PRRs recognize conserved microbial patterns and signals of cell {{c1::damage}}
{{c1::DAMPs}} are molecules released by injured cells that activate innate sensors
add.extra: Damage-associated molecular patterns

add.cloze: PRR {{c1::location}} gives context: a molecule normal in one compartment can signal infection in another
add.extra: Surface, endosome, or cytosol

add.cloze: PRR activation makes macrophages release inflammatory {{c1::cytokines}} and chemokines
add.extra: Also enhanced phagocytosis, endothelial activation, and leukocyte recruitment

add.cloze: Phagolysosomes kill microbes with acid, lysosomal enzymes, ROS, and {{c1::NO}}
add.extra: NO = nitric oxide

add.cloze: Neutrophils can trap microbes in extracellular traps called {{c1::NETs}}
add.extra: They also kill by phagocytosis, granule contents, and ROS

add.cloze: Neutrophil recruitment: rolling → activation → firm {{c1::adhesion}} → transmigration → {{c2::chemotaxis}}
{{c1::Chemokines}} switch leukocyte integrins to a high-affinity state
Defective β2 integrins (CD18) impair firm {{c1::adhesion}} of neutrophils
add.extra: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency; rolling (selectins) is spared

add.cloze: NK cells kill when {{c1::activating}} signals outweigh inhibitory signals
add.extra: HLA class I gives the main inhibitory signal

add.cloze: NK cells perform ADCC by binding antibody-coated targets with {{c1::CD16}}
{{c1::Chemokines}} are cytokines that direct cell migration along concentration gradients
Type I interferons create an {{c1::antiviral}} state in cells
TNF activates {{c1::endothelium}}, recruits leukocytes, and amplifies inflammation
Low CH50 with normal AH50 suggests a {{c1::classical}} pathway defect
add.extra: Normal CH50 + low AH50 → alternative pathway

add.cloze: Recurrent Neisseria with low CH50 and low AH50 suggests a {{c1::terminal}} complement defect
add.extra: C5–C9

add.cloze: Plant proteins are lower in {{c1::saturated}} fat than fatty animal proteins

q.v: A researcher is characterizing an unknown genetic pathogen isolated from a patient's tissue sample. Biochemical analysis of the pathogen's genetic material reveals that it is composed of a single-stranded polymer that utilizes a pentose sugar containing hydroxyl (-OH) groups at both the 2' and 3' carbon positions. When this polymer is hydrolyzed into its constituent nitrogenous bases, which of the following structural features will be uniquely present in one of the bases compared to those found in a double-stranded 2'-deoxyribose polymer?
o: A methyl group attached to the C5 position of a pyrimidine ring
A hydrogen atom rather than a methyl group at the C5 position of a pyrimidine ring
A ribose sugar lacking a 3' hydroxyl group
A purine ring directly linked to an amino acid acceptor stem
A double-stranded helical backbone stabilized by thymine pairing
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the genetic material as RNA based on single-stranded structure and ribose sugar with 2' and 3' OH groups) -> Step 2 (Deduce that RNA utilizes uracil instead of thymine, which structurally lacks the C5 methyl group present on thymine).

r.A: A methyl group (H3C) on the pyrimidine ring is characteristic of thymine, which is used in DNA rather than RNA.
r.C: Both ribose and deoxyribose contain a 3' hydroxyl group; they differ only at the 2' carbon position.
r.D: Nitrogenous bases are attached to the sugar-phosphate backbone, whereas amino acids attach to the 3' CCA end of the complete tRNA molecule.
r.E: RNA is single-stranded and utilizes uracil rather than thymine.

q.s: Slide 3: RNA vs DNA

q.v: An oncology research team is developing a novel therapeutic agent designed to silence a specific mutated oncogene in human tumor cells. The synthetic molecule acts by directing the degradation of selective mRNAs and inducing the establishment of compact chromatin structures to turn off gene expression. A closely related endogenous class of noncoding RNA molecules also regulates gene expression, but typically functions through which of the following primary mechanisms instead?
o: Processing and chemically modifying ribosomal RNAs in the nucleolus
Modifying small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs) and small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs)
Blocking the translation of selective mRNAs without directing chromatin compaction
Functioning as an adaptor between mRNA codons and amino acids
Mediating telomere synthesis and X-chromosome inactivation
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the therapeutic agent as mimicking small interfering RNAs [siRNAs] based on mRNA degradation and chromatin compaction) -> Step 2 (Identify the closely related regulatory RNA as microRNA [miRNA], which typically regulates gene expression by blocking translation of selective mRNAs).

r.A: Processing and chemically modifying rRNAs is the specific function of small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs).
r.B: Modifying snoRNAs and snRNAs is the function of small cajal RNAs (scaRNAs).
r.D: Serving as adaptors between mRNA and amino acids is the function of transfer RNAs (tRNAs).
r.E: Telomere synthesis, X-chromosome inactivation, and ER protein transport are functions of other diverse noncoding RNAs.

q.s: Slide 5: Table 6-1 Principal Types of RNAs Produced in Cells

q.v: A molecular biologist is analyzing a newly discovered bacterial gene in Escherichia coli to optimize recombinant protein production. Sequencing of the region immediately upstream of the transcription start site reveals a -35 sequence of 5'-TTGACA-3' and a -10 sequence of 5'-TATAAT-3', separated by a 17-base spacer region. If a mutation drastically increases the guanine-cytosine (G-C) content specifically within the -10 consensus sequence while keeping the 17-base spacer length intact, which of the following steps of transcription initiation will be most directly impaired?
o: Initial recognition of the -35 element by the core RNA polymerase subunits
The local unwinding and opening of approximately 10 base pairs of the DNA double helix
The synthesis of the required RNA primer prior to ribonucleotide addition
The release of the sigma factor after approximately 10 nucleotides have been added
The binding of the Rho protein to the nascent RNA transcript
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the -10 sequence [5'-TATAAT-3'] as the prokaryotic Pribnow box) -> Step 2 (Deduce that replacing its high A=T content with G-C base pairs directly impairs the ~10bp DNA opening required during step 2 of prokaryotic transcription initiation).

r.A: Promoter recognition is mediated specifically by the sigma factor within the holoenzyme, not by the 4-subunit core enzyme alone.
r.C: Unlike DNA replication, transcription initiation does not require a primer.
r.D: Sigma factor release occurs after ~10 nucleotides are synthesized to transition into efficient elongation, which happens downstream of DNA opening.
r.E: Rho factor binds to growing naked mRNA during transcription termination, not during promoter opening.

q.s: Slide 10 & Slide 13: Transcription - Initiation in Prokaryotes

q.v: During an in vitro experiment studying bacterial gene expression, a researcher introduces a mutation into a prokaryotic gene that prematurely stops translation by ribosomes, leaving a long stretch of newly synthesized mRNA completely devoid of ribosomes ('naked RNA') while RNA polymerase is still actively transcribing downstream. Which of the following events is most likely to be facilitated by this exposed stretch of nascent mRNA?
o: Decrease in the elongation rate of RNA polymerase from 40-50 nucleotides/sec to 20 nucleotides/sec
Spontaneous formation of a lariat intermediate via an internal adenine nucleotide
Binding of a hexameric termination factor that moves toward the paused RNA polymerase to cause dissociation
Recruitment of poly-A polymerase to cleave the transcript 20 nucleotides downstream
Immediate export of the naked mRNA across the nuclear envelope prior to translation
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that simultaneous transcription and translation normally occur in prokaryotes, and absence of ribosomes exposes naked RNA) -> Step 2 (Connect naked RNA to Rho-dependent termination, where factor rho binds sites on naked RNA without ribosomes and moves toward paused RNA pol to cause dissociation).

r.A: An elongation rate of 20 nucleotides per second is characteristic of eukaryotic RNA polymerase, whereas prokaryotes transcribe at 40-50/s.
r.B: Lariat formation occurs during eukaryotic pre-mRNA intron splicing, which is unique to eukaryotes.
r.D: Polyadenylation via cleavage ~20 nucleotides downstream of AATAAA is a eukaryotic mRNA modification.
r.E: Prokaryotes lack a nucleus and translate mRNA co-transcriptionally; nuclear export is required only for eukaryotic mRNAs.

q.s: Slide 16 & Slide 17: Transcription - Elongation and Termination

q.v: A genetics laboratory is investigating a line of cultured human cells that exhibit defective ribosome biogenesis. Ultracentrifugation of the cellular RNA reveals a complete absence of the 5S ribosomal RNA subunit and a severe deficiency in transfer RNAs (tRNAs), while the 18S, 5.8S, and 28S ribosomal RNA subunits are synthesized in normal quantities. The enzyme defective in this cell line is also responsible for transcribing which of the following?
o: All protein-coding messenger RNAs (mRNAs)
Small nucleolar RNA (snoRNA) genes
MicroRNA (miRNA) and small interfering RNA (siRNA) genes
The tandemly repeated genes located in the nucleolar organizing regions (NOR)
Some small nuclear RNA (snRNA) genes and genes for other small RNAs
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the defective enzyme as eukaryotic RNA polymerase III based on the loss of tRNA and 5S rRNA synthesis while Pol I products [18S, 5.8S, 28S] are spared) -> Step 2 (Determine that RNA polymerase III also transcribes some snRNA genes and genes for other small RNAs).

r.A: All protein-coding genes (mRNAs) are transcribed by eukaryotic RNA polymerase II.
r.B: Small nucleolar RNA (snoRNA) genes are transcribed by eukaryotic RNA polymerase II.
r.C: Both miRNA and siRNA genes are transcribed by eukaryotic RNA polymerase II.
r.D: Genes in the nucleolar organizing regions (encoding 18S, 5.8S, and 28S rRNAs) are transcribed by RNA polymerase I.

q.s: Slide 21: Table 6-2 The Three RNA Polymerases in Eucaryotic Cells

q.v: A researcher is studying the regulation of a human tissue-specific gene that requires a specific transcription factor to bind an enhancer located 5,000 base pairs upstream of the TATA box. Although the specific transcription factor binds the enhancer normally and DNA-bending proteins successfully loop the DNA, transcription fails to initiate because the enhancer-bound activator cannot physically communicate with the general transcription factors and RNA polymerase II at the promoter. Which of the following components of the eukaryotic transcription initiation complex is most likely mutated?
o: Sigma factor
Mediator complex
Internal transcribed spacer 1 (ITS1)
Poly-A-binding protein
Factor rho
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the process as eukaryotic transcription activation via distal enhancer looping to the promoter) -> Step 2 (Identify the Mediator complex as the bridging protein group that connects specific transcription factors/activators bound at enhancers to the general transcription factors and RNA Pol II at the promoter).

r.A: Sigma factor is a prokaryotic initiation factor; eukaryotes utilize general transcription factors (such as TFIIB and TFIID) instead.
r.C: Internal transcribed spacers (ITS1, ITS2) are non-coding regions removed during post-transcriptional processing of pre-rRNA.
r.D: Poly-A-binding proteins bind to the 3' poly(A) tail of mature eukaryotic mRNA after transcription termination and cleavage.
r.E: Factor rho is a prokaryotic transcription termination factor that dissociates RNA polymerase from DNA.

q.s: Slide 20, Slide 22 & Slide 23: Transcription in Eukaryotes

q.v: Cytogenetic analysis is performed on a patient's karyotype to evaluate a chromosomal abnormality involving the short arms of chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21, and 22. The geneticist notes that these specific acrocentric chromosomes contain specialized regions with hundreds of tandem gene copies that organize the nucleolus. When a single transcriptional unit from these regions is transcribed and subsequently undergoes post-transcriptional processing, which of the following occurs?
o: Introns are excised via a lariat intermediate to join three coding exons into a mature mRNA
External and internal transcribed spacers (ETS, ITS1, and ITS2) are removed to yield 18S, 5.8S, and 28S subunits
RNase P cleaves the 5' end and tRNA nucleotidyltransferase adds a 3' CCA sequence
A 7-methylguanosine cap is added via a 5'-to-5' triphosphate bridge
The transcript is cleaved 20 nucleotides downstream of an AATAAA consensus sequence
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the acrocentric chromosomal regions [13, 14, 15, 21, 22] as nucleolar organizing regions [NORs] containing rDNA units) -> Step 2 (Recall that each rDNA transcriptional unit is processed post-transcriptionally by removing external and internal spacers [ETS, ITS1, ITS2] to yield the 18S, 5.8S, and 28S rRNA subunits).

r.A: Intron removal via a lariat intermediate to join exons is the mechanism of pre-mRNA splicing mediated by snRNPs.
r.C: 5' cleavage by RNase P and 3' CCA addition by tRNA nucleotidyltransferase are specific modifications of tRNA processing.
r.D: Addition of a 7-methylguanosine cap via a 5'-to-5' triphosphate bridge is a 5' modification of eukaryotic pre-mRNA.
r.E: Cleavage downstream of AATAAA followed by polyadenylation is a 3' modification of eukaryotic pre-mRNA.

q.s: Slide 26, Slide 27 & Slide 28: rRNA Transcription & Processing

q.v: A molecular genetics lab is investigating an experimental cell line with a temperature-sensitive mutation in an enzyme required for tRNA maturation. When shifted to the non-permissive temperature, primary tRNA transcripts accumulate that have had their introns successfully removed, their 5' ends properly cleaved, and their 3' portions trimmed, but they cannot be charged with an amino acid because they lack the terminal 3' CCA sequence. Which of the following enzymes is operational immediately prior to the defective step to prepare the 3' end of the tRNA?
o: RNase P
An exonuclease
tRNA nucleotidyltransferase
Poly-A polymerase (PAP)
Guanylyltransferase
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the defective step as the addition of CCA to the 3' end by tRNA nucleotidyltransferase) -> Step 2 (Identify the enzyme that prepares the 3' portion of the tRNA transcript by trimming it as an exonuclease, whereas the 5' portion is removed by the endonuclease RNase P).

r.A: RNase P is an endonuclease that removes the 5' portion of the primary tRNA transcript, not the 3' portion.
r.C: tRNA nucleotidyltransferase is the defective enzyme itself that adds the CCA sequence to the 3' end, rather than the enzyme that trims the 3' end.
r.D: Poly-A polymerase (PAP) adds a template-independent poly(A) tail to the 3' end of mRNA, not tRNA.
r.E: Guanylyltransferase (adding a GMP molecule) is one of the three enzymatic steps involved in 5' mRNA capping.

q.s: Slide 30: Modification of tRNA

q.v: A 4-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician due to progressive, symmetric muscle weakness and hypotonia ('floppy baby syndrome'). Genetic testing confirms a diagnosis of spinal muscular atrophy caused by a deficiency in the survival motor neuron (SMN) protein, which impairs the assembly of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs) into the spliceosome. Which of the following biochemical reactions will be most directly impaired in the anterior horn cells of this patient's spinal cord?
o: Removal of a phosphate group from the 5' end of nascent pre-mRNA followed by methylation of GMP
Nucleophilic attack by the 2'-OH group of a specific branch-point adenine nucleotide on the 3' end of the upstream exon
Phosphorylation of the Tyr-Ser-Pro-Thr-Ser-Pro-Ser heptapeptide repeats on the RNA polymerase II tail
Recognition of the -35 and -10 consensus sequences upstream of the transcription start site
Cleavage of the internal transcribed spacers (ITS1 and ITS2) from the 45S pre-rRNA transcript
q.p: Step 1 (Connect spinal muscular atrophy and decreased SMN protein to defective snRNP/spliceosome assembly) -> Step 2 (Identify the biochemical mechanism mediated by snRNPs during pre-mRNA splicing: a specific adenine nucleotide's 2'-OH in the intron attacks the 3' end of the upstream exon to form a lariat).

r.A: Dephosphorylation, GMP addition, and methylation describe 5' mRNA capping, which does not require snRNPs.
r.C: Phosphorylation of the 52 heptapeptide repeats on the C-terminal domain (CTD) of RNA Pol II initiates transcription elongation and recruits processing factors.
r.D: The -35 and -10 consensus sequences are prokaryotic promoter elements recognized by the bacterial sigma factor.
r.E: Cleavage of internal transcribed spacers is part of nucleolar rRNA processing, which is mediated by snoRNAs rather than spliceosomal snRNPs.

q.s: Slide 32, Slide 33 & Slide 34: Modification of mRNA - mRNA splicing

q.v: A researcher is studying the co-transcriptional processing of a nascent eukaryotic pre-mRNA transcript. After RNA polymerase II has transcribed approximately 25 nucleotides, a specialized protein complex is recruited by the phosphorylated C-terminal domain (CTD) of the polymerase to modify the 5' end of the transcript. This modification stabilizes the transcript and marks it as 'complete' by creating which of the following chemical structures?
o: A 7-methylguanosine linked to the primary transcript via a 5'-to-5' triphosphate bridge
A covalently closed lariat loop linking a 5' guanosine to an internal branch-point adenine
A template-independent string of adenine nucleotides bound by stabilizing proteins
A G-C rich stem-loop hairpin structure followed by 6 to 7 single-stranded uracils
An invariant 3'-CCA trinucleotide sequence covalently linked to phenylalanine
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the process occurring after ~25 bases of RNA Pol II transcription recruited by the CTD as 5' mRNA capping) -> Step 2 (Identify the chemical structure formed by the three capping enzymes [removing a phosphate, adding GMP, methylating GMP] as a 7-methylguanosine attached via a 5'-to-5' triphosphate bridge).

r.B: A covalently closed lariat loop is the excised intron intermediate formed during pre-mRNA splicing.
r.C: A template-independent string of adenines bound by poly-A-binding proteins describes 3' polyadenylation.
r.D: A G-C rich hairpin loop followed by 6-7 uracils is the structure required for prokaryotic Rho-independent termination.
r.E: An invariant 3'-CCA sequence linked to an amino acid such as phenylalanine describes the acceptor stem of a mature, charged tRNA.

q.s: Slide 31 & Slide 38: Modification of mRNA - mRNA 5' capping & C-terminal domain (CTD)

q.v: A researcher is analyzing a human cell line with a targeted deletion in a class of regulatory RNAs that normally downregulate gene expression without directly cleaving the target transcript or inducing compact chromatin structures. Instead, these molecules act primarily by blocking the translation of selective mRNAs. Which of the following enzymes is directly responsible for transcribing the genes that encode this specific class of regulatory RNA?
o: RNA polymerase I
RNA polymerase II
RNA polymerase III
Poly-A polymerase
tRNA nucleotidyltransferase
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the regulatory RNA that blocks translation of selective mRNAs without directing degradation/chromatin compaction as microRNA [miRNA]) -> Step 2 (Determine that miRNA genes are transcribed by eukaryotic RNA polymerase II).

r.A: RNA polymerase I is exclusively responsible for transcribing the 5.8S, 18S, and 28S ribosomal RNA genes.
r.C: RNA polymerase III transcribes tRNA genes, 5S rRNA genes, and some snRNA genes, rather than miRNA genes.
r.D: Poly-A polymerase adds a template-independent poly(A) tail to the 3' end of mRNA and does not transcribe genes from DNA.
r.E: tRNA nucleotidyltransferase adds the CCA sequence to the 3' end of tRNAs during post-transcriptional processing.

q.s: Slides 5 & 21: Table 6-1 Principal Types of RNAs Produced in Cells & Table 6-2 The Three RNA Polymerases in Eucaryotic Cells

q.v: A molecular biology laboratory is investigating a rare congenital ribosomopathy caused by a defect in the chemical modification and processing of ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) within the nucleolus. Further analysis reveals that the small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs) required for this rRNA processing are themselves unmodified and non-functional. A deficiency in which of the following principal RNA types is the most likely upstream cause of this defect in snoRNA maturation?
o: Small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs)
Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs)
Small cajal RNAs (scaRNAs)
Transfer RNAs (tRNAs)
Messenger RNAs (mRNAs)
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that rRNAs are chemically modified by snoRNAs, which are defective in this scenario) -> Step 2 (Identify that small cajal RNAs [scaRNAs] are specifically used to modify snoRNAs and snRNAs).

r.A: Small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs) function in nuclear processes such as pre-mRNA splicing and are themselves targets of modification by scaRNAs.
r.B: Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) turn off gene expression by directing mRNA degradation and establishing compact chromatin structures.
r.D: Transfer RNAs (tRNAs) serve as adaptors between mRNA and amino acids during protein synthesis rather than modifying snoRNAs.
r.E: Messenger RNAs (mRNAs) code for proteins and do not directly catalyze the chemical modification of snoRNAs.

q.s: Slide 5: Table 6-1 Principal Types of RNAs Produced in Cells

q.v: A genetics lab is sequencing a region of human genomic DNA to identify the cause of a hereditary enzyme deficiency. They isolate the double-stranded DNA segment corresponding to the coding region of the affected gene and determine that the template (antisense) strand has the sequence: 5'-ATGAGCGTCGATAATAAAGACGACGATCA-3'. Which of the following sequences correctly represents the primary RNA transcript synthesized from this segment in the 5' to 3' direction?
o: 5'-ATGAGCGTCGATAATAAAGACGACGATCA-3'
5'-AUGAGCGUCGAUAAUAAAGACGACGAUCA-3'
5'-TGATCGTCGTCTTTATTATCGACGCTCAT-3'
5'-UGAUCGUCGUCUUUAUUAUCGACGCUCAU-3'
5'-UACUCGCAGCUAUUAUUUCUGCUGCUAGU-3'
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that the given 5' to 3' strand is the template/antisense strand, which must be read 3' to 5' to synthesize antiparallel RNA) -> Step 2 (Determine the complementary RNA sequence using A-U and G-C base pairing and orient it from 5' to 3': 5'-UGAUCGUCGUCUUUAUUAUCGACGCUCAU-3').

r.A: This sequence is identical to the DNA template strand and contains thymine instead of uracil.
r.B: This sequence would be produced only if the given DNA strand were the sense (coding) strand rather than the antisense template strand.
r.C: This sequence is antiparallel and complementary to the template strand, but it contains thymine (DNA) rather than uracil (RNA).
r.E: This sequence is written in the 3' to 5' orientation (reading left to right as complementary to the 5' to 3' template) rather than the standard 5' to 3' direction.

q.s: Slide 7: Transcription - Overview

q.v: During an in vitro transcription assay using purified Escherichia coli components, a researcher observes that the RNA polymerase holoenzyme successfully binds to the promoter, opens the 10-base-pair Pribnow box, and synthesizes short RNA fragments of 8 to 10 nucleotides. However, the enzyme fails to transition into the highly processive elongation phase. This arrest is most likely caused by a mutation that prevents which of the following molecular events?
o: Synthesis of a short RNA primer by primase
Phosphorylation of the 52-repeat C-terminal domain (CTD)
Release of the sigma factor from the core enzyme
Binding of the Rho (ρ) factor to the nascent RNA transcript
Recruitment of general transcription factors TFIIB and TFIID
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that in prokaryotes, initiation involves the holoenzyme adding ~10 nucleotides without needing a primer) -> Step 2 (Identify that after ~10 nucleotides are added, the polymerase must release the sigma factor to become more efficient and enter the elongation phase).

r.A: Transcription initiation does not require a primer, unlike DNA replication.
r.B: Phosphorylation of the C-terminal domain (CTD) initiates elongation in eukaryotic RNA polymerase II, not in E. coli.
r.D: Binding of the Rho factor to growing mRNA is involved in prokaryotic transcription termination, not the transition to elongation.
r.E: TFIIB and TFIID are eukaryotic general transcription factors and do not function in prokaryotic transcription initiation.

q.s: Slide 14: Transcription - Initiation in Prokaryotes

q.v: A researcher is comparing the kinetics of gene expression between a pathogenic bacterium and human host cells in culture. A specific coding region under investigation is exactly 2,000 nucleotides in length. Based on the standard rates of transcription elongation, which of the following correctly compares the approximate time required to transcribe this region and the cellular compartment where translation of the resulting transcript begins?
o: 40–50 seconds in bacteria with co-transcriptional translation; 100 seconds in human cells with cytoplasmic translation after nuclear export
100 seconds in bacteria with co-transcriptional translation; 40–50 seconds in human cells with cytoplasmic translation after nuclear export
40–50 seconds in bacteria with translation after nuclear export; 100 seconds in human cells with co-transcriptional translation in the nucleus
20 seconds in bacteria with co-transcriptional translation; 40–50 seconds in human cells with cytoplasmic translation after nuclear export
100 seconds in bacteria with cytoplasmic translation; 20 seconds in human cells with co-transcriptional translation in the nucleus
q.p: Step 1 (Calculate transcription time using elongation rates of 40–50 nucleotides/sec in prokaryotes [2000/50 = 40s to 2000/40 = 50s] and 20 nucleotides/sec in eukaryotes [2000/20 = 100s]) -> Step 2 (Pair with the localization principle that prokaryotic mRNA is translated simultaneously/co-transcriptionally, whereas eukaryotic mRNA must be stabilized and exported from the nucleus before translation).

r.B: This option reverses the elongation rates; prokaryotes transcribe faster (40–50 nt/s) than eukaryotes (20 nt/s).
r.C: Prokaryotes lack a nucleus and translate co-transcriptionally, whereas eukaryotes must export mRNA from the nucleus for translation.
r.D: This option uses the raw rate numbers as time durations rather than dividing the 2,000-nucleotide length by the respective rates.
r.E: This option both miscalculates the transcription duration and reverses the cellular locations of translation between prokaryotes and eukaryotes.

q.s: Slides 16 & 29: Transcription - Elongation & RNA Processing

q.v: A molecular biologist is studying a human gene that is normally expressed at low basal levels. To upregulate its expression in response to a hormone, a specific transcription factor binds to a distal control element located several thousand base pairs upstream of the promoter. Before RNA polymerase II can begin transcribing this gene, which of the following must occur at the promoter sequence?
o: A sigma factor must bind directly to the -10 and -35 consensus sequences
General transcription factors must bind to the promoter prior to RNA polymerase II recruitment
Internal and external transcribed spacers (ITS and ETS) must be cleaved from the DNA
Poly-A-binding proteins must attach to the TATA box to unwind the double helix
Small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs) must assemble on the enhancer to form a lariat
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the process as eukaryotic transcription regulation involving specific transcription factors at distal enhancers and a promoter) -> Step 2 (Determine that in eukaryotes, general transcription factors such as TFIIB and TFIID must bind to the generic promoter sequence prior to the recruitment of RNA polymerase).

r.A: Sigma factors and -10/-35 consensus sequences are features of prokaryotic transcription initiation, not eukaryotic RNA polymerase II.
r.C: Internal and external spacers are removed from pre-rRNA transcripts during post-transcriptional processing, not cleaved from DNA before transcription.
r.D: Poly-A-binding proteins bind to the 3' poly(A) tail of processed mRNA, not to the DNA TATA box.
r.E: snRNPs assemble on pre-mRNA introns to mediate splicing via a lariat intermediate, not on DNA enhancers.

q.s: Slides 20, 22 & 23: Transcription in Eukaryotes

q.v: In an experiment investigating ribosome biogenesis in human cells, a researcher uses radiolabeled uridine to track the synthesis and maturation of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) in the nucleolus. She isolates a single nascent primary rRNA transcript synthesized from one transcriptional unit within a nucleolar organizing region (NOR) before any cleavage occurs. Which of the following sets of components will be present within this single unprocessed precursor molecule?
o: 18S, 5.8S, 28S, and 5S rRNA subunits
18S, 5.8S, and 28S rRNA subunits along with external and internal spacers (ETS, ITS1, ITS2)
Only the 18S and 28S rRNA subunits linked by a 5'-to-5' triphosphate bridge
5S rRNA and tRNA linked by intergenic spacers (IGS)
28S, 5.8S, and 18S rRNA subunits with a 3' CCA sequence attached
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that each rDNA transcriptional unit in the NOR is transcribed by RNA polymerase I as a single precursor) -> Step 2 (Recognize that this primary transcript encodes three of the four rRNA subunits [18S, 5.8S, and 28S] separated by external and internal spacers [ETS, ITS1, ITS2] that are later removed by post-transcriptional processing).

r.A: The 5S rRNA subunit is not encoded within the NOR transcriptional unit; it is transcribed separately by RNA polymerase III.
r.C: The transcriptional unit also includes the 5.8S rRNA subunit and spacers, and a 5'-to-5' triphosphate bridge is a feature of mRNA 5' capping.
r.D: 5S rRNA and tRNAs are transcribed by RNA polymerase III, and intergenic spacers (IGS) lie between tandem rDNA units rather than within the processed primary transcript.
r.E: The 3' CCA sequence is added post-transcriptionally to tRNAs, not to rRNA precursors.

q.s: Slides 26 & 28: Transcription in Eukaryotes & rRNA Transcription & Processing

q.v: A researcher is studying the maturation of transfer RNA (tRNA) in eukaryotic cells. A primary tRNA transcript is synthesized by RNA polymerase III and subsequently undergoes multiple enzymatic modifications, including intron removal and trimming of both the 5' and 3' ends. Before the correct amino acid can be attached to this tRNA, which of the following enzymatic reactions must occur?
o: Cleavage of the 5' leader sequence by an exonuclease
Removal of the 3' trailer sequence by the endonuclease RNAse P
Addition of a 7-methylguanosine cap via a 5'-to-5' triphosphate bridge
Addition of a CCA sequence to the 3' end by tRNA nucleotidyltransferase
Addition of a template-independent poly(A) tail by poly-A polymerase
q.p: Step 1 (Trace tRNA processing: intron removal, 5' end removal by endonuclease RNAse P, and 3' trimming by an exonuclease) -> Step 2 (Identify that tRNA nucleotidyltransferase must add the CCA sequence to the 3' end so the correct amino acid can be added to the CCA site).

r.A: The 5' portion of the primary tRNA transcript is removed by RNAse P, which is an endonuclease, not an exonuclease.
r.B: The 3' portion of the tRNA is trimmed by an exonuclease, whereas RNAse P is the endonuclease that cleaves the 5' portion.
r.C: Addition of a 7-methylguanosine cap via a 5'-to-5' triphosphate bridge is a modification specific to the 5' end of mRNA.
r.E: Addition of a poly(A) tail by poly-A polymerase occurs at the 3' end of mRNA, not tRNA.

q.s: Slide 30: Modification of tRNA

q.v: A molecular hematology lab is characterizing the β-globin mRNA transcripts from a 6-month-old infant who presented with severe anemia and was diagnosed with β-thalassemia. Sequencing of the patient's β-globin gene reveals a single-nucleotide mutation within the intron between exon 1 and exon 2 that replaces the branch-point nucleotide required for the initial nucleophilic attack during splicing. Which of the following chemical reactions is directly prevented by this specific mutation?
o: Attack of the 2'-OH group of a specific intronic adenine on the 3' end of exon 1
Attack of the 3'-OH group of exon 1 on the 5' end of exon 2
Cleavage of the pre-mRNA 20 nucleotides downstream of the AATAAA sequence
Removal of a phosphate group from the 5' end of the primary transcript prior to GMP addition
Dephosphorylation of the Tyr-Ser-Pro-Thr-Ser-Pro-Ser repeats on RNA polymerase II
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the mutated structure as the specific adenine [A] nucleotide at the branch point inside the intron involved in pre-mRNA splicing) -> Step 2 (Determine that the first step of splicing requires the 2'-OH of this specific intronic adenine to attack the 3' end of the upstream exon [exon 1] to form the covalently linked lariat intermediate).

r.B: The reaction of the 3'-OH group of exon 1 with the 5' end of exon 2 is the second step of splicing, which occurs only after the intronic adenine has attacked the 5' splice site.
r.C: Cleavage downstream of the AATAAA consensus sequence is part of 3' polyadenylation, not intron splicing.
r.D: Removal of a 5' phosphate group prior to GMP addition and methylation is the mechanism of 5' mRNA capping.
r.E: The heptapeptide repeats belong to the C-terminal domain (CTD) of RNA polymerase II, which is phosphorylated to initiate elongation and recruit processing factors.

q.s: Slides 32, 33 & 35: Modification of mRNA - mRNA splicing & β-thalassemias

q.v: A biochemist is studying the mechanism of eukaryotic mRNA 5' capping using radiolabeled nucleotide precursors. She observes that after RNA polymerase II transcribes approximately 25 bases, capping factors are recruited to the C-terminal domain (CTD) of the polymerase to form a 7-methylguanosine cap connected via a 5'-to-5' triphosphate bridge. Which of the following sequences of three enzymatic actions is required to synthesize this structure at the 5' end of the nascent transcript?
o: Addition of GMP -> removal of a phosphate group -> methylation of the ribose sugar
Removal of a phosphate group -> addition of a GMP molecule -> methylation of the GMP
Methylation of the 5' terminal base -> addition of GTP -> cleavage of two phosphate groups
Cleavage of the transcript 20 bases downstream -> addition of GMP -> binding of poly-A-binding proteins
Phosphorylation of the 5' end -> attachment of 7-methylguanosine -> formation of a lariat structure
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the process of eukaryotic mRNA 5' capping occurring after ~25 bases are transcribed) -> Step 2 (Recall the exact 3-enzyme modification sequence: 1. removing a phosphate group from the 5' end, 2. adding a GMP molecule, and 3. methylating the GMP).

r.A: A phosphate group must be removed from the 5' end of the transcript before the GMP molecule is added, and the methylation occurs on the guanine base (N7) of GMP.
r.C: Methylation is the third and final enzymatic step performed after GMP is added, not the first step.
r.D: Cleavage 20 bases downstream of a consensus sequence and binding of poly-A-binding proteins are steps in 3' polyadenylation, not 5' capping.
r.E: The 5' end of the primary transcript already has तीन phosphates (one of which is removed), and lariat formation occurs during intron splicing.

q.s: Slides 31 & 38: Modification of mRNA - mRNA 5' capping & C-terminal domain (CTD)

myLectures.note: Tim Howard, Regulation of Gene Expression and Translation, 2026-11-06 (course packet lists Peter Fuerst). 53 B&B notes and 19 one-word clozes. Your 30 cards: 15 fully covered, 13 partly, 2 not covered by B&B. No previous lecture JSONs were provided, so cross-lecture duplicates were not checked. Antibiotic notes are mechanism-only from the slide 43 inhibitor table. Left out: macrolide 'blocks translocation' and aminoglycoside 'blocks initiation complex formation' notes (the slide table describes these differently), and side effects, the tRNA D/T-arm, eEF-2/toxins, RNA polymerase types, silencers and mutation-severity notes (not taught). Not in B&B: DNA-binding motifs (helix-turn-helix, zinc finger, leucine zipper, HLH), major-groove recognition, mRNA export proteins (hnRNPs, export receptor, CBC to eIF4E/4G), 5'→3' / N→C direction, ATP-driven scanning, nucleolar assembly, polyribosomes, and cycloheximide/puromycin/anisomycin.
